summary: The Junior Elettrica is Alfa Romeo's first battery-electric car and the only pure-EV grade in the Junior range here, a single front-drive spec using the same 115kW motor and 51kWh usable Stellantis pack as its platform twin the Jeep Avenger, but with an Italian chassis tune and a $58,990 list price. Australian reviewers are near-unanimous that the Junior steers and rides better than almost anything else this size — the same testers call the pricing hard to defend against a Volvo EX30 or Kia EV3, and the Elettrica asks about $13,000 more than the Ibrida hybrid that makes up most of the model's sales. Opinion splits on whether the badge, the driving character and $232-a-year servicing offset a 400-litre boot, a cramped rear seat, no crash-test rating at all and a national network of only eight dealers.
pros: Cheapest electric car in Australia to service by a wide margin: Alfa's own schedule averages $232.32 a year over five years at 12-month/15,000km intervals, against $621.17 a year for the Ibrida hybrid version of the same car.

Reviewers rate the chassis the best part of the car — CarsGuide scored the Junior 9/10 for driving and called the steering 'communicative and direct', where the mechanically related Jeep Avenger is criticised for over-light steering.

Charging is competitive for a 51kWh car: 100kW DC takes 20-80 per cent in 27 minutes and an 11kW three-phase AC charger fills it in 5 hours 45 minutes, so a home three-phase supply is genuinely usable.

At $58,990 list and $65,649 drive-away in Melbourne it sits comfortably under the $75,000 FBT threshold, so a novated lease keeps the full exemption — and Alfa's own calculator itemises the $2,995 dealer delivery rather than burying it.
Five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, unlike the platform-mate Jeep Avenger whose five years is capped at 100,000km.
cons: No crash-test rating exists at all — neither ANCAP nor Euro NCAP has assessed the Junior, so a buyer is choosing on six airbags and a feature list against five-star-rated rivals like the Volvo EX30 and Kia EV3.
Not rated to tow anything: 0kg braked and unbraked, where the Junior Ibrida hybrid is rated at 1,100kg braked and a Chery E5 at 750kg.

The battery costs you boot and rear space: 400 litres behind the second row versus 415 in the Ibrida, reviewers describe the rear seat as 'even tighter' with minimal headroom and awkward door openings, and there is no spare wheel, only a repair kit.

Ownership risk is real — Alfa Romeo Australia runs just eight dealers nationally and has said it has no plans to expand, on brand volume of a few hundred cars a year, and the same 51kWh Stellantis drivetrain in the Jeep Avenger has been discounted to $40,000 drive-away from $49,990 list.

The 207kW Elettrica Veloce sold in Europe has been explicitly ruled out for Australia, so the only battery-electric Junior on offer is the 115kW/260Nm car that takes 9.0 seconds to 100km/h and tops out at 150km/h.

summary: The Q4 e-tron is Audi's MEB-platform medium electric SUV, sold in Australia as a conventional SUV and a lower-roofed Sportback, each in rear-drive 45 and quattro 55 form. Australian reviewers rate the cabin quality, driving position and packaging highly and note it carries more usable space than its compact footprint suggests, but they are lukewarm about its handling and point out it costs meaningfully more than the mechanically related Volkswagen Group EVs. The critical decision inside the range is the price step: the 45 grades sit under the $91,661 luxury-car-tax and FBT threshold while both 55 quattro grades clear it, which changes the ownership maths far more than the extra performance does.
pros: Both 45 grades list under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT/FBT threshold, so they attract no luxury car tax and stay eligible for the novated-lease FBT exemption
Biggest boot in its premium class: 520L in the SUV and 535L in the Sportback, versus 490L in a BMW iX1 and just 340L in a Mercedes EQA
175kW DC charging across the whole range since the 82kWh battery update, Audi quotes 10-80 per cent in about 28 minutes
Sportback 45 is the efficiency pick at 540km WLTP, and CarsGuide measures the Sportback body using roughly 0.5kWh/100km less than the SUV
Genuinely roomy for the footprint, with reviewers singling out front and rear legroom, the driving position and cabin storage
cons: Both 55 quattro grades list at $97,936, above the $91,661 threshold, so they cop luxury car tax (about $2,932) and lose the FBT exemption entirely
No spare wheel of any kind, just a tyre inflation kit, on every variant
CarsGuide criticises rear visibility in the Sportback 55 and says the heavier 55 is less agile than the lighter rear-drive 45
Braked towing is capped at 1000kg for the 45 and 1200kg for the 55 quattro, well short of a Tesla Model Y (1588kg) or Polestar 4 (up to 2000kg)
CarExpert notes it is pricier than the mechanically related Volkswagen Group EVs, with only so-so charging speed and unremarkable handling, and a facelifted Q4 has already been revealed overseas

summary: Audi's new-generation Q5 e-hybrid quattro is the plug-in the brand badged TFSI e last time round, and its headline is price parity: at $96,900 for the SUV and $100,400 for the Sportback it costs exactly the same as the 200kW TFSI quattro sport petrol while making 270kW/500Nm and adding 82km of WLTP electric range from a 20.7kWh usable battery. That undercuts the Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e and the BMW X3 30e while carrying more claimed electric range than the BMW, and reviewers rate the PPC-platform Q5's new-found ride comfort and cabin technology highly. The reservations are consistent and not about the powertrain: capacitive touch panels have replaced most physical controls, the steering is over-assisted, the battery costs 82 litres of boot, and with the PHEV FBT exemption gone since April 2025 the case rests entirely on charging at home.
pros: 270kW/500Nm and 5.1sec to 100km/h for exactly the same $96,900 (SUV) / $100,400 (Sportback) as the 200kW TFSI quattro sport petrol — 70kW more for no extra money, and it undercuts the Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e ($99,900) and BMW X3 30e ($104,800)
82km WLTP electric range from a 20.7kWh usable (25.9kWh gross) battery, about 45 per cent more capacity than the old Q5 55 TFSI e, so a typical 30-45km Melbourne commute runs on electricity alone
11kW three-phase AC charging fills the pack 0-100 per cent in about 2.5 hours, up from 7.2kW on the superseded Q5 TFSI e, which makes daytime top-ups practical rather than overnight-only

75g/km combined CO2 is well under Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car threshold, so it pays $8.40 per $200 duty instead of the $10.40 (SUV) or $14.00 (Sportback) per $200 an equivalently priced petrol Q5 attracts — worth roughly $970 on the SUV and $2,800 on the Sportback

2000kg braked towing plus standard 20-inch Audi Sport wheels, sport suspension, red calipers, black styling pack, privacy glass and auxiliary air-conditioning that the same-priced petrol does not get; five-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with the high-voltage battery covered eight years/160,000km
cons: The battery under the boot floor costs 82 litres: 438L seats-up in the SUV and 433L in the Sportback, against 520L in the petrol and diesel Q5, and 1358L/1300L folded versus 1473L — the Mercedes GLC 350e carries 590L and the BMW X3 30e 460L

The 3.3L/100km ADR label figure only holds if you start every trip charged: Audi's own WLTP figure with the battery discharged is 7.4-8.4L/100km for the 270kW car and an independent charge-sustaining test returned 7.8L/100km, so an apartment-dwelling buyer is running a 2170kg petrol SUV on 95 RON

AC-only charging capped at 11kW with no DC fast-charge hardware at all, where the Mercedes GLC 350e accepts up to 60kW DC — a flat battery on a road trip stays flat until you find a destination charger

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and both variants sit above the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and far above the $75,000 FBT phase cap, so the novated-lease concessions that once justified the plug-in premium no longer apply

Reviewers are consistent that the new Q5 trades away driver engagement and usability: steering with too much electronic assist, climate and most secondary functions moved to capacitive touch panels, a tight rear seat with a high floor hump, and a tyre repair kit rather than a spare

summary: The Q6 e-tron is Audi's first car on the 800-volt PPE platform it shares with the Porsche Macan Electric, sold here as a boxy SUV and a lower-roofed Sportback that Audi and the Australian outlets both file as an SUV. Reviewers rate the cabin, the screens and the charging hardware as a clear step above the cheaper MEB-based Q4, but consistently mark the ride down as firm and busy on the entry grades that cannot be optioned with air suspension. The commercial catch is that Audi Australia's own certified range figures land well below the European numbers quoted at launch, and every grade lists above the $91,661 fuel-efficient threshold, so nothing in the range attracts the novated-lease FBT exemption.
pros: 800V architecture charges at 225kW on the entry grade and 270kW on quattro and SQ6 grades, 10-80 per cent in a claimed 21 minutes, against 175kW in the Audi Q4 e-tron
Braked towing of 2000kg on RWD grades and 2400kg on quattro and SQ6 grades, double the Q4 e-tron's 1000-1200kg and well clear of a Tesla Model Y's 1588kg
526L boot and 1529L with the 40:20:40 bench down in the SUV, plus a 64L frunk that swallows the charging cables
The Sportback body is the efficiency pick and costs nothing extra in entry form: 173Wh/km and 493km certified against 182Wh/km and 466km for the SUV, at the same $99,900 list price
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, six years of roadside assistance and a capped six-year service plan at $2,080
cons: The cheapest grade lists at $99,900, so every variant clears the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT/FBT threshold - unlike the Q4 e-tron 45, no Q6 is eligible for the novated-lease FBT exemption and all attract luxury car tax

Australia's certified WLTP figures are far below the European numbers used at launch: the performance grade is homologated here at 558km, not the 641km quoted in Audi's own launch material, and the quattro at 542km rather than 625km
Chasing Cars calls the entry RWD grade's ride 'very firm, tightly controlled' and notes the $4,900 adaptive air suspension that fixes it cannot be ordered on that grade at all
Audi added the $99,900 entry grade in March 2025, undercutting the launch Q6 e-tron performance by $15,600 for near-identical equipment, which has hurt residuals on the earlier car
Choosing the Sportback body costs 15L of boot with the seats up and 156L with them down, and $5,000 extra on the quattro and SQ6 grades

summary: Reviewer consensus across CarExpert, CarsGuide and EV Central is that the BMW i4 eDrive35 remains genuinely engaging and comfortable to drive, even as BMW pared the local range back to this single grade for 2026, dropping the eDrive40 and M50 and readying the model for replacement by the Neue Klasse i3. CarsGuide scored the driving experience 10/10, but reviewers consistently flag pricing that undercuts few direct rivals, real-world range well short of the claimed figure, and cabin materials that feel a step below what BMW buyers expect. CarExpert's overall verdict of "Good" reflects a competent EV being overtaken by newer rivals on range and technology.
pros: Engaging, car-like driving dynamics with precise steering and confident handling praised across reviews
Comfortable, well-damped ride and a notably quiet, refined cabin at speed
Strong multimedia system with 12.3-inch digital cluster and 14.9-inch curved touchscreen
Fast DC charging (180kW, 32 minutes 10-80%) and now standard M Sport styling
cons: Real-world range (reviewers observed roughly 370km) falls well short of the claimed 448km
Expensive for what it offers, undercutting few direct rivals despite being the sole remaining variant
Interior materials feel plasticky and lack the polish reviewers expect of a BMW
Shorter warranty than some rivals, and the model is being phased out ahead of the incoming i3

summary: Australian reviewers rate the electric 5 Series as the most convincing large executive EV to drive, with CarExpert marking both the eDrive40 and the M60 xDrive "Very Good" for a chassis that stays composed and quiet where rivals feel inert. The disagreement is entirely about money and range: at $155,900 to $215,900 before on-roads the i5 asks Mercedes EQE and Porsche Taycan money, and reviewers consistently record real-world consumption well above the claim, so the 550km and 506km certified figures are not what buyers see. The M60's $60,000 premium buys an M5-rivalling 3.8-second car, but it also cuts range and is the harder case to argue on value.
pros: Rear-drive eDrive40 is certified at 550km from an 81.2kWh usable pack, and the 442kW M60 still manages 506km rather than the sub-450km a performance EV usually concedes
205kW DC charging gives a 10-80 per cent top-up in about 30 minutes, and BMW includes a five-year Chargefox subscription
CarExpert rates the ride/handling balance above the EQE's, calling perceived build quality "head and shoulders above" Mercedes-Benz
M60 xDrive delivers 442kW/820Nm and 0-100km/h in 3.8 seconds, effectively an electric M5 for $4000 less than the M60 Touring
Standard 17-speaker Bowers & Wilkins audio, panoramic glass roof and Merino leather on both grades, not option-boxed
cons: Real-world efficiency badly undershoots the claim — CarExpert logged 18.6kWh/100km in the eDrive40 against a 16.6kWh/100km claim, and 21.3kWh/100km in the M60 against 18.0
CarExpert's own reviewer notes the petrol 520i carries comparable standard equipment for far less, making the $155,900 entry hard to justify
Option packages inflate the price fast: the Comfort Package alone adds $5700 to a car already over $150,000
M60 xDrive rides low enough to scrape its undercarriage on ordinary driveways, and rear legroom is tight for taller adults despite the size
Large luxury EVs hold value poorly in Australia, and roughly $19,000 (eDrive40) to $37,000 (M60) of the list price is Luxury Car Tax that is not recovered at resale

summary: The facelifted iX is BMW's flagship electric SUV and, since the mid-2025 update, Australia gets exactly one grade: the xDrive45 M Sport at $142,900 before on-road costs. Reviewers are near-unanimous that the bigger 94.8kWh usable pack fixes the old xDrive40's biggest weakness, and that the ride, refinement and cabin quality are a class above the mainstream large EVs, but they split on whether the styling and the screen-led interior justify the money against an Audi Q6 e-tron, Polestar 3 or Cadillac Lyriq. The bigger caveat for buyers is money rather than metal: heavy new-car discounting and soft premium-EV residuals mean this is a car to negotiate hard on and hold for a long time.
pros: The 94.8kWh usable pack lifts the claimed range to 602km WLTP best case (522km on the Australian car's standard 22-inch wheels), against just 425km for the xDrive40 it replaced
2500kg braked towing is unusually strong for a large EV SUV and more than double the BMW iX1's 1200kg, with a 500L boot growing to 1750L
22kW three-phase AC charging is rare at any price and lets the big pack refill overnight on a home three-phase supply; DC peaks at 175kW for 10-80% in about 34 minutes
300kW/700Nm dual-motor all-wheel drive for a 5.1-second 0-100km/h, with the air-sprung ride and hush that Australian reviewers consistently rate above the Tesla Model X and Polestar 3
Dealers advertise drive-away deals well under the $149,800 a $142,900 list price implies in Victoria, so the sticker is genuinely negotiable
cons: Australia gets the xDrive45 M Sport only - the longer-range xDrive60 and the M70 performance flagship are sold in Europe and the US but not offered here, so there is no way to buy more range or more speed
The 602km headline is the best-case end of BMW's own 490-602km WLTP band; the Australian-spec car is certified at 522km, and carsales measured about 450km at constant highway speed
Depreciation on large premium EVs is punishing - independent US data puts the iX at 62-69% lost over five years, and one-year-old EVs in Australia are averaging 25% falls
Almost everything routes through the touchscreen, and reviewers single out the awkward door handles, the missing blind on the panoramic roof and the polarising front end
At $142,900 it clears the Luxury Car Tax and sits far above both the $75,000 and $91,661 FBT exemption thresholds, so a novated lease gets no FBT relief

summary: Australian reviewers rate the iX1 as one of the best small electric SUVs on sale, praising BMW's typically composed ride and precise steering alongside a genuinely upscale, well-finished cabin with quality materials and slick infotainment. It carries a clear price premium over mainstream EV rivals, and its roughly 400-450km real-world range trails segment leaders like the Tesla Model Y, but reviewers feel the driving experience and interior finish justify the extra spend for buyers prioritising refinement and brand prestige over outright value. CarExpert has named it its Best EV Small SUV in consecutive years, reflecting a broad consensus that BMW has successfully electrified its smallest SUV.
pros: Composed, well-damped ride and precise steering that reviewers say outclasses cheaper EV rivals
Upscale, well-finished interior with quality materials and an intuitive, slick infotainment system
Surprisingly spacious cabin for a compact SUV, with rear seat space rivalling the front
Back-to-back CarExpert Choice Award winner for Best EV Small SUV
cons: Premium pricing sits well above mainstream small EV SUVs and undercuts few direct rivals
Real-world range (reviewers report high-17s to high-18s kWh/100km) trails key rivals such as the Tesla Model Y
490L boot is smaller than the petrol X1's due to the rear-mounted motor and battery pack
Expensive scheduled servicing over a typical ownership period

summary: The iX2 is the coupe-roofed version of BMW's iX1 electric small SUV, sharing its 230kW dual-motor drivetrain and 64.8kWh usable pack but trading a little rear headroom for a sleeker tail and a slightly bigger 525-litre boot. Australian reviewers consistently rate the powertrain, cabin quality and body control highly while calling out the 395km ADR range as short for the money, and a ride that is firmer than the iX1's on the standard 19-inch M wheels. A $7,700 price cut in March 2026 dropped it to $79,900 and simultaneously deleted the front-drive eDrive20, so the range is now a single dual-motor grade.
pros: 230kW/494Nm dual-motor all-wheel drive gets it to 100km/h in 5.6 seconds, quicker than a Volvo EX40 Twin Motor and most of the segment
525-litre boot is roughly 35L larger than the iX1's despite the coupe roofline, expanding to 1400L
$7,700 cut in March 2026 brought it to $79,900 before on-roads, only $2,000 above the iX1 xDrive30 and now below the LCT threshold for fuel-efficient vehicles
Adaptive M suspension and a boost paddle give it genuinely engaging body control that reviewers rank above the Mercedes-Benz EQA
1200kg braked towing capacity with the optional bar, which several small electric SUVs cannot match
cons: 395km ADR range is short for an $80k EV — CarExpert measured 19.1kWh/100km against the 18.5kWh/100km claim, implying closer to 350km in mixed driving
Firmer, busier ride than the iX1, and reviewers report the 20-inch wheel option makes it noticeably worse over sharp bumps
Sloping roofline costs rear headroom, and the raised battery floor leaves taller adults sitting knees-up
Now a one-grade range — the cheaper front-drive eDrive20 was discontinued in Australia in 2026, so there is no lower entry point
Buyers of the pre-cut $87,600 car lost close to 9 per cent of list overnight, which weighs on used values

summary: The second-generation iX3 is the first Neue Klasse BMW, built on a dedicated 800V platform with a Gen6 cylindrical-cell battery, and Australian reviewers have been close to unanimous that it is the new benchmark premium electric SUV — steering, braking feel and regeneration are singled out as the best of any EV they have driven. Its range claim is the longest of any new vehicle on sale in Australia — 793km WLTP as the local car is actually specified, against the 805km headline BMW quotes for a European base car without the M Sport pack Australia fits as standard — and at $109,900 before on-roads it undercuts the Porsche Macan, Audi Q6 e-tron and Polestar 3 rather than matching them. The disagreement is over the tech-first cabin: the 43-inch Panoramic Vision strip impresses everyone, but reviewers split on whether burying climate and steering-wheel adjustment in a screen-heavy iDrive is livable, and several flagged rear-seat harshness on passive dampers as an open question for Australian roads.
pros: 793km WLTP on the standard-fit 20-inch wheels is the longest range of any new vehicle on sale in Australia — Polestar 3 claims 706km and the Audi Q6 e-tron 542km — and the no-cost alternative 20-inch aero wheel lifts it to 802km
800V architecture charges at up to 400kW, adding a claimed 372km in 10 minutes and 10-80 per cent in about 21 minutes
Undercuts the premium electric SUVs it is benchmarked against by thousands: rivals from Porsche, Audi and Polestar sit in the $120,000-$140,000 band
345kW/645Nm dual-motor drivetrain does 0-100km/h in 4.9 seconds, and reviewers rate the steering feel and near-98-per-cent regenerative braking as the best in any EV they have driven
2000kg braked tow rating and a 520L boot plus a 58L frunk — the first BMW EV with front storage
cons: One grade only at launch: the $109,900 50 xDrive. The $89,900 rear-drive iX3 40 is announced but not orderable until Q4 2026, so early buyers pay a $20,000 premium for a variant that will shortly stop being the entry point
Air-conditioning and even steering-wheel adjustment are screen-only, and reviewers called the Panoramic iDrive laggy, illogically nested and steep enough to need a lengthy instructional briefing
Rear-seat ride was described as harsh over sharp inputs, and there is no driver-adjustable damper option — a live risk on Australian roads given launch cars were assessed on smooth Spanish tarmac
No spare tyre of any kind, only run-flats; one launch car was stranded by a puncture

Real-world consumption of 17.3-18kWh/100km in testing implies roughly 600-650km rather than the near-800km lab claim, the optional 22-inch wheels cut the WLTP figure to 737km, and BMW's five-year warranty trails the seven years Kia offers on the EV9

summary: The xDrive25e is the first plug-in hybrid X1 BMW Australia has ever sold locally, added mid-2026 as the only PHEV in a range that otherwise runs mild-hybrid petrol or the battery-electric iX1. It pairs the base car's 1.5-litre three-cylinder with an 80kW motor and a 14.2kWh usable battery for 180kW, 6.8sec to 100km/h and a WLTP electric range BMW Australia quotes at 67-82km depending on wheels — enough to cover most Melbourne commutes on grid power. Reviewers rate the underlying X1 highly (CarExpert's Best Luxury Small SUV two years running, CarsGuide's best small car under $80,000), but no Australian outlet has road-tested the PHEV yet, and the case for it over the cheaper petrol or the FBT-exempt iX1 is a tax and charging-access argument rather than a driving one.
pros: 67-82km of WLTP electric range from a 14.2kWh usable battery clears the daily commute for most buyers, and beats the Mazda CX-60 PHEV's 76km and the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 86km on usable-battery-per-dollar within a genuinely premium small SUV

At $79,500 before on-roads it sits $1,309 under the ordinary $80,809 LCT threshold, so no luxury car tax applies at all — and at 53-75g/km CO2 combined it is comfortably inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car limit, so stamp duty is charged at the flat green rate
180kW and 477Nm for 6.8sec to 100km/h makes it the second-quickest X1 behind the $93,900 M35i, and 1.7 seconds quicker than the $66,700 sDrive20i it is based on
1,700kg braked towing is unusually strong for a compact PHEV — the Cupra Formentor VZe manages 1,500kg and most small plug-ins are rated at 750kg or not rated at all
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and not tied to servicing inside the BMW network, with the high-voltage battery separately covered for six years or 100,000km
cons: The battery costs the X1 50 litres of boot, dropping it from 540 litres in the petrol car to 490 — and Carwow notes the plug-in is the smallest boot in the whole X1 line-up, below even the mild-hybrid grades

Once the battery is flat it is a 1.5-litre three-cylinder hauling roughly 1,855kg: BMW's own charge-sustaining figure is 6.3-7.1L/100km, three times the 2.3-3.3L/100km combined label, so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home

It lost the FBT exemption that PHEVs held until 1 April 2025, while the iX1 xDrive30 sitting $7,300 above it at $86,800 keeps it — on a novated lease that gap can outweigh the sticker difference entirely

Charging is AC-only at 11kW with no DC capability, so a flat battery is a one-hour-45-minute stop on a wallbox and cannot be topped up usefully on the road; the Cupra Formentor VZe offers 50kW DC for $10,510 less

Only one grade is offered and the M Sport package with 19-inch wheels is mandatory, which pushes the car to the pessimistic end of BMW's 67-82km range band and leaves no cheaper entry point into the X1 PHEV

summary: The X3 30e xDrive is the only plug-in hybrid in BMW Australia's G45 X3 range, pairing a 2.0-litre turbo petrol with a 19.7kWh usable battery for 220kW/450Nm and a WLTP electric range in the 81-90km band — roughly double the previous X3 PHEV and enough for most Australian buyers to commute on electricity alone. Reviewers rate the ride and the EV-mode refinement highly, and several nominate the 30e as the pick of the X3 range, but they are consistent about the trade-offs: the battery costs 110 litres of boot space, the brake pedal loses the feel of the petrol cars, and the engine audibly strains once the charge is gone. At about $105,000 before on-roads it sits well above both LCT thresholds, and with the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids gone since April 2025 the case rests entirely on charging at home every night.
pros: 81-90km WLTP electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery — roughly double the 41km of the previous X3 xDrive30e — with reviewers reporting 70-80km in real Australian conditions, so a typical 30-45km commute runs on electricity alone
11kW three-phase AC charging is standard (up from 7.4kW on the pre-update car), giving a full charge in about 2 hours 15 minutes rather than an overnight-only proposition
2000kg braked towing and 220kW/450Nm for a 6.2-second 0-100km/h means the plug-in doesn't give away capability to the 20 xDrive petrol it costs more than

38g/km combined CO2 puts it comfortably under Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car threshold, so it attracts the $8.40-per-$200 duty rate instead of the $14.00-per-$200 tier a $100,000-plus petrol X3 pays — worth roughly $2,900 at this price

Five years/unlimited kilometres vehicle warranty with a separate six-year/100,000km high-voltage battery warranty, and M Sport package, panoramic roof and adaptive LED headlights are standard rather than optional
cons: The battery sits under the boot floor and costs 110 litres: 460L seats-up versus 570L in the 20 xDrive and M50, and 1600L versus 1700L folded — the Mercedes GLC 300e and Volkswagen Tiguan eHybrid also carry more claimed electric range

The 1.6L/100km label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: Parkers' WLTP charge-sustaining figure is 37.2mpg (about 7.6L/100km), and BMW Blog recorded around 14L/100km driving a depleted 30e in Sport mode, so a buyer without home charging is running a 2065kg petrol SUV

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and at $104,800 the X3 30e is above both the $80,809 ordinary and $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT thresholds and far above the $75,000 FBT cap — the concessions that made this car a novated-lease case are gone
AC-only charging at 11kW with no DC fast-charge capability, where the Mercedes GLC 300e accepts up to 60kW, and no vehicle-to-load or vehicle-to-home output

Multiple reviewers flag a soft, indistinct brake pedal from the regenerative blending — carsales called it 'squashy' versus the petrol variants — and CarExpert notes the engine 'sounds and feels like it has to work hard' climbing hills on a low battery

summary: The Atto 1 is a 3,990mm four-seat city hatch that broke Australia's sub-$25,000 barrier for a new battery-electric car, and it carries a five-star ANCAP rating rather than the safety compromise that price usually implies. Reviewers agree it is comfortable, nimble and better finished than its price suggests, and that the 220km Essential is a second-car proposition rather than a household's only vehicle. Where they split is whether the $4,000 step to the 310km Premium is essential or merely nice: some rate the base car complete, others call the Essential's range and 65kW motor the limit of the concept.
pros: At $23,990 before on-road costs the Essential is the cheapest new EV on sale in Australia, roughly $6,000 under the BYD Dolphin Essential and the MG 4 Urban 43.
Five-star ANCAP (2025, carried over from the European Dolphin Surf on confirmed identical spec) with six airbags, AEB, lane support and speed-sign recognition standard on both grades.
The Premium's 115kW/220Nm makes it genuinely quick for a city car at a claimed 9.1s to 100km/h, and it accepts 85kW DC charging where rivals at this price often cap out around 50kW.
Soft, long-travel suspension over a 2,500mm wheelbase in a 3,990mm body gives an unusually settled urban ride plus a turning circle that suits multi-storey car parks.
BYD's 6-year/150,000km vehicle warranty and 8-year/160,000km battery cover apply with no dealer-servicing condition attached.
cons: Only four seats: the rear bench is a 50/50-split two-place unit, so unlike the five-seat MG 4 or BYD Dolphin it cannot carry a fifth occupant at all.
The Essential's 220km WLTP range is the shortest of any EV on sale here and shrinks sharply at 100km/h, which makes the $4,000 Premium upgrade close to compulsory for anyone leaving the suburbs.
Australian reviewers repeatedly criticise the driver-monitoring and speed-warning chimes, which revert to on at every start and need several touchscreen taps to silence.
Almost all secondary controls live in the rotating touchscreen with few physical shortcuts, and the car ships with a repair kit rather than a spare wheel.
It gets noticeably noisy above about 80km/h, and the soft suspension that flatters it around town turns bouncy on coarse higher-speed roads.

summary: The Atto 2 is BYD's smallest SUV in Australia and, from $31,990 before on-road costs, the cheapest electric SUV on sale here — a point almost every local reviewer leads with. Testers consistently find it comfortable, quiet and easy to live with, and note real-world efficiency that beats the claim, but they are equally consistent that its 51.13kWh battery and 82kW DC charging peak make it a city and suburbs car rather than a country-trip one. Opinion splits on whether the soft, light-steering setup reads as relaxed or as vague, and the missing ANCAP rating is the recurring reservation.
pros: Cheapest electric SUV in Australia at $31,990 before on-road costs, undercutting the Chery E5 and Jaecoo J5 EV by roughly $4,000-$5,000 in Dynamic form
Real-world efficiency beats the 17.1kWh/100km claim — CarExpert recorded 13.7, Chasing Cars 14.2 and RACV 12-13.9kWh/100km, so the 345km WLTP figure holds up in suburban use
Both grades get the full active-safety set as standard, including AEB with pedestrian and cyclist detection, blind-spot monitoring, rear cross-traffic alert and adaptive cruise
Six-year/150,000km vehicle warranty is unconditional — no dealer-servicing strings — plus eight years/160,000km on the Blade battery
Premium's $4,000 walk-up is unusually well filled: 12.8-inch rotating screen, panoramic roof, 360-degree camera, heated and ventilated power driver's seat and eight speakers
cons: No ANCAP rating at all, and BYD has no plans to have it locally tested; reviewers note it lacks a driver monitoring system, which rules out five stars under current criteria
82kW DC charging peak means roughly 38-40 minutes for 10-80 per cent — slow enough that CarsGuide, CarExpert and Chasing Cars all flag it as the car's main road-trip limitation
Australia gets only the 51.13kWh battery; the 64.8kWh long-range version sold in Europe is not offered here, so 345km WLTP is the ceiling
No spare wheel on either grade — CarsGuide called this "unacceptable in Australia"
Soft suspension and very light, low-feedback steering leave it wallowy at speed, and several testers had to repeatedly switch off oversensitive lane-keeping and speed alerts

summary: The Atto 3 is the car that made BYD a volume brand in Australia, and after successive price cuts it remains one of the cheapest electric SUVs on sale, with a genuinely spacious cabin and a tow rating most rivals at the price cannot match. Australian reviewers are broadly positive but not unanimous: Chasing Cars found the chassis fluent and nicely balanced, while CarsGuide scored its driving dynamics a flat 6/10, and everyone flags coarse-surface road noise and the deliberately weird interior as the things buyers must forgive. It is showing its age on charging hardware, and the same aggressive discounting that makes it good value new has punished resale for earlier owners.
pros: Essential lists at $39,990 before on-road costs, undercutting essentially every other new electric SUV in Australia
Rated to tow 750kg braked, where the MG 4, BYD Dolphin and several similarly priced EVs are rated at zero
LFP Blade battery covered for 8 years/160,000km with a guaranteed 70 per cent state of health, on top of the 6-year/150,000km vehicle warranty
The 2025 update swapped the widely criticised Atlas Batman tyres for Continental EcoContact 6Q rubber and grew the rotating touchscreen to 15.6 inches
Five-star ANCAP (2022 test) with 91 per cent adult occupant protection
cons: Only a 7kW single-phase AC onboard charger on both grades, so a full home charge takes around nine hours where 11kW rivals need under six
DC charging peaks at just 70kW on the Essential and 88kW on the Premium, making 10-80 per cent a 35-38 minute stop
Independent tests returned 16.8-18.7kWh/100km against the 14.9 claim, cutting the Premium's real-world range to roughly 320-380km rather than 420km
Reviewers consistently criticise intrusive road noise and an over-designed cabin with tiny door bins and poor small-item storage
BYD's repeated new-car price cuts have hammered resale, with three-year retained value forecast at about 51 per cent

summary: Australia's cheapest new electric car, the Dolphin pairs a soft, comfortable ride with a surprisingly well-equipped, upscale-feeling cabin for the price, according to CarExpert, CarsGuide and WhichCar. Reviewers agree it is happiest as a city runabout: refined and efficient around town, but wind noise, mixed rear visibility and (on the base Essential) modest power blunt its appeal on the open road. It is not a driver's car, but on value and everyday livability it comfortably outpoints most petrol light hatches at a similar price.
pros: Lowest entry price of any new EV in Australia
Comfortable, well-controlled ride for the segment
Roomy cabin and quality-feeling trim materials for the price
Strong standard equipment including a large rotating touchscreen
Five-star ANCAP safety rating with comprehensive driver assist tech
cons: Underpowered Essential struggles with highway overtaking
Slow 7kW AC home charging versus rivals' 11kW
Small boot and restricted rear visibility
6-year/150,000km warranty trails some rivals' 7-year cover
Steeper resale depreciation risk as BYD repeatedly cuts new prices

summary: The BYD Seal is a fast-charging, long-range electric sedan that undercuts the Tesla Model 3 on price while matching it on performance, especially in dual-motor Performance guise. Australian reviewers rate the equipment list, warranty and everyday value highly, but consistently flag a boot smaller than key rivals, an unsettled ride on rougher roads, and a touchscreen-heavy interior with few physical controls. Repeated BYD price cuts have also softened resale values across the range, a factor increasingly raised by reviewers and even BYD's own local distributor.
pros: Strong value against the Tesla Model 3, with a well-equipped cabin and quick acceleration in Performance guise (390kW/670Nm, 0-100km/h in 3.8s)
Long WLTP range from the 82.56kWh Blade LFP battery: 570km (Premium) and 520km (Performance), with 150kW DC fast charging
Strong after-sales backing with a 6-year/150,000km vehicle warranty and 8-year/160,000km battery warranty
cons: 400L boot trails key rivals like the Tesla Model 3 (594L) and Toyota Camry (524L), with a narrow opening
Ride quality criticised as unsettled and bouncy over bumps, lacking the composure of segment rivals
Interior tech feels dated relative to newer BYD models, with too many functions buried in touchscreen menus rather than physical controls
Reviewers and BYD's own Australian distributor have flagged softening resale values as BYD continues to cut new-car prices across its range

summary: The Seal 6 is Australia's cheapest plug-in hybrid sedan, and reviewers agree the price is the argument: at $34,990 before on-roads it undercuts the petrol-hybrid Toyota Camry it targets while adding a plug, a 491-litre boot and a five-star ANCAP result. Where they are far less generous is the way it drives — the ride and steering draw the sharpest criticism of any recent BYD, and the 55km electric range is the shortest in the brand's local plug-in line-up. Only one grade is offered on the sedan body, so buyers wanting the sunroof, heated seats or DC charging have to move to the Touring wagon.
pros: At $34,990 before on-road costs it is the cheapest plug-in hybrid sedan on sale in Australia, undercutting the non-plug-in Toyota Camry hybrid it is aimed at ($39,990) while adding 55km of electric-only running
491-litre boot with the seats up and 1370 litres folded — larger than BYD's own Seal battery-electric sedan (400/950L), so the plug-in hardware costs almost nothing in load space

Five-star ANCAP rating (2023-2025 criteria) with 92 per cent adult occupant protection, the highest adult score in ANCAP's release batch, and maximum points in the full-width frontal, side impact and oblique pole tests
65-litre tank behind a frugal charge-sustaining engine gives roughly 1350km between fills on our arithmetic (BYD claims over 1400km), so it does not trade touring range for the plug
Six-year/150,000km warranty with no servicing conditions attached, and the drive battery separately covered for eight years/160,000km
cons: 55km of WLTP electric range is the shortest of any BYD plug-in hybrid sold here — half the Seal 6 Touring's 100km and well under the Sealion 6 Essential's 92km — so the petrol engine is involved on most days beyond a short commute

Charging is AC-only and capped at 3.3kW, with no DC fast-charge capability at all (the Touring gets 6.6kW AC and 27kW DC), so the 10.08kWh pack takes about three and a half hours from a home wallbox and cannot be topped up on a road trip

CarExpert's launch drive described the ride as "loose and slovenly" with a floating feel at highway speed, numb steering and both understeer and snap-oversteer at the limit — the driving experience is the car's clear weak point rather than a minor demerit

The 1.1L/100km label figure assumes you start every trip with a full battery; once the pack is depleted it drinks around 5L/100km and CarExpert measured 6.1L/100km in the mechanically similar Touring, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is left with an ordinary hybrid carrying extra weight

summary: The Sealion 5 is BYD's cheapest plug-in hybrid and, at $33,990 before on-roads for the Essential, the cheapest PHEV on sale in Australia — a front-drive medium SUV that sits just below the Sealion 6 on price while beating it on boot space. Australian reviewers agree the value case is unarguable and that ride comfort and rear-seat room are better than the price suggests, but they split on the driving experience, with several calling the steering lifeless and the 1.5-litre engine coarse under load. The consistent reservations are the 3.3kW AC-only charging, the absence of an ANCAP rating, and how quickly running costs climb once the battery is flat.
pros: At $33,990 before on-road costs the Essential is the cheapest plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia, undercutting BYD's own Sealion 6 Essential by $9,000 and the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV by more again
463-litre boot with the seats up (1,410 litres folded) is larger than the physically bigger Sealion 6's 425 litres, so the battery packaging costs less practicality than usual in the class

Premium's 18.3kWh battery is rated at 85km of WLTP electric range (100km on the NEDC figure BYD Australia quotes), enough for a typical Melbourne commuter to run several days between charges without starting the engine
High-voltage battery is covered for 8 years/160,000km, two years beyond the 6-year/150,000km unconditional vehicle warranty, and the drive unit for 8 years/150,000km
CarsGuide and CarExpert both rate interior material quality and ride comfort above the price point, and Chasing Cars singles out rear-seat space as genuinely family-sized
cons: Charge-sustaining fuel use is the number that matters: BYD quotes 4.5L/100km (Essential) and 4.6L/100km (Premium) with the battery below 25 per cent against a 1.2-1.3L/100km label, EV Central measured 4.9L/100km and Chasing Cars 8.1L/100km on country roads — a buyer who cannot charge at home loses most of the reason to own it
3.3kW AC onboard charger and no DC fast-charging at all: 4.5 hours to fill the Essential and about 6 hours the Premium, so an away-from-home top-up is effectively impossible
No ANCAP rating as at mid-2026 — the Sealion 5 is still on ANCAP's list to be tested rather than carrying a result, unlike the five-star Sealion 6
Front-wheel drive only, rated to tow just 750kg braked, and supplied with a tyre repair kit rather than a spare wheel

Reviewers repeatedly criticise the steering as light and lifeless and the 1.5-litre engine as noisy under load, with CarsGuide also noting limited steering-column adjustment and some high-speed instability

summary: Australian reviewers consistently rate the Sealion 6 as the value pick of the plug-in hybrid SUV class, with the Essential holding the title of the country's cheapest new PHEV and offering a genuinely usable electric-only range. Opinions are more mixed on dynamics: reviewers like the improved, comfort-biased suspension tune but mark it down for body roll and light, indirect steering next to rivals such as the Cupra Formentor. Most agree the 425-litre boot is a real compromise versus segment rivals, and that running costs climb sharply once the battery is depleted.
pros: Essential undercuts the Toyota RAV4 PHEV and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV by a wide margin at $42,990 before on-roads, reviewers' benchmark for value in the class
Usable electric-only range for a budget PHEV: up to 92km (Essential) or 140km (Dynamic Extended Range) on a full charge, enough to cover most Melbourne commutes without touching the engine
Generous standard equipment for the price, including a rotating touchscreen (12.8in Essential/Dynamic, 15.8in Premium), dual-zone climate and vehicle-to-load power
Five-star ANCAP rating (assessed under 2023 Euro NCAP criteria) with seven airbags standard across the range
8-year/160,000km battery warranty outlasts the vehicle's own 6-year/150,000km unconditional term
cons: 425-litre boot with the rear seats up trails segment rivals like the Toyota RAV4 and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV, the direct cost of packaging the battery under the floor

Once the battery is depleted the Sealion 6 drinks far more than its 0.8-1.1L/100km label figure suggests — reviewers measured 4.8-6.0L/100km in charge-sustaining running — so the economics case weakens sharply for anyone who cannot charge at home
Soft, comfort-tuned suspension brings noticeable body roll and light, indirect steering that reviewers rate well behind more dynamically composed rivals
No spare wheel, a tyre-repair kit only, and BYD's Australian resale value and dealer/service network remain relatively unproven for a car this new to the range
