summary: Australian reviewers largely agree the Sealion 7 is one of the most convincing mainstream electric SUVs yet from a Chinese brand, praising its spacious, well-finished cabin, strong value against the Tesla Model Y, and a confident five-star ANCAP safety rating. The dual-motor Performance adds genuinely quick acceleration while keeping the comfortable, easy-to-live-with character of the range. Verdicts are more mixed on dynamics, with several outlets noting body roll, a ride that can feel soggy on the open road and jiggly around town, and lingering infotainment glitches.
pros: Spacious, well-finished cabin with generous rear-seat room and dual driver displays
Strong value against the Tesla Model Y, undercutting it while matching much of its specification
Five-star ANCAP safety rating (2025) with comprehensive standard driver-assist tech
Performance variant adds genuine pace (4.5s 0-100km/h) without losing everyday comfort
cons: Noticeable body roll and a ride that reviewers describe as soggy at speed and jiggly around town
Some tech gremlins and infotainment software glitches reported in early ownership
Real-world range and efficiency trail the claimed WLTP figures by a noticeable margin
BYD's Australian resale value and dealer/service network are still relatively unproven for the brand

summary: The Sealion 8 is BYD's first three-row model in Australia, a large seven-seat plug-in hybrid that undercuts the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-80 PHEV by roughly $11,000-$14,000 at the entry point while claiming far more electric range on paper — up to 152km, though on the lenient NEDC cycle rather than WLTP. Reviewers broadly agree on the value case, the presentation of the cabin and the generous second row, and agree that the 359kW AWD grades offer more performance than a family SUV needs. Where they diverge is ride and refinement: some rate it quiet and well-resolved, while CarExpert and Chasing Cars both flag inconsistent damping and road noise at speed.
pros: The 35.6kWh battery in the AWD grades is the largest plug-in pack in any seven-seat SUV sold here — roughly two and a half times the Kia Sorento PHEV's 13.8kWh — and BYD claims 152km of electric running from it.
Sharp entry pricing: $56,990 before on-roads for the Dynamic FWD against $70,880 for the cheapest Kia Sorento PHEV and $68,100 for the Mazda CX-80 PHEV Touring.
Braked towing of 1800kg (Dynamic FWD) or 2000kg (both AWD grades) comfortably beats the Kia Sorento PHEV's 1010kg, which is the usual weak point of a plug-in seven-seater.
Warranty is six years/150,000km with no servicing conditions attached, and the high-voltage battery carries a separate eight-year/160,000km cover.

Combined tailpipe CO2 of 22-24g/km puts every grade under Victoria's 120g/km green-passenger-car duty threshold and well inside the LCT fuel-efficient test, and all three list prices sit below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold so no luxury car tax is payable.
cons: Only 270 litres of boot behind the third row — enough for a school run, not a seven-up holiday — and there is no spare wheel at all, just a puncture repair kit.
Every electric range figure is NEDC. No WLTP number exists for this model in any market, and RACV's own conversion puts the realistic equivalents nearer 88km (FWD) and 130km (AWD).

The plug-in compromise is visible in BYD's own numbers: the 1.0-1.1L/100km label assumes a charged battery, and BYD quotes 5.3L/100km (FWD) or 6.3L/100km (AWD) once the pack falls below 25 per cent — so a buyer who cannot charge at home is simply running a 2.3-2.6 tonne SUV on petrol.

The third row is described by CarsGuide as strictly for smaller kids, with tight access, and Chasing Cars criticises cabin noise, front-seat support and the reliance on touchscreen controls for basic functions.
CarsGuide calls the 359kW AWD grades' performance irrelevant in a family car, yet they carry a $7,000-$14,000 premium over the Dynamic FWD and add around 265kg of kerb weight.

summary: Australian reviewers treat the Shark 6 as the ute that reset the segment's value equation: it was the first plug-in hybrid dual-cab sold here, and at $55,900-$62,900 before on-roads it undercuts the Ford Ranger PHEV by a wide margin while riding and accelerating better than any diesel rival. The consistent caveat is capability rather than comfort - payload sits below the class norm, the 1.5-litre cars stop at 2500kg braked towing, and there is no low-range transfer case, so reviewers steer heavy haulers and serious off-roaders elsewhere. BYD has also run repeated drive-away and cashback campaigns on the Shark 6, which makes list-price resale harder to read than for the segment's established diesels.
pros: Cheapest plug-in hybrid dual-cab in Australia at $55,900 before on-roads for the Dynamic cab-chassis, roughly $20,000 under the Ford Ranger PHEV while making more power (321kW/650Nm, or 350kW/700Nm in the Performance)
Electric range holds up in the real world: Australian testers covered about 80km on battery alone against BYD's claim, enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute without the engine starting
8-year/160,000km battery warranty runs two years past the 6-year/150,000km unconditional vehicle warranty, on long 12-month/20,000km service intervals averaging about $550 a year
Five-star ANCAP with a ride reviewers rate as SUV-like - coil-sprung double wishbones front and rear make it quieter and more composed on-road than any leaf-sprung diesel dual-cab
The 2026 Performance finally delivers the segment-benchmark 3500kg braked towing for $5,000 over the Premium, and reviewers found it stayed planted with close to three tonnes behind it
cons: Payload trails the class: 790kg on the Premium, 725kg on the Performance and 750kg on the cab-chassis once the 150kg factory tray is fitted, against roughly a tonne for a HiLux or Ranger

With the battery depleted it drinks 7.9L/100km (1.5-litre) or 10.5L/100km (Performance), not the 1.3-2.0L/100km label figure - a buyer who cannot charge at home pays diesel-ute running costs for premium 95RON petrol
No low-range transfer case and limited articulation; reviewers found it out of its depth beyond formed dirt roads even with the Performance's new Crawl mode
The Dynamic cab-chassis arrives with no tray at all - the factory-approved Ironman 4x4 unit adds about $5,000 plus $1,155 fitment, so it lands dearer than the Premium pickup it appears to undercut
2.6-2.8 tonne kerb weight and a ladder-frame PHEV driveline push Melbourne comprehensive quotes above comparable mid-size PHEV SUVs, with quotes on the Premium reported past $2,000

summary: Cadillac's first Australian model is a 2.8-tonne dual-motor electric SUV that a permanent $32,000 cut has re-priced from $122,000 to $90,000 before on-road costs, dropping it under the fuel-efficient LCT threshold and into FBT-exempt novated-lease territory. Reviewers agree on the hushed ride, the 530km WLTP range and the distinctive styling, but split hard on the cabin: CarExpert and carsales rate it genuinely luxurious, while Chasing Cars judges the materials and rear-seat packaging not good enough at any price. The unresolved risks are a three-outlet retail network across Australia and New Zealand, no tow rating at all, and the resale damage the cut inflicts on every car sold before it.
pros: The permanent cut from $122,000 to $90,000 before on-road costs puts it under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold, so it now qualifies for the FBT exemption on a novated lease — it did not at launch.
530km WLTP from a 102kWh pack, and a 22.1kW three-phase AC onboard charger roughly double the 11kW most rivals fit, so a full charge on three-phase takes about five hours rather than overnight-plus.
793 litres behind the second row and 1,722 litres folded, against 526/1,536L in a Polestar 4 and 333L behind row two in a seven-seat Kia EV9.

Five years unlimited-kilometre warranty plus five years of complimentary scheduled servicing at 12-month/12,000km intervals, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, and a year of free public charging upgradable to three years or a 7kW home charger.

Genuinely quiet: active noise cancellation that pre-empts road impacts and a 19-speaker AKG Studio system with Dolby Atmos are what every Australian reviewer singles out, alongside 388kW/610Nm and 0-100km/h in 5.3 seconds.
cons: The $32,000 cut is a resale problem as much as a bargain — every Lyriq sold at $117,000 to $124,000 was re-based overnight to $90,000, and Cadillac does not report sales to VFACTS, so there is no local residual data to argue with.
Not rated to tow anything in Australia, where a Kia EV9 pulls 2,500kg braked and a Zeekr 7X 2,000kg.

Three retail outlets across Australia and New Zealand — the Rosebery Experience Centre in Sydney, a Port Melbourne test-drive venue and Auckland — with the promised Brisbane site still unopened, so servicing and panel repair mean a long trip for most buyers.
Super Cruise is not approved for Australian roads and the adaptive cruise ships without lane centring; there is also no head-up display and no native navigation at $90,000.

At 2,774kg and a claimed 22.5kWh/100km it is markedly thirstier than a Polestar 4 Dual Motor's 18.7kWh/100km, and Chasing Cars rates the rear seat's high floor and hard ISOFIX bracing covers as genuinely uncomfortable.

summary: The Optiq is the cheapest way into General Motors' relaunched Cadillac brand in Australia, and reviewers consistently praise its distinctive, well-finished cabin, quiet running and unusually generous standard equipment for $80,000 before on-road costs. The consensus criticism is just as consistent: 425km of WLTP range and a 110kW DC charging ceiling are the weakest numbers among luxury mid-size electric SUVs on sale here, and Australia takes the superseded 224kW powertrain rather than the US car's 328kW update. Opinion divides mainly on the ride, which most describe as composed and connected but firmer and less plush than the badge implies.
pros: At $80,000 before on-road costs it undercuts the BMW iX3 ($89,900), Genesis GV60 ($88,300) and Lexus RZ ($84,500), and sits well under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold that governs the novated-lease FBT exemption
Genuinely big for the class: a 744-litre boot with the rear seats up (1603 litres folded) and a 2954mm wheelbase that reviewers rate for near-limousine rear knee room

Heavily specified in its single grade — 33-inch curved display with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto (features GM deleted from its US EVs), 19-speaker AKG Dolby Atmos audio, heated/ventilated/massaging front seats, Brembo front brakes, panoramic glass roof and 21-inch wheels
22.1kW three-phase AC charging is unusually quick for the segment and adds roughly 100km of range per hour at home, which softens the weak DC rate for overnight chargers
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with no servicing strings attached, an eight-year/160,000km battery warranty, and a five-star Euro NCAP result (2025) scoring 83% for adult occupant protection
cons: 110kW is the lowest DC fast-charging peak of any luxury mid-size electric SUV sold in Australia — a Polestar 4 accepts 200kW — so road trips mean noticeably longer stops
425km of WLTP range is short for an $80,000 EV in 2026, and the 19.9kWh/100km WLTP consumption claim is high for the class (CarExpert measured 17.9kWh/100km on test)

Australia gets the superseded 224kW/480Nm dual-motor drivetrain while the US MY26 car has 328kW/675Nm and 150kW charging, and GM Australia has given no timing for bringing the update here; the Optiq-V is ruled out entirely

Firm-riding on 21-inch wheels with no adaptive dampers available, which several Australian reviewers judged short of the plushness a luxury badge implies, and the steering is described as vague on-centre

New-brand ownership risk: Cadillac does not report Australian sales, retails through a handful of metropolitan experience centres, permanently cut the larger Lyriq's price by $32,000 during 2026, and had still not confirmed Optiq service pricing at launch

summary: The Vistiq is Cadillac's three-row flagship EV for Australia, sold in a single fully-loaded Platinum grade at $116,000 before on-road costs — sharp enough to undercut a Kia EV9 GT-Line and well under a Volvo EX90 or Hyundai Ioniq 9. Australian reviewers rate the cabin, the AKG audio and the genuinely usable third row highly, and are near-unanimous that the drivetrain is far quicker than the class needs. Where they diverge is whether the Australia-only 91kWh pack is enough: 461km of WLTP range and a 130kW DC charging ceiling are both below what the price and the badge imply, and the brand's tiny local footprint makes resale the open question.
pros: At $116,000 before on-roads it undercuts the Kia EV9 GT-Line ($121,000), Hyundai Ioniq 9 and Volvo EX90 while arriving in top Platinum trim only — 22-inch wheels, adaptive air suspension, rear-wheel steering, four-zone climate, a 33-inch curved display and 23-speaker AKG audio are all standard, with no options ladder to climb
Third row is adult-sized rather than the usual '5+2' afterthought, and the second-row captain's chairs leave a walk-through aisle to reach it
459kW/880Nm dual-motor AWD covers 0-100km/h in 4.2 seconds, quicker than any EV9 including the GT
Five years of complimentary scheduled servicing and roadside assistance comes on top of the 5-year/unlimited-km warranty, with the battery covered for 8 years/160,000km
cons: DC charging peaks at just 130kW — the US car gets 190kW, and the 800V Kia EV9 recharges materially faster, so long trips cost more time than the price suggests
461km WLTP from the Australia-only 91kWh usable pack (the US car gets 102kWh) trails the Kia EV9 Earth's 521km and the Ioniq 9, in a 5.2m SUV that is thirsty at a claimed 22kWh/100km
Six seats only in Australia — the US seven-seat bench is not offered — with 430L behind the third row and no front boot under the long bonnet
Resale is the brand risk: Cadillac sells through a handful of Australian stores and the closely related Lyriq took a permanent $32,000 price cut in 2026, which drags residuals across the range

summary: The Chery E5 (rebranded from Omoda E5 during 2025, with the Omoda name now being reserved for a separate model line launching later) is one of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia, a small front-wheel-drive EV pitched squarely on price and standard equipment rather than dynamic polish. Australian reviewers consistently praise its value proposition, long warranty and cheap servicing, well-equipped cabin, but mark it down for unsettled ride quality, an over-cautious safety-assist calibration, and a boot that trails class rivals. For MY26 the range was simplified to a single Ultimate grade with a smaller but more efficient battery, holding range steady at 430km WLTP while sharpening the price further.
pros: One of the cheapest new electric SUVs on sale in Australia, undercutting most EV rivals
Long ownership package: 7-year vehicle / 8-year battery warranty plus affordable capped-price servicing (around $227/visit)
Well-equipped cabin for the price, with dual 12.3-inch screens, wireless charging and soft-touch trim
Solid 430km WLTP range from a modest, efficient battery
cons: Ride quality criticised as jittery and easily upset by rough surfaces around town, with some testers also describing wallowy handling at speed
Safety-assist calibration is poor: abrupt lane-keep intervention and over-sensitive driver-attention warnings that reviewers end up disabling
Small 300-litre boot (seats up) trails rivals offering closer to 450 litres
Slower DC fast-charging (around 80kW max) than newer rivals in the segment

summary: The Tiggo 7 Super Hybrid is the cheapest plug-in hybrid SUV on sale in Australia, and Australian reviewers agree the powertrain is the reason to buy it: an 18.4kWh LFP battery good for about 90km of electric range, 40kW DC fast charging almost nobody else offers at this price, and roughly 4-6L/100km once the battery is flat. Where they part company is the chassis and the software — NRMA, CarExpert and The Beep all criticise the stiff, jarring ride, the disconnected steering and an occasional driveline shunt, while carsales and CarsGuide are more forgiving on the basis of what it costs. Nobody argues it is good to drive; the case rests on running costs, the seven-year warranty and a transaction price that Chery keeps discounting.
pros: About 90km of WLTP electric range from the 18.4kWh LFP pack — more than a BYD Sealion 5 Essential's 71km and enough for most Melbourne commutes on electricity alone
40kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 20 minutes) plus 3.3kW vehicle-to-load, where the BYD Sealion 6 and Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV have no DC capability at all

Stays efficient with the battery depleted: Chery claims under 6.0L/100km charge-sustaining and Australian testers recorded 4.1-5.8L/100km, so the car is not punishing for a buyer who forgets to plug in
Seven-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing condition, a separate eight-year unlimited-kilometre battery warranty, and capped-price servicing quoted at $3,174 across seven years
Five-star ANCAP rating applied to petrol and Super Hybrid Tiggo 7 variants built from June 2025, and both grades sit far below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold
cons: Ride and steering are the consistent complaint: NRMA calls the suspension stiff and jarring with steering that gives almost no feedback, CarExpert reports unexplained driveline power surges like a clutch dump, and The Beep describes vague steering and lazy throttle response

The plug-in packaging costs you the underfloor storage and the spare wheel entirely — the Super Hybrid gets a tyre repair kit only, where the petrol Tiggo 7 has a two-level boot floor and underfloor bin
No braked tow rating published — Chery quotes only 750kg unbraked, so a caravan or a boat rules the car out where a petrol mid-size SUV would not

The 1.4L/100km label figure is a laboratory number that assumes you start every trip charged; without home charging you are running a 1,788kg SUV on its petrol engine at 4-6L/100km and the plug-in premium never pays back
Chery has run repeated $5,000 drive-away campaigns and $2,000 build-clearance cashbacks on this car since launch, so the street price keeps resetting and resale is unproven

summary: The Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid is the cheapest seven-seat plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia, and Australian reviewers agree the powertrain is the reason to buy it: a 1.5-litre turbo petrol engine and 150kW motor in a single-speed dedicated hybrid transmission, an 18.4kWh LFP battery good for 90km of WLTP electric range, and roughly 6L/100km once the battery is flat. Where they split is the chassis and the third row — CarsGuide and EV Central rate the value and the powertrain calibration highly, while Chasing Cars, carsales and the NRMA mark down a floaty, underdamped ride, screen-buried controls and a rearmost row that has no top-tether or ISOFIX anchorages at all. As a two-row family SUV with occasional seats seven and eight it is compelling; as a genuine three-row people mover it is compromised by 117 litres of boot behind the third row and kerbside-only access to it.
pros: The cheapest seven-seat PHEV in Australia at $42,990 before on-road costs for the Urban — roughly $25,000 under a Mitsubishi Outlander Exceed PHEV and about $30,000 under a Kia Sorento PHEV, both of which also seat seven

90km of WLTP electric-only range (56 miles, Chery UK) from the 18.4kWh LFP pack, enough to cover most Melbourne commutes on electricity, and Chery quotes 1200km combined; 40kW DC fast charging takes 30-80 per cent in about 20 minutes, which neither the Outlander PHEV nor a BYD Sealion 6 offers at all

Seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing-exclusivity condition, plus a separate eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty and seven years of capped-price servicing totalling $3,174.15

The petrol engine drives the wheels directly through the DHT in parallel mode rather than acting only as a generator, so highway consumption settles at 5.4-6.1L/100km on a flat battery instead of collapsing the way a range-extender's does

Five-star ANCAP rating from 2025 covering all variants including the Super Hybrid, with 86 per cent child occupant protection and nine airbags, and at $46,990 the top Ultimate still sits about $34,000 under the ordinary $80,809 LCT threshold
cons: Only 117 litres of boot with all seven seats in use — less than a Kia Sorento's 179 litres and a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 191 litres — so the third row and the weekly shop are effectively mutually exclusive

No top-tether or ISOFIX anchorages in the third row at all, which ANCAP explicitly flags, and third-row access is via the kerbside door only, putting children out on the traffic side on a right-hand kerb

The 1.3L/100km combined label figure is meaningless in use: Chery itself points buyers to about 6.0L/100km charge-sustaining (47.1mpg WLTP with the battery depleted), and Australian testers recorded 5.4-6.1L/100km, so a buyer without home charging is running a 1.9-tonne seven-seater on premium 95-octane at ordinary-SUV cost

No braked towing rating whatsoever — 750kg unbraked only — where the 2.0-litre petrol Tiggo 8 and most seven-seat rivals are rated for a caravan or a boat, and neither grade carries a spare wheel (inflator kit only)

Reviewers are consistent that the ride is soft and floaty with poor body control at speed, the climate and drive-mode functions are buried in the touchscreen, and Chery's aggressive national drive-away pricing plus a current $2,000 cashback offer leaves resale value unproven

summary: The Tiggo 9 Super Hybrid is Chery Australia's flagship: a 4.8-metre seven-seat plug-in hybrid sold only as a PHEV here, in a 225kW front-drive Elite at $52,990 and a 315kW all-wheel-drive Ultimate at $59,990 before on-road costs. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous that the powertrain is the story — the Ultimate's 34.5kWh pack returns a genuine 146km WLTP electric range that testers repeatedly measured at 138-145km, and 71kW DC charging is something no Outlander PHEV or BYD Sealion 6 offers. Where they diverge is the body around it: CarExpert, carsales and the NRMA rate the equipment and refinement well above the price, while CarsGuide, Chasing Cars and bttr.reviews mark down a third row with no airbag coverage, a floaty 20-inch ride and hard interior plastics, and there is still no ANCAP rating.
pros: 146km of WLTP electric range on the Ultimate — the longest of any plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia and roughly double a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 84km — from a 34.5kWh CATL NMC pack, with Australian testers independently recording 138km, 143km and 145km before the engine started

71kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 18 minutes) plus 6.6kW AC and 6.6kW vehicle-to-load, where the Outlander PHEV, Kia Sorento PHEV and BYD Sealion 6 offer no meaningful DC capability at all

Seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing-exclusivity condition, a separate eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty, and seven years of capped-price servicing totalling about $3,174
315kW/580Nm and 0-100km/h in 5.4 seconds in the Ultimate, with a 1500kg braked tow rating and a 70-litre tank, where the Tiggo 7 and Tiggo 8 Super Hybrids are not rated to tow anything braked at all

At $59,990 the top Ultimate sits nearly $21,000 below the ordinary $80,809 LCT threshold and undercuts a seven-seat Kia Sorento PHEV by roughly $25,000, so no luxury car tax is payable on either grade
cons: Only 143 litres of boot with all seven seats up — less than a Kia Sorento's 179 litres and a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 191 litres — and the curtain airbags do not extend to the third row, which CarExpert and carsales both call an outright oversight; there is no ANCAP rating for the Tiggo 9 either way

The 1.3-1.4L/100km combined label figure is a fiction for anyone who cannot charge: Australian testers measured 5.9L/100km (carsales), 6.3L/100km (CarExpert) and 7.1L/100km (CarsGuide) once the battery was flat, and the car demands 95-octane premium, so a 2.2-tonne SUV with no home charger costs about the same to fuel as a petrol Kluger

Reviewers are consistent that the Ultimate's 20-inch wheels leave the ride busy over sharp edges with excessive body pitch, that the steering is over-light beyond 80km/h, and that the cabin mixes a good 15.6-inch screen with obviously cheap hard plastics

Third-row access is awkward and kerbside-biased, the boot floor does not lie flat with the third row folded, and neither grade carries a spare wheel — the repair kit is velcroed to the boot carpet with no dedicated stowage for it or the charging cable

The Elite arrived in May 2026 at $7,000 under the Ultimate that launched six months earlier, and Chery discounts hard on national drive-away campaigns, so residual values for both grades are unproven and the depreciation assumption here is inherited from the Tiggo 7 and Tiggo 8 rather than observed

summary: The Formentor VZe is the sole plug-in hybrid in Cupra's coupe-styled small SUV range, and the MY26 update roughly doubled its battery to 20kWh usable for a claimed 114km of WLTP electric range — enough that most Melbourne commuters would rarely start the 1.5-litre engine. Reviewers agree the second-generation drivetrain is smooth and genuinely quick at 200kW, but they split on whether it is worth $68,990: CarExpert found it the least resolved car in the range to drive, with heavy steering and a soft-front/stiff-rear ride, and pointed buyers at a Skoda Kodiaq PHEV for similar range and more space. The recurring practical complaint is that the battery costs it a third of its boot and its spare wheel.
pros: 114km of WLTP electric range from a 20kWh usable battery is roughly double the previous VZe's 58km and beats every PHEV SUV near the price — Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV claims 86km, Mazda CX-60 PHEV 76km
50kW DC fast charging plus 11kW AC is rare on a plug-in hybrid: most PHEV rivals, including the Outlander and CX-60, have no DC capability at all
200kW/400Nm and 7.2sec to 100km/h makes it quicker than the 150kW petrol Formentor V that sits $11,500 below it
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional — it is not tied to servicing inside the Cupra network — and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km

Priced at $68,990 before on-roads it sits under both the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold and Victoria's green-car duty test at 43g/km CO2, so no luxury car tax applies and stamp duty is charged at the flat green rate
cons: The battery cuts the boot from roughly 450 litres in the petrol Formentor to 345 litres, and deletes the spare wheel entirely — CarsGuide lists 'small boot in PHEV' and 'no spare wheel' as its headline dislikes

Once the battery is flat it is an ordinary 1.5-litre turbo hauling 1,730kg, and the 1.7L/100km label figure is meaningless — expect roughly 6.5L/100km on petrol alone, so the economics collapse for a buyer without home charging

CarExpert judged the VZe the most disconnected car in the Formentor range to drive, citing heavy, feel-free steering from the extra front-axle mass and suspension that is too soft at the front and too stiff at the rear

The plug-in hybrid lost its FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and Cupra's own MY24 run-out saw the previous VZe cut from $64,990 to $47,990 drive-away — with Formentor sales down 61.3 per cent in the first half of 2026, resale risk is real
No vehicle-to-load outlet, a 40-litre fuel tank that limits touring range once the battery is depleted, and a 1,500kg braked tow rating that trails the petrol VZx's 1,800kg

summary: The Tavascan is Cupra's only battery-electric model in Australia now that the Born has been withdrawn, and it is a coupe-roofed mid-size SUV built on the same MEB platform as the Volkswagen ID.5 and Skoda Enyaq. Australian reviewers consistently rate the chassis above its rivals — Chasing Cars and CarsGuide both single out the steering and body control as sharper than a Tesla Model Y or BYD Sealion 7 — while criticising the haptic controls, the 135kW DC charging peak and the complete absence of connected services. Buyers should note this two-grade range is in run-out: Cupra announced an updated line-up on 30 June 2026, arriving from late August, which adds a cheaper entry grade and repositions the VZ above the $75,000 FBT cap.
pros: Reviewers rate the chassis the best in the segment: Chasing Cars called the Endurance's chassis 'agile and adjustable' with crisp steering, and CarsGuide judged the ride a genuine step above the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7 it is priced against

Both grades sit under the $75,000 FBT-exemption cap for novated leases, the VZ by just $510 — and the replacement VZ announced for late August 2026 is priced at $75,490, which forfeits that concession, so the run-out car is materially cheaper to salary-package
540 litres seats-up and 1,550 litres seats-down with a power tailgate and kick sensor, and a completely flat rear floor that makes the middle seat genuinely usable for an adult

Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is factory-backed and unconditional — it is not tied to servicing inside the Cupra network — with the high-voltage battery separately covered for 8 years/160,000km including a 70 per cent capacity floor
The 250kW VZ runs 0-100km/h in 5.5 seconds and adds DCC adaptive dampers, a fixed panoramic roof and matrix high beam over the 210kW Endurance, none of which the base car can be optioned with
cons: This range is superseded from late August 2026 by an updated line-up with a 10.25-inch driver display, physical steering wheel buttons and a $55,490 entry grade — the run-out car means older cabin tech and an immediate resale hit
135kW DC peak is slow for 2026: a Kia EV5 or Zeekr 7X at similar money refills faster, and Chasing Cars called the 28-minute 10-80 per cent claim disappointing for a 77kWh pack
No vehicle-to-load, no head-up display and no connected services at all — no smartphone app, no remote preconditioning and no over-the-air updates, features that cars $15,000 cheaper now include

Cupra is a marginal brand here — just 257 Tavascans delivered in Australia to the end of May 2026, the same as the Skoda Elroq it shares a platform with — so parts, specialist repairers and resale all carry small-volume risk
Chasing Cars measured 18.3kWh/100km in the real world for about 421km against the 531km WLTP claim, and criticised the grainy handover between regenerative braking and the rear drum brakes

summary: The S07 is Australia's first Deepal model, a mid-size electric SUV sold in a single RWD grade and visibly benchmarked against the Tesla Model Y. CarExpert's 2025 review called it competently executed but derivative, marked down for a bouncy ride, a wide turning circle and overreactive driver-assist alerts, while praising its equipment list and quiet cabin. CarsGuide's follow-up in 2026 found Deepal had used over-the-air updates to fix several of those early complaints, lifting its verdict to 7.4/10 and noting the car is a more convincing daily proposition now than at launch, even if it remains an unexciting drive with slower DC charging than key rivals.
pros: Strong standard equipment for the price, including a large tilting touchscreen, augmented-reality head-up display and 14-speaker Sony audio
Quiet, comfortable cabin with well-insulated highway cruising and good seat ergonomics
Deepal has shown it will fix early software and driver-assist niggles via over-the-air updates rather than leaving them unresolved
Undercuts the Tesla Model Y and roughly matches the Kia EV5 on list price while offering a longer 7-year vehicle warranty
cons: Bouncy ride quality with excessive body roll in corners, and a poor 11.5m turning circle for a rear-wheel-drive car
Driver-assistance systems (lane-keep, driver monitoring) were criticised as intrusive and overreactive at launch, and remain only partly resolved
Capped-price servicing runs dearer over the ownership period than rivals like the Kia EV5
Slower DC fast-charging than key mid-size EV SUV competitors
As Australia's newest EV brand with no resale history, and evidence of the brand already discounting hard via drive-away deals well below list price, resale value is genuinely unproven

summary: The Mustang Mach-E is a coupe-profiled mid-size electric SUV and Ford Australia's only battery-electric passenger car, updated for 2026 with more power, a standard heat pump and a 15.5-inch portrait touchscreen. Australian reviewers consistently like how it drives — genuinely rear-drive-flavoured, precise steering, strong straight-line pace — and rate the cabin as quiet and upmarket, but they are split on the firm suspension, with CarExpert calling the ride 'far too firm' while CarsGuide found the 2026 retune acceptable. The recurring verdict is that the Select makes the value case and the Premium does not, because Chinese and Korean rivals deliver more space and equipment for less money.
pros: Extended-range Premium claims 600km WLTP from 88kWh usable, further than a Tesla Model Y Long Range RWD or Kia EV6 GT-Line, and Chasing Cars still saw 465km on a highway loop
GT makes 434kW/955Nm for 2026 (up 76kW) and undercuts a Kia EV6 GT on both price and outputs
2026 update adds a standard heat pump across the range, which reduces the cold-weather range penalty
Cheap to service for a $65k-plus EV: 12-month/15,000km intervals at roughly $158 a year, about $790 over five years
Rear-drive chassis is genuinely playful in Untamed mode, with steering CarsGuide described as light yet precise
cons: 402-litre boot is small for the class and the tapered roofline limits what fits, versus 513L in a Kia EV5 and 526L in a Polestar 4 — and the frunk shrank to 49L for 2026 to make room for the heat pump
Not rated to tow anything in Australia (0kg braked), where European Mach-Es are rated to 1000kg and rivals like the EV6 tow 1600kg
Ride is firm to the point of bump-crashiness on suburban roads, and the GT's MagneRide dampers were judged to make it worse rather than better
Real-world efficiency is poor: Chasing Cars averaged about 19kWh/100km and 19.6kWh/100km on the highway against a 17.7kWh/100km claim, which hurts anyone relying on public charging

Electronic door releases with a B-pillar button and no conventional handle, no spare wheel, and no charging cable included; Ford also ran an Australian stop-sale in late 2025 over two door-latch and related recalls

summary: The plug-in hybrid Ranger keeps the hardware that makes the diesel version work — 3500kg braked towing, a full-size dual-cab tub and the same off-road gear — and adds a 6.9kW mains outlet that Australian reviewers rate as its single best feature. The compromise is an 11.8kWh battery: testers here recorded 27-34km of real electric range against Ford's 49km ADR claim, and once it is flat the 2.3-litre petrol drinks 7.0-10.5L/100km. Opinion splits on value: after Ford's mid-2026 repricing to $59,000-$70,000 drive-away it finally undercuts the BYD Shark 6, but that rival still carries roughly triple the battery.
pros: Braked towing stays at 3500kg with a 6580kg gross combination mass, where the BYD Shark 6 PHEV is rated to 2500kg — it is the plug-in ute that can still pull a full-size caravan.
Pro Power Onboard supplies up to 6.9kW of 240V mains from the tub and cabin, which reviewers treat as a genuine replacement for a site generator or a camp setup.
Ford's MY26.5 repricing dropped the range to $59,000-$70,000 drive-away, about $10,000-$14,000 below the 2025 launch prices, and added an XL grade below where the range previously started.
Five years/unlimited km warranty with no condition to service inside the dealer network, an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty, and capped servicing at $399 per visit on 12-month/15,000km intervals.
cons: The 11.8kWh battery is about a third of the BYD Shark 6's, and Australian testers recorded 27-34km of usable electric range against the 49km ADR claim.

AC charging only and capped at 3.5kW — roughly four hours from a wallbox, seven from a household socket, and no DC fast charging — so the economics collapse for anyone who cannot plug in at home overnight.
With the battery depleted, reviewers measured 7.0-10.5L/100km, and 9.3L/100km loaded to GVM, against the 2.9L/100km ADR label; on a long tow it is no cheaper to run than a V6 diesel Ranger.
The battery sits between the rear chassis rails and raises the tub floor about 27-31mm, and Ford advises against fitting an aftermarket tray or canopy — ruling out a standard trade fit-out.
Payload falls from 973kg on the entry grades to about 808kg on the heaviest, so an accessorised plug-in Ranger runs out of GVM well before the diesel does.

summary: The Taikon 5 is the first model from Forthing, a Dongfeng sub-brand distributed in Australia by Ateco, and it landed in June 2026 as the cheapest mid-size electric SUV on sale here. The battery-electric grades share one 150kW front-drive powertrain and a 64.4kWh LFP pack rated at 427km WLTP, so the Luxury-to-Exclusive step buys trim rather than range; a range-extender version of the same body is sold alongside them and is excluded here. No Australian outlet had road-tested it at the research date, and the New Zealand launch reviews that exist split over whether the electric version's softer, less resolved ride is a fair trade for its sharper acceleration and low price.
pros: Cheapest mid-size electric SUV in Australia at launch: $38,990 drive-away for the BEV Luxury, roughly $6,000 under a GAC Aion V Premium and $8,000 under a Leapmotor C10 Style on a comparable drive-away basis
1500kg braked towing on both BEV grades per Forthing's own June 2026 spec sheet, matching a Leapmotor C10 where the similarly priced GAC Aion V has no published towing rating at all
541-litre boot expanding to 1480 litres, against 427/978 litres for a GAC Aion V and 300/1079 litres for a Chery E5

Unconditional seven-year/200,000km vehicle warranty with no dealer-servicing strings, plus an eight-year/200,000km battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent capacity; roadside assistance extends to five years but only if every scheduled service is done at a Forthing service centre

Base Luxury already includes a 14.6-inch screen, wireless CarPlay and Android Auto, 10-way power driver's seat with ventilation and massage, 19-inch alloys, 3.5kW V2L, AEB, adaptive cruise and blind-spot monitoring
cons: Unrated by ANCAP at launch, and the car ships without driver-attention monitoring or e-call, which rules out a five-star result under the current protocol
80kW peak DC charging is slow for the segment, giving 30-80 per cent in about 30 minutes against roughly 24 minutes for 10-80 per cent on a 180kW GAC Aion V
Only 14 Forthing dealers nationally (three in Victoria) and no capped-price servicing programme announced, so servicing costs and resale are entirely unproven
Forthing Australia publishes drive-away pricing only, and the campaign is restricted to new stock vehicles with no options while stock lasts, so there is no published list price for this car anywhere
No energy-consumption figure is published in Australia at all, and the 427km WLTP claim sits 27km above the 400km WLTP figure Forthing quotes for the identical 64.4kWh car in New Zealand

summary: GAC's first small car for Australia undercuts the BYD Dolphin Premium and MG 4 Essence while offering more battery, more power and far more rear legroom than either, and Australian reviewers consistently rate its ride comfort and cabin packaging above its price. The disagreement is over the software and the ownership case: CarExpert and EV Central found the touchscreen-only controls buggy and the driver-assist warnings intrusive, while CarsGuide and Chasing Cars were more forgiving and focused on the value. Everyone flags the same unknowns — a brand with no Australian resale history, roughly 30 dealers, no capped-price servicing and no ANCAP rating yet.
pros: 60kWh (58kWh usable) LFP pack and 430km WLTP range beat the BYD Dolphin Premium's 427km for $1000 less list price
150kW/210Nm and a 7.3-second 0-100km/h make it quicker than every rival under $40,000, including the MG 4 Essence 64
2750mm wheelbase and 905mm of rear legroom give it back-seat space a Toyota Corolla hatch cannot match, despite being 105mm shorter
Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and two years longer than BYD's six or MG's seven
11kW AC charging as standard, against 7kW on the BYD Dolphin
cons: No ANCAP rating as at July 2026 — testing is deferred until the local eCall system goes live, so buyers are taking GAC's five-star target on trust
Climate and audio are buried in the 14.6-inch touchscreen with almost no physical controls, and reviewers report menu lag and outright bugs
87kW DC peak is slow for a 60kWh pack: about 40 minutes for 10-80 per cent, where an MG 4 64 manages a similar job faster
No capped-price servicing programme; GAC quotes $199-$640 a visit at dealer discretion and about $1607 over five years
Roughly 30 dealers nationally and no Australian resale track record, so residual values and parts supply are unproven

summary: The Aion V is the first electric SUV from GAC, which launched in Australia in December 2025, and it undercuts most mid-size rivals while quoting a longer 510km WLTP range than the Geely EX5 or BYD Atto 3. Reviewers rate the cabin quality, quietness and standard equipment highly and find the ride comfortable if unexciting, but consistently criticise the touchscreen-only controls and the intrusive driver-monitoring and speed-sign systems. Both grades share one 150kW front-drive powertrain and a 75.26kWh LFP battery, so the choice between them is purely about trim rather than range or performance.
pros: 510km WLTP range from a 75.26kWh LFP pack, ahead of the Geely EX5 (475km) and BYD Atto 3 (420km) at similar money
180kW DC charging with a claimed 24-minute 10-80 per cent, roughly double the Geely EX5's peak rate
8-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 8-year/200,000km battery warranty for private buyers, longer than BYD's 6 years or Geely's 7 (commercial use drops to 5 years/150,000km)
Heat pump, V2L, panoramic sunroof, surround-view camera and heated/ventilated front seats are standard on the $42,590 base Premium
5-star ANCAP rating (2025 datestamp, valid to December 2031) applying to both grades
cons: No towing rating published in Australia at all, against 1500kg braked for a BYD Sealion 7 or Leapmotor C10
Everything runs through the 14.6-inch touchscreen, with no volume dial and mirror adjustment buried in menus
Driver-monitoring and speed-limit warnings are intrusive and reset to on at every start, a recurring complaint across Australian reviews
Highway consumption climbs past 25kWh/100km against the 16.7kWh/100km WLTP claim, so the 510km figure is urban-biased
Brand-new to Australia with about 19 dealers as at March 2026 and no capped-price servicing scheme, leaving resale and running costs unproven

summary: The EX2 is Geely's second Australian model and its cheapest, a rear-wheel-drive electric light hatch that opened for order in July 2026 at $26,490 before on-road costs. Reviewers rate the packaging highly for the money — 375 litres of boot plus a 70-litre frunk, genuine rear legroom and a cabin that reads above its price — but early drives split on the chassis, with Chasing Cars criticising body control and tyre grip while CarExpert found it agile and fun around town. The bigger caveats are objective: the base car's 252km WLTP range and 14.2-second 0-100km/h, and no ANCAP result at the research date.
pros: Second-cheapest new EV in Australia at $26,490 plus on-road costs, undercut only by the BYD Atto 1 Essential at $23,990
375-litre boot plus a 70-litre frunk beats the Hyundai Inster's 280 litres from a 4,135mm-long body
Rear-wheel drive with multi-link independent rear suspension, rare in a light hatch where the BYD Dolphin and MG 4 Urban rivals are front-drive or pricier
Seven-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with eight years on the high-voltage battery, matching the Geely EX5
Launch offer running 12 July to 31 August 2026 adds a 7kW home charger (installation excluded) and a free premium paint upgrade
cons: The 60kW Complete takes a claimed 14.2 seconds to 100km/h, which reviewers flag as marginal for freeway merging; the 85kW Inspire is still 11.5s
252km WLTP on the Complete is the shortest range of any EV in this price band — the Inspire's 345km costs $4,500 more
DC charging peaks at just 60kW (Complete) and 80kW (Inspire), and AC at 6.6kW, so it is a poor road-trip car
No ANCAP or Euro NCAP crash rating published as at July 2026, unlike the five-star Geely EX5
Chasing Cars' pre-launch drive found poor body control under brakes and through corners plus noisy, low-grip tyres, a criticism CarExpert's short local drive did not reproduce

summary: The EX5 is Geely's first model for the Australian market, a mid-size front-wheel-drive electric SUV pitched on comfort and value below better-known rivals like the Tesla Model Y. Reviewers consistently praise its quiet, cushioned ride and roomy, lounge-like rear seating, but mark it down for a smaller-than-expected boot, touchscreen-only climate controls, and driving dynamics that favour softness over sharpness. A mid-2026 update brought a larger 68.39kWh battery lifting range to 475km (Complete) and 450km (Inspire), addressing the main complaint about the original 2025 launch cars.
pros: Comfortable, well-cushioned ride tuned for Australian roads
Quiet cabin with strong urban energy efficiency
Sharp pricing relative to rivals such as Leapmotor C10 and Tesla Model Y
Spacious, lounge-like rear seat comfort
Long 7-year vehicle / 8-year battery warranty
cons: Boot space (302-410L) trails key rivals like the Leapmotor C10 (581L)
Modest ~100kW DC fast-charging rate
Touchscreen-only controls for climate and headlights are fiddly
No official towing rating in Australia as at mid-2026
Noticeable body roll and 'floaty' suspension feel when driven briskly

summary: The Starray EM-i is Geely's first plug-in hybrid for Australia and undercuts almost every mid-size PHEV SUV on the market, with 83km of WLTP electric range in the $37,490 Complete and 136km in the $41,490 Inspire Extended Range. Australian reviewers agree the powertrain and the equipment list are the reasons to buy it — Chasing Cars measured 5.1L/100km over 5,000km of long-term use and 95km of real electric range — and they agree just as consistently that the chassis and the driver-assist software are not sorted, with CarExpert, carsales and Chasing Cars all describing an under-damped rear end and an adaptive cruise system that cuts speed for no reason. It is a value argument, not a driving one, and it rests on a brand with roughly two years of Australian sales history behind its resale values.
pros: The $41,490 Inspire Extended Range carries a 29.8kWh usable pack for 136km of WLTP electric range — more than double a BYD Sealion 6 Dynamic's 81km and enough to keep most Melbourne commuters off petrol entirely
60kW DC fast charging on the Extended Range (30-80 per cent in a claimed 16 minutes) and 30kW on the Complete, where the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and BYD Sealion 6 offer no DC charging at all

Seven-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus a separate eight-year unlimited-kilometre battery warranty guaranteed to 70 per cent capacity, and capped-price servicing quoted at $1,932 over five years
Five-star ANCAP rating (90 per cent adult occupant, 87 per cent child occupant) and both grades sit more than $35,000 below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold, so no luxury car tax applies either way
Stays genuinely cheap with the battery flat: Chasing Cars recorded 5.1L/100km cumulatively over five months and 5,000km, and 95.2km of real electric range at 14.2kWh/100km on a gentle run
cons: Ride and body control are the consistent complaint: carsales calls the suspension 'far too under damped, especially from the rear' and reports porpoising, Chasing Cars describes 'pogo-like body control' on country roads, and its own long-term test concluded the ride is too soft for Australian speeds

The driver-assist software misbehaves rather than merely nags — carsales recorded the adaptive cruise cutting 30-40km/h for no reason on country roads, and multiple testers report an aggressive lane-keep that adds heavy steering weight and resets at every restart

Charge-sustaining fuel use is real money: with the battery depleted testers recorded roughly 5.9-7.0L/100km (Chasing Cars) and the UK's Auto Express managed 6.6L/100km, so a buyer without home charging is running a 1,730-1,815kg SUV on a 1.5-litre naturally aspirated engine and the plug-in premium never pays back
The 428-litre boot is small for a mid-size SUV — NRMA singles it out as a weakness, it needs the floor removed to reach the quoted 528 litres, and there is no spare wheel, only a repair kit

Geely has sold cars in Australia for about two years and has already run EOFY campaigns at 6 per cent off plus 0.88 per cent finance on the Starray EM-i and EX5, so transaction prices keep resetting and there is no resale record to anchor a residual against

summary: The GV60 is Genesis's E-GMP-based electric SUV, and the 2027 update swaps the old 77.4kWh pack for an 84kWh one while cutting the entry price by roughly $15,000 so the Advanced RWD lands under the luxury car tax threshold. Australian reviewers rate its cabin materials, noise suppression and low-speed ride among the best in the class, but consistently argue it is still priced above what an emerging luxury brand can command against the Hyundai and Kia relatives that share its hardware. The 448kW Magma adds genuine performance-car pace and heads the two-grade range, though it costs $15,000 more than a mechanically similar Ioniq 5 N and neither GV60 grade is rated to tow.
pros: At $88,300 before on-road costs the Advanced RWD sits below the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold, so no LCT is embedded in its price — a roughly $15,000 cut on the superseded Luxury grade
The 84kWh 800V pack claims 561km WLTP in the Advanced and a 10-80 per cent DC charge in 18 minutes on a 350kW charger, with 400V/800V compatibility and V2L

Ownership costs are covered: five years of complimentary scheduled servicing at 15,000km/12-month intervals, roadside assistance for up to 10 years, and an 8-year/160,000km high-voltage battery warranty on top of the 5-year/unlimited-km vehicle cover
CarExpert rates the low-speed ride and suppression of wind, tyre and suspension noise as among the best of any EV, with soft-touch materials almost everywhere in the cabin
The Magma's dual-motor 448kW/740Nm drivetrain (478kW/790Nm in Boost) claims 0-100km/h in 3.4 seconds with an e-LSD, Drift Mode and a simulated gearshift system
cons: Neither grade is rated to tow — both the Advanced RWD and the Magma are listed at 0kg braked, where the superseded AWD grades were rated to 1600kg
432 litres behind the rear seats (400 in the Magma) is small for a mid-size SUV costing $88,000-plus, there is no spare wheel, and no internal V2L socket
The Magma asks $15,000 more than a mechanically near-identical Hyundai Ioniq 5 N, and CarExpert measured 25.6kWh/100km against the 21.5kWh/100km claim — roughly 330km of real-world range
Genesis runs only about nine Australian retail sites, all in NSW, VIC, QLD and WA, with nothing in SA, TAS, ACT or NT, which limits servicing access and thins the used-buyer pool
Body control loosens over bigger compressions on country roads, and CarExpert still judges the Advanced roughly $20,000 too expensive to be competitive against Chinese and Hyundai-group rivals

summary: Australian reviewers rate the Electrified GV70 as one of the most convincingly luxurious mid-size electric SUVs on sale, with a quiet, richly trimmed cabin, 800V charging at up to 350kW and 360kW of dual-motor pace in Boost mode. The trade-off is efficiency and packaging: 462km of WLTP range and a 503-litre boot both trail the Audi Q6 e-tron and BMW iX3 it is priced against, and testers describe the suspension tune as comfortable and quiet but soft rather than sharp. It is sold as a single $132,800 grade at fixed national agency pricing through a retail network of roughly nine sites that reaches only New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland and Western Australia.
pros: Genesis Australia's 5-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is genuinely unconditional — its own terms allow servicing by 'a Genesis outlet, authorised Genesis repairer or suitably qualified motor vehicle repairer' — and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km
Five years or 75,000km of scheduled servicing is included in the purchase price, which few rivals at this price match
800V architecture charges at up to 350kW DC, taking 10-80 per cent in about 19 minutes, and adds 3.6kW vehicle-to-load outlets both inside and outside the car
Rated to tow 1,800kg braked with a 159kg towball limit, and carries a 22-litre front boot for cables on top of the 503-litre rear one
320kW/605Nm rising to 360kW/700Nm in Boost mode gives a 4.4-second 0-100km/h from the only grade offered, with no options list to navigate
cons: 462km of WLTP range and a claimed 20.0kWh/100km both trail the $122,500 Audi Q6 e-tron and the BMW iX3; CarsGuide recorded 21.0kWh/100km on test
The 503-litre boot is the smallest of its named rivals and 39 litres down on the petrol GV70's 542 litres

One grade only at $132,800 with no cheaper entry point — that is above both the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold and the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so novated-lease buyers get no EV FBT exemption

Genesis retails from around nine sites across NSW, Victoria, Queensland and WA only, leaving buyers in South Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory with no local studio for sales or service
Reviewers call the suspension 'spongey in corners' — it prioritises glide over body control, where the German rivals are sharper

summary: Australian reviewers rate the Cannon Alpha PHEV as the most electric-capable dual-cab ute on sale here, pairing a 37.11kWh battery with a class-benchmark 3500kg braked tow rating that no other plug-in ute matches. They are equally unanimous that the 2810kg kerb weight blunts it, leaving a 685kg payload and body control that wallows next to a conventional diesel dual-cab. Verdicts split hard on whether the size and equipment justify the money — CarsGuide scores it 8.5 and calls it a genuine HiLux alternative, Chasing Cars gives it 6.5 for unpredictable throttle response and the full-size spare standing up in the tub — but every reviewer agrees the running-cost case collapses for a buyer who cannot charge at home.
pros: Class-benchmark 3500kg braked towing across both grades, matching a diesel Ford Ranger or Toyota HiLux where most plug-in utes are rated to 2500kg, which is the single reason ute buyers look past a plug-in hybrid

The largest plug-in battery in any Australian ute at 37.11kWh: GWM claims 115km electric-only, though that is quoted on the superseded NEDC cycle and independent testers returned 85-100km from a full charge
7-year/unlimited-km unconditional warranty with no servicing strings attached, plus 8-year/unlimited-km battery cover and $4615 capped-price servicing across those seven years
50kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 24 minutes) is rare on a plug-in ute — the Ford Ranger PHEV is AC-only — and 6kW vehicle-to-load runs site tools off the traction battery
Five-star ANCAP (2024 criteria) and, at $59,990 before on-road costs for the Lux, roughly $12,000 under a Ford Ranger PHEV
cons: The 1.7L/100km label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: GWM's own charge-sustaining number is 7.9L/100km, the NRMA measured 10-11L/100km on the motorway and over 15L/100km towing 2000kg, so a buyer without home charging is running a thirsty 2.8-tonne petrol ute
685kg payload falls well short of the one-tonne rating dual-cab buyers expect, and towing at the full 3500kg drops usable payload to about 435kg to stay inside the 6745kg GCM

Packaging the battery under the floor forces the full-size spare to stand upright in the tub, costing working floor space and fouling tonneau covers — CarsGuide, Chasing Cars and the NRMA all single this out

At 2810kg kerb it carries roughly half a tonne over a diesel dual-cab, and reviewers consistently describe loose body control, numb steering and a driver-monitoring system that is intrusive and hard to switch off

GWM has run repeated national drive-away campaigns on this ute (as low as $57,490 drive-away for the Lux, several thousand under a nominal drive-away price), which is good news at purchase and bad news for resale

summary: The H6 GT is the coupe-roofline sibling of the Haval H6, but its plug-in hybrid is a genuinely different car underneath: a 35.43kWh pack claiming 183km of electric range against the standard H6 PHEV's 19.09kWh and 100-106km, for about $3,500 more. Reviewers agree the EV range and the 321kW/4.6sec Hi4 all-wheel-drive performance are extraordinary at the price, and agree just as consistently that the 392L boot is small for a 4.7m SUV, the brake pedal is poor and the driver-assist calibration is intrusive. The electric range is quoted on NEDC only, and independent tests returned 130-150km, so the claim is best read as an upper bound rather than a number to budget against.
pros: A 35.43kWh ternary-lithium pack claiming 183km of electric range - nearly double the 19.09kWh and 100-106km of the cheaper standard Haval H6 PHEV, and more electric range than any other plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia under $60,000

321kW/642Nm from the second-generation Hi4 dual-motor all-wheel-drive system for a claimed 4.58sec 0-100km/h, quicker than the 268kW standard H6 Ultra PHEV AWD (4.8sec) and well clear of any BYD Sealion 6

DC fast charging at up to 48kW on CCS2 (30-80 per cent in about 26 minutes) plus 6.6kW AC, so the pack can be usefully topped up mid-trip rather than only overnight - most PHEVs in this price bracket cannot DC charge at all

Seven-year/unlimited-km warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus separate eight-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery and five years of roadside assistance and capped-price servicing

GWM is currently advertising the $52,990 list price as a $52,990 national drive-away figure (a $2,000 saving on the $54,990 indicative drive-away), so the on-road costs the calculator adds are in practice being absorbed by the campaign
cons: The coupe roofline costs it real practicality: 392L seats-up and 1390L folded, against 560L/1445L in the standard H6 PHEV and 425L in a BYD Sealion 6, which Chasing Cars called 'piddly for its 4727mm length' - and rear headroom suffers too

The 0.6L/100km combined-cycle label is meaningless once the battery is flat: Australian testers recorded about 5.0L/100km (CarsGuide), 5.4L/100km (RACQ and Chasing Cars) and 6.0L/100km (EV Central), with Chasing Cars seeing 9.5L/100km at motorway speed, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is worse off than in a conventional hybrid

Electric range is quoted on the NEDC cycle only - no WLTP figure has ever been published for this car, CarsGuide recorded the WLTP rating as still pending at launch - and real-world tests returned 130-140km (EV Central) and about 150km (Chasing Cars) against the 180-183km claim

At 2045-2075kg it carries roughly 450kg more than the petrol H6 GT, there is no spare wheel on the PHEV (a repair kit only, because the rear motor takes the space), and reviewers are unanimous about the spongy brake pedal - the NRMA called it 'one of the worst brake pedal actions in recent memory'

Pricing has fallen three times since launch, from $55,990 drive-away in Q1 2025 to $53,990 and now $52,990, which is good for a buyer today but is documented evidence that resale values will be dragged down by the next campaign

summary: The plug-in Haval H6 undercuts almost every mid-size PHEV rival while claiming 100-106km of electric range and a 560L boot, and the mid-2025 update added Australian-signed-off suspension tuning that reviewers agree fixed the previous car's biggest flaw. Testers are consistent that the powertrain is smooth and genuinely quick in 268kW Hi4 all-wheel-drive form, and equally consistent that the driver-assist and stability-control calibration still needs work. Its case rests on being charged nightly: with a flat battery it uses 5.4-6.7L/100km in Australian testing, which is no better than the cheaper non-plug-in H6 Hybrid.
pros: Claims 106km of electric range (2WD) from a 19.09kWh LFP pack for $43,490 list - more than the $42,990 BYD Sealion 6 Essential's 92km, and enough that most Melbourne commuters would rarely start the engine
560L boot seats-up and 1445L folded, versus 425L in the BYD Sealion 6, and the floor-mounted pack costs it nothing against the petrol H6's seats-up figure
Seven-year/unlimited-km warranty with no dealer-servicing condition attached, plus separate eight-year/unlimited-km cover on the drive battery, against BYD's six years
DC fast charging at up to 34kW (30-80 per cent in under 30 minutes) is rare in a sub-$50,000 plug-in hybrid, so the battery can be topped up on a trip rather than only overnight
The $49,490 Ultra PHEV AWD's Hi4 dual-motor system makes 268kW/760Nm for a claimed 4.8sec 0-100km/h, quicker than any Sealion 6, and tows 1500kg braked
cons: The 1.0-1.1L/100km ADR label figure is meaningless once the battery is flat: Australian testers recorded 5.4L/100km (carsales), 5.8L/100km (Chasing Cars) and 6.2-6.7L/100km (CarExpert, CarsGuide), so a buyer without home charging is worse off than in the cheaper H6 Hybrid at 5.2L/100km
Electric range is quoted on the NEDC-derived ADR 81/02 cycle and no WLTP figure is published, and independent tests returned 89km (Chasing Cars) and 95.8km (carsales) against the 100-106km claim
Reviewers repeatedly flag the safety-system calibration: over-eager lane-keeping, and traction and stability control that carsales found cuts power abruptly in the wet
No spare wheel on any PHEV variant - a repair kit only - and kerb weight climbs to about 1980kg in Hi4 AWD form, roughly 250kg above the petrol H6

GWM sells almost exclusively on capped drive-away campaigns (the $43,490 Lux PHEV has been advertised at $40,990-$44,990 drive-away with a free wall charger), which supports the transaction price but not the resale value

summary: The Ora 5 is GWM's replacement for the axed Ora hatch: a 4.47m front-drive electric small SUV sold here in two grades, both with the same 150kW motor and 58.3kWh LFP battery. Reviewers agree it is a lot of electric car for the money and unusually quiet at highway speed, and note the rare inclusion of a space-saver spare, but they split sharply on the suspension, which CarExpert calls too firm and Chasing Cars calls floaty yet busy. The consistent criticisms are over-eager driver-monitoring alerts, a touchscreen that swallows the regen and drive-mode controls, and a claimed efficiency figure real-world testing does not reach.
pros: 435km WLTC range from a 58.3kWh usable battery for an under-$35,000 list price, against 345km for the BYD Atto 2 it is aimed at
Seven-year unlimited-kilometre warranty (eight on the battery) with capped-price servicing at $195 a visit, $1,365 across the seven years
Carries a space-saver spare wheel, still uncommon in this class, plus 6kW vehicle-to-load and 120kW DC charging for 10-80% in about 30 minutes
362-litre boot expanding to 1,060 litres with the 60/40 rear seats folded, and a 750kg braked tow rating where the MG 4 manages 500kg and the BYD Dolphin none at all

Both grades ride on the same 18-inch wheels and battery, so the $3,000 step to Ultra buys equipment (panoramic roof, powered tailgate, heated and ventilated seats, dual-zone climate) without costing range
cons: The claimed 15.5kWh/100km is optimistic: CarExpert observed about 18kWh/100km in mixed driving, which cuts real range to roughly 325km
Driver-monitoring and seatbelt warnings misfire repeatedly, and regenerative braking strength is adjustable only through the 14.6-inch touchscreen with almost no physical controls
Ride quality is the main point of reviewer disagreement - firm and bump-sensitive to CarExpert, floaty with mild rear-end instability at speed to Chasing Cars - and neither rates it as settled
Unrated by ANCAP at the time of writing, with testing still under way

GWM publishes no list price at all - only a Victorian drive-away figure ($33,990 Lux, $36,990 Ultra) - so the list prices shown here are backed out of those figures and are estimates, not sourced numbers; the outgoing Ora hatch it replaces was also withdrawn after weak local sales, so expect softer resale than a BYD or MG equivalent

summary: The Elexio is Hyundai's China-built mid-size electric SUV, mechanically close to the Kia EV5 but sold only as a single 160kW front-driver on an 88.1kWh LFP pack in two grades, $58,990 and $61,990 before on-road costs. Australian reviewers consistently rate its locally tuned ride and steering above the EV5's, and the 562km/546km WLTP claims are among the longest at the price, but they are equally consistent that the 38-minute 10-80% DC charge and the button-free 27-inch screen are the weak points. Where opinion splits is value: some call it well-priced against a Tesla Model Y, others note a BYD Sealion 7 or Geely EX5 does the same job for less, which is why Hyundai has been running drive-away campaigns since launch.
pros: 562km WLTP on the base grade's 18-inch wheels and 546km on the Elite's 20s, longer than the Kia EV5 Air Long Range's 555km claim from the same 88.1kWh pack
Australian-tuned suspension: Chasing Cars and CarExpert both rate its body control and highway composure clearly above the mechanically related Kia EV5
506L boot expanding to 1,540L, 1,250kg braked towing and a 4kW three-pin V2L outlet, so it tows and camps like the EV5 rather than a Kona Electric (rated 0kg)
24-month/30,000km service intervals with capped-price servicing quoted at about $1,897 over four years, roughly $475 a year

Warranty is 5 years/unlimited km unconditionally, extending to 7 years/unlimited km only if every scheduled service is completed within the Hyundai dealer network; the high-voltage battery is covered 8 years/160,000km either way
cons: 400V architecture peaking at 150kW takes 38 minutes for 10-80%, against roughly half that in Hyundai's own 800V Ioniq 5, and AC charging is capped at 10kW
Tested consumption runs 20-20.8kWh/100km against the 18.2kWh/100km ADR/WLTP claim, and Chasing Cars measured a real-world 424km rather than the Elite's 546km
27-inch screen with no physical switchgear for climate or drive modes, and reviewers report the head-up display disappears behind polarised sunglasses
Front-wheel drive only at 160kW/310Nm and 8.9s to 100km/h, with no AWD grade to answer the Kia EV5 Earth or GT-Line
No spare wheel, tyre mobility kit only, and Hyundai was already discounting to $55,990/$59,990 drive-away within months of launch, which points to soft early resale

summary: Australian reviewers consistently praise the Inster's cleverly packaged, unexpectedly roomy cabin and its agile, fun-to-drive character in city conditions, with several noting it feels bigger inside than its tiny footprint suggests. The main point of criticism across CarsGuide, Zecar and Carscoops is value: at its current pricing the Inster sits noticeably above key budget-EV rivals like the BYD Dolphin and GWM Ora, undercutting its case as an affordable city runabout. Interior plastics are widely described as hard and budget-grade, and the rear bench is limited to two occupants rather than three.
pros: Cleverly packaged, surprisingly spacious cabin for such a small footprint, helped by sliding and fully-folding rear seats
Agile, easy-to-park city manners with light, precise steering
Distinctive, likeable styling that reviewers describe as fun and characterful
Extended Range and Cross variants add usefully more range and ground clearance over the entry Standard Range
cons: Priced noticeably higher than key budget-EV rivals such as the BYD Dolphin and GWM Ora, undermining its value case
Rear seating limited to four occupants in total, with only two rear seatbelts rather than three
Hard, budget-feeling interior plastics and no wireless Apple CarPlay/Android Auto
Standard Range's real-world range is modest for anything beyond city and inner-suburban driving

summary: Australian reviewers consistently rate the Ioniq 5 as one of the most complete mid-size electric SUVs on sale, praising its distinctive retro-futuristic styling, spacious and flexible cabin, and quick 800V DC charging. Ride comfort has improved with recent updates and is composed around town, though some testers still find body control loosens up over undulating country roads. The Ioniq 5 N adds genuine sports-car pace and track ability while retaining the practicality of the donor SUV, making it a standout among performance EVs, albeit at a steep price premium.
pros: Distinctive, spacious interior with a flat floor and sliding rear seats
Fast 800V charging architecture supports rapid top-ups on road trips
Comfortable, grown-up highway ride with low wind and tyre noise
Ioniq 5 N offers genuine performance-car dynamics in a practical SUV body
cons: Body control can feel loose and float-y over undulating roads at speed
Real-world efficiency trails some rivals, particularly on the AWD and N variants
Boot space is only average for the class
N Line Premium and N variants push well into luxury-car pricing territory

summary: The Ioniq 6 is now a one-model range in Australia: Hyundai withdrew the standard Dynamiq and Epiq grades in the first half of 2026 after selling only 1,214 cars locally, and has not confirmed local timing for the facelifted non-N versions, leaving the 478kW Ioniq 6 N as the only variant you can order. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous that the N is the most convincing electric performance car at the price, rating its steering feel and rear-biased balance above the heavier Ioniq 5 N. They part company on liveability: Chasing Cars calls the ride quality excellent, while CarExpert found the damping harsh over sharp edges even in its softest setting, and all note the 371-litre boot and tight rear headroom make it the least practical N.
pros: 478kW/770Nm with N Grin Boost and 0-100km/h in 3.2 seconds undercuts a BMW M3 ($169,100) and Mercedes-AMG C63 ($187,900) by more than $50,000
487km WLTP range plus 800V charging at 10-80 per cent in 18 minutes makes it genuinely usable between track days, unlike most sub-$150k performance EVs
N e-Shift simulated eight-speed and N Drift Optimiser give real driver involvement; CarExpert and Chasing Cars both rate its handling above the Ioniq 5 N
Warranty runs 7 years/unlimited km and explicitly covers non-competitive track use, with capped-price servicing around $1,312 over five years on 24-month/30,000km intervals
cons: 371-litre boot behind a structural brace, no frunk and a separate bootlid rather than a liftback - well short of a 524-litre Toyota Camry, and less usable than the Ioniq 5 N
CarExpert recorded 22.0kWh/100km against the 18.7kWh/100km claim, cutting real touring range to roughly 380km on a 2166kg kerb weight
Suspension transmits sharp edges and potholes into the cabin even on the softest damper setting, and rear headroom is a problem for anyone over about 190cm
At $115,000 before on-road costs it sits well above the $91,661 fuel-efficient threshold, so it cannot be novated FBT-exempt the way an $80,900 Tesla Model 3 Performance can

Hyundai has pulled every standard Ioniq 6 grade from sale in Australia, so there is no cheaper version to step down to and resale is exposed to an orphaned nameplate that was recently discounted by up to $34,142

summary: Hyundai sells its three-row electric SUV in Australia as a single loaded Calligraphy grade, and reviewers agree it is the most convincing long-distance family EV on the market — 600km WLTP, 233kW DC charging and a third row adults actually fit in. The disagreement is entirely about price and polish: at $119,750 before on-roads it is the dearest car Hyundai has ever sold here, several thousand above a comparably equipped Kia EV9, and testers split over whether the firm 21-inch ride and a cabin borrowed from much cheaper Hyundais justify it. Real-world efficiency reports vary widely, from about 12.7kWh/100km around town to 23.4kWh/100km on country touring.
pros: 600km WLTP range from the 110.3kWh pack is the longest claim of any three-row EV sold here — about 80km more than a Kia EV9 Earth and 95km more than an EV9 GT-Line
800V E-GMP charging takes 10-80 per cent in about 24 minutes, and Australian testers have measured over 200kW against the 233kW peak
Rated to tow 2500kg braked with trailer pre-wiring and Trailer Stability Assist standard, matching the EV9 and beating most large EVs
Third row seats adults rather than children — a 175cm CarsGuide tester fit comfortably — with its own climate zone, reclining backrests and USB-C outlets
One grade means no upselling: Nappa leather, 14-speaker Bose, heat pump, head-up display, surround-view and Highway Driving Assist 2 are all standard
cons: At $119,750 plus on-road costs it clears both the $75,000 and $91,661 FBT caps, so there is no novated-lease exemption, and a Kia EV9 Earth covers the same brief for $13,250 less

Hyundai's unconditional cover is five years/unlimited km — the advertised seven years lapses unless every service is done inside the Hyundai dealer network, where Kia's seven years has no such condition
Only one battery and one drivetrain are offered, with no cheaper rear-drive entry point; the six-seat layout ($2,000) and digital side mirrors ($3,000) are options, not lower-priced grades
338 litres behind the third row is modest for a 5.06m, 2.7-tonne vehicle, and there is no spare wheel at any price — only a tyre mobility kit

summary: Australian reviewers see the Kona Electric as a competent, easy-to-live-with small SUV with genuinely spacious packaging and a comfortable, relaxed ride around town, backed by Hyundai's dealer network. The Extended Range base grade is widely rated the pick of the range as strong value, while the Standard Range's real-world range and slow 100kW charging are seen as behind newer rivals, and the step up to Premium is questioned as not clearly worth the extra outlay. Recent price cuts of roughly $8,000 across the range have sharpened its position against cheaper Chinese EVs without changing the fundamental verdict: a sound, unexciting choice rather than a class leader.
pros: Spacious, well-packaged interior for the class, with strong rear legroom and a rare space-saver spare wheel
Comfortable, well-damped ride that soaks up potholes and speed bumps around town
Easy-to-use dual-screen infotainment with thoughtful right-hand-drive ergonomics
Extended Range grade seen by reviewers as strong value following 2026 price cuts, undercutting the Premium by around $10,000 for similar underlying capability
cons: Standard Range's real-world range (around 350km) looks light for a modern EV, especially for interstate trips
100kW DC fast-charging trails newer 800V rivals and is described by reviewers as not great for the segment
Chassis gets bouncy and less composed at highway speed or when pushed harder
Premium trim's price premium over Extended Range is questioned as not clearly justified by the added equipment

summary: The Jaecoo J5 EV is the battery-electric member of Chery's Jaecoo J5 small-SUV line, sold in Australia in a single fully-loaded EV Summit grade alongside separate petrol and hybrid J5s that share the body but not the drivetrain. Australian reviewers rate it as one of the cheapest ways into a well-equipped electric SUV, praising the 130kW DC charging, the eight-year warranty and a $1,520 eight-year servicing bill, while splitting sharply over how it drives. Testers who liked the neutral suspension tune still found real-world consumption in the mid-to-high teens, which puts genuine range nearer 350km than the 402km WLTP claim.
pros: Cheapest end of the electric small-SUV class at $35,990 before on-road costs, and Jaecoo has run a flat $36,990 national drive-away offer continuously since launch — which is around $1,400 less than the Victorian on-roads would otherwise cost
130kW DC peak charging and 10.3kW three-phase AC, both well ahead of the 80kW-class Chery E5 it shares a 58.9kWh LFP pack with

Eight-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty and a separate eight-year unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty, with eight years of capped-price servicing totalling $1,520; roadside assistance also runs to eight years but only if renewed at each scheduled service at an authorised Jaecoo dealer
Rated to tow 1,250kg braked on the manufacturer's own spec sheet — double the 750kg most cheap Chinese electric SUVs, including the Chery E5, BYD Atto 2 and GWM Ora 5, are limited to

Unusually complete equipment for the money: powered and heated/ventilated front seats, 360-degree camera, powered tailgate, glass roof, 50W wireless charging and a 13.2-inch screen, all standard on the only grade
cons: Real-world consumption of mid-to-high teens kWh/100km against a 14.3kWh/100km claim leaves usable range around 350km, roughly 50km short of the WLTP figure

Front-drive chassis struggles to deploy 155kW/288Nm: reviewers report wheelspin and pronounced torque steer under moderate throttle, plus very light steering and an inconsistent brake pedal with a delay in the regenerative blending

Ride is criticised as sharp over coarse or broken bitumen despite the otherwise neutral tune, and the 235/55 R18 tyres carry a repair kit rather than a spare — the closely related Chery E5 gets a spare
No ANCAP rating as at July 2026; Jaecoo says it expects five stars but the car is untested, unlike the BYD Atto 2 and Kia EV3 it is cross-shopped against
Jaecoo is a 2025-vintage nameplate in Australia with no resale, parts or reliability record, and the permanent drive-away discounting works against used values
