summary: The J7 SHS is Chery's Jaecoo sub-brand undercutting the plug-in hybrid mid-size SUV class on equipment-per-dollar, and Australian reviewers are near-unanimous that the powertrain is the best part of the car: 90km of WLTP electric range from an 18.3kWh battery, a claimed 1200km combined range and an eight-year unlimited-kilometre warranty that carries no dealer-servicing condition. Where they disagree is the chassis — CarExpert and EV Central call the ride acceptable for the money, while CarsGuide, carsales and Chasing Cars mark it down for numb steering, loose body control and a fidgety, noisy ride on coarse Australian surfaces. Nobody rates it class-leading to drive, and the 340-litre boot, the missing braked tow rating and a service network of roughly 50 sites are the recurring practical objections.
pros: 90km of WLTP electric-only range from the 18.3kWh LFP battery — more than the BYD Sealion 6 Premium AWD's 81km and enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute on electricity alone

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty with no compulsory dealer-servicing condition, plus a separate eight-year unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent residual capacity — longer than BYD's 6-year and MG's 7-year cover
The petrol engine drives the front wheels directly in parallel mode as well as running as a generator in series mode, so highway efficiency does not collapse the way it does in a range-extender
40kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 20 minutes) is unusual at this price — the Sealion 6 and Outlander PHEV have no DC capability at all
Five-star ANCAP rating from 2025 testing, and both SHS grades sit far below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold so no luxury car tax applies
cons: 340-litre boot (to the cargo cover) is well down on the 424 litres of the front-drive petrol J7 and the 425 litres of a BYD Sealion 6 — the direct cost of packaging the battery — and the SHS is the only J7 with no spare wheel

Jaecoo quotes 5.9L/100km once the battery is depleted, not the 1.0L/100km combined label figure, and carsales measured about 6.0L/100km in charge-sustaining running with 8-9L/100km on the motorway, so the running-cost case largely evaporates for a buyer who cannot charge at home
No braked towing rating at all on the SHS (750kg unbraked only), where the petrol J7 is rated to 1350kg braked and a Sealion 6 Premium AWD tows 1300kg

Reviewers consistently criticise the steering as disconnected and artificial, the body control as loose when pushed and the ride as fidgety and noisy on coarse-chip roads, with abrupt regenerative braking and hesitant low-speed throttle response

Jaecoo launched in Australia in 2025 with about 50 service locations nationally and has already run repeated $3000 factory bonuses and cashback offers, so resale value is unproven and the transaction price keeps resetting

summary: The J8 SHS Summit is Jaecoo's flagship and its first car above $50,000: a single $59,990 seven-seat plug-in hybrid with a 34.5kWh battery, 315kW/580Nm from a 1.5-litre turbo and three motors, and a 70-litre tank that stretches combined range past 1,100km. Australian reviewers agree the equipment list and the electric range are extraordinary for the money — CarExpert measured 124km on a charge against a 134km WLTP figure — and equally agree the chassis is the weak point, describing a floaty, under-damped ride, heavy body roll and steering with no meaningful feel, none of it locally tuned. The third row is the other consistent objection: it is a 5+2 with no airbag coverage, no ISOFIX and roadside-only access, where the BYD Sealion 8 gives you all three.
pros: 134km of WLTP electric range from a 34.5kWh usable battery — roughly double the BYD Sealion 8's electric range and enough that most owners will only burn petrol on trips, with CarExpert observing 124km from a full charge in Australian conditions

70kW DC fast charging plus 6.6kW AC, where the BYD Sealion 8, Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and Mazda CX-80 PHEV have no DC capability at all, so a mid-trip top-up takes about 25 minutes rather than an overnight plug-in

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with no dealer-servicing exclusivity condition, matched by an eight-year unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty guaranteeing 70 per cent residual capacity, and eight years of capped-price servicing averaging about $485 a year

315kW/580Nm and a claimed 5.8-second 0-100km/h make it quicker than a Sealion 8 Premium AWD while towing 1600kg braked, and at $59,990 it sits $24,000 below the fuel-efficient LCT threshold so no luxury car tax applies
2021 litres of cargo space with both rear rows folded, and a 738-litre load bay with just the third row down — genuinely van-like for a $60,000 seven-seater
cons: Only 200 litres behind the third row when all seven seats are in use — less than a Toyota Corolla's boot, and well down on the Sealion 8's 270 litres, so it cannot carry seven people and their luggage

The 1.2L/100km ADR combined label is meaningless as a running cost: CarExpert measured 6.6L/100km once the battery was flat and closer to 10L/100km in stop-start city driving, so a buyer without home charging is running a 2275kg SUV on a 1.5-litre engine at large-petrol-SUV consumption

Reviewers are unanimous on the chassis — CarsGuide calls the ride wallowy and floaty with excessive bounce over speed bumps, carsales criticises the body roll, vague steering and poor bump absorption, and EV Central found the steering too light for anything but town work; there is no Australian suspension tuning

The third row has no airbag coverage and no child-seat anchor points, headroom suits nobody taller than an average 10-year-old, and the single-fold middle seat is on the traffic side rather than the kerb side — the Sealion 8 offers third-row ISOFIX and dedicated rear climate controls

Jaecoo's electric range is quoted only as 169km NEDC in Australia, with no local WLTP homologation published; the 134km figure here comes from the identical UK-market Jaecoo 8 SHS-P, and the brand's Australian resale record above $50,000 is entirely unproven

summary: The Avenger is Jeep's first battery-electric model and its only small SUV in Australia, sold here in three front-wheel-drive grades sharing a 115kW motor and a 51kWh usable battery. Australian reviewers consistently rate it one of the better-driving cars Jeep has produced, and its light 1520kg kerb weight makes it genuinely efficient, but the same reviewers call the pricing hard to justify against Chinese and Korean rivals and single out a three-star crash rating, a bare rear seat and cheap cabin plastics. Opinion splits on whether the Jeep character and 200mm of ground clearance offset a spec sheet that a Kia EV3 or Skoda Elroq beats on range, space and safety for similar money.
pros: Efficient for a high-riding SUV: 51kWh usable stretches to 396km WLTP at a claimed 15.6kWh/100km, and Australian testers recorded 14.3kWh/100km in mixed driving — better than the claim.
Lightest car in its class at 1520kg, more than 200kg under a BYD Atto 3, which is why it matches rivals' range on a much smaller battery and why reviewers praise its steering and body control.
Genuinely more capable off-sealed-road than its rivals: 200mm of ground clearance, selectable terrain modes and hill descent control, none of which a Volvo EX30 or Kia EV3 offers.
Cheap and predictable to maintain: servicing is capped at $250 per visit at 12-month/12,500km intervals, with roadside assistance renewed for life while it is serviced through the Jeep network.
Slow sales have made it heavily negotiable — Jeep Australia has run the Longitude at $40,000 drive-away with premium paint included, roughly $16,000 below the equivalent of its $49,990 list price.
cons: Three-star ANCAP rating (shared with Euro NCAP, 2023): 59 per cent for vulnerable road user protection and 53 per cent for safety assist, with no child presence detection, against five stars for the Volvo EX30, Kia EV3 and Skoda Elroq.

Rear seat and boot are the weakest part of the car: 355L behind the second row versus 470L in a Skoda Elroq, no rear air vents, no centre armrest and no rear door pockets, so it suits couples rather than families.
Only 115kW and 260Nm for about nine seconds to 100km/h, and reviewers repeatedly criticise over-light steering and brakes that give dead travel and then bite too hard.

Ownership risk is real: Jeep Australia is down to three models with a shrinking dealer network, the Avenger sold just 92 cars here in 2025, the five-year warranty is capped at 100,000km, and $16,000 discounts point to poor resale.

summary: The Musso EV is the first genuinely affordable battery-electric dual-cab sold in Australia, landing from $60,000 drive-away against the $92,990-plus LDV eT60, and Australian reviewers agree it drives far better than any ladder-frame ute because it is a monocoque with independent rear suspension rather than a converted diesel. That same architecture is the catch: braked towing stops at 1800kg where the Ranger PHEV and GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV both manage 3500kg, ground clearance is 181mm, and there is no low range, so reviewers read it as a tradie's or fleet runabout rather than a tow vehicle. Opinion splits on whether the money is well spent - CarsGuide scored it 7.4/10 and praised the SUV-like ride, while CarExpert found the interior hollower than the diesel Musso's and the performance short of its 152kW/339Nm claim.
pros: Cheapest electric ute in Australia by a wide margin: $60,000 drive-away for the 2WD against $92,990 before on-roads for the LDV eT60, and it is line-ball with the petrol-burning BYD Shark 6 and Ford Ranger PHEV rather than carrying an EV premium
905kg payload on the 2WD (805kg AWD) beats the BYD Shark 6's 790kg and the GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV's 685kg, and the self-levelling rear shocks keep it sitting flat when loaded
Capped-price servicing totals $1,996 over seven years/140,000km - about $285 a year, roughly half what a diesel dual-cab costs to maintain

KGM's seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional (you may service outside the dealer network if you keep the invoices) and the high-voltage battery is covered for 10 years/unlimited kilometres; only the extra roadside assistance is conditional on servicing at a KGM dealer

Reviewers consistently rate the ride and steering above every ladder-frame rival - the monocoque body, McPherson-strut front and multi-link rear make it quiet and composed on broken Melbourne roads in a way a leaf-sprung HiLux is not
cons: 1800kg braked towing and a 180kg towball limit, against the 3500kg that the Ford Ranger PHEV, GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV and every mainstream diesel dual-cab offer - a 2.0-tonne caravan or a car trailer is simply out of the question
No ANCAP or Euro NCAP rating at all, so a fleet or salary-packaging buyer with a five-star purchasing policy cannot order one despite the eight airbags and full driver-assist suite

Not a genuine off-roader: 181mm of ground clearance (34mm less than the diesel Musso), no low-range transfer case, the battery pack slung under the body, and the tub is about 200mm shorter than a Ranger's

KGM sold 4116 cars in Australia in 2025, down 23.7 per cent, and the only precedent for an electric ute here - the LDV eT60 - is trading around 40-50 per cent of its new price after two to three years, so residual risk on this body style is real and unproven

KGM publishes drive-away pricing only and no list price, and CarExpert's tester recorded 21kWh/100km against the AWD's 26kWh/100km claim while CarsGuide saw 20kWh/100km urban against the 2WD's 23kWh/100km - useful in practice, but it means the official numbers cannot be taken at face value either way

summary: KGM's first electric SUV for Australia arrives as a single fully-equipped front-drive grade carrying the largest battery in its price class - 80.6kWh of BYD LFP Blade - but Australian reviewers agree that battery buys less range than it should, with a 462km WLTP claim that trails the smaller-batteried Geely EX5 and testers recording between 18.2 and 21.7kWh/100km. Where they part company is whether the fundamentals compensate: CarsGuide scored it 7.1/10 for interfaces that simply work and a genuinely roomy cabin, while CarExpert and The Driven both flagged missing equipment for the money and 339Nm regularly overwhelming the front tyres. The counterweight is running cost - $2,114 of capped-price servicing over seven years and an unconditional seven-year warranty - set against no ANCAP rating at all and just 168 Torres of any kind sold in Australia across the whole first half of 2025.
pros: Capped-price servicing totals $2,114 over seven years/140,000km (about $302 a year) with a complimentary first service inside six months or 5,000km, and KGM's seven-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional - you may service outside the KGM dealer network provided you keep records proving the work met KGM's specification - while the BYD Blade pack carries a separate 10-year/unlimited-kilometre warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent state of health

The 80.6kWh battery is the biggest in the sub-$60,000 mid-size electric SUV class - Geely EX5 68.4kWh, MG S5 62kWh, BYD Atto 3 60.5kWh - and it supports 3.5kW vehicle-to-load, 120-130kW DC charging (10-80 per cent in about 37 minutes) and 10.5kW three-phase AC
1,500kg braked towing where the Geely EX5 is not rated to tow at all and the MG S5 and BYD Atto 3 stop at 750kg, plus a 465-litre boot that opens out to 1,526 litres with the rear seats folded

One grade, no options list to navigate and no cheaper trim that deletes equipment: 18-inch alloys, powered sunroof, twin 12.3-inch screens, synthetic leather, heated and ventilated front seats, 360-degree camera, eight airbags and full driver-assist including lane centring and junction-assist AEB are all standard

A $5,010 factory bonus off the recommended retail price was running at the research date, taking the car to $53,690 drive-away with metallic paint included - available for a limited time and while stocks last, so it is a buying-window discount rather than a permanent repositioning
cons: 462km WLTP from 80.6kWh is the weakest efficiency in the class - the Geely EX5 gets 475km from 68.4kWh - and CarExpert measured 21.7kWh/100km against the 18.7kWh/100km claim; worse, 462km is the identical figure KGM published for the superseded 73.4kWh pack while Europe rates the 80.6kWh car at 503km, so the Australian range claim may simply be a carried-over number

No ANCAP rating at all, and no KGM or SsangYong model is ANCAP-rated, so a fleet or salary-packaging buyer with a five-star purchasing policy cannot order one despite the eight airbags and full driver-assist suite

Front-wheel drive only with no AWD option offered, and CarsGuide, CarExpert and The Driven independently report the 339Nm overwhelming the front Nexen tyres off the line, with regenerative braking that feels inconsistent

KGM sold 168 Torres in the first half of 2025 against 24,034 Toyota RAV4s, and the brand's total 2025 Australian volume of 4,116 was down 23.7 per cent - thin dealer coverage, and a $5,010 factory bonus on new stock pushes used values down further; CarsGuide's own verdict is that rivals come 'from brands that might hold their value better'

No spare wheel (a repair kit only), climate control is touchscreen-only so you must leave CarPlay to change the temperature, and there is no built-in navigation, no wireless phone mirroring and no wireless charging pad - a cable is mandatory

summary: Kia's compact electric SUV pairs a genuinely spacious, well-finished cabin with suspension tuning that Australian reviewers rate as composed and comfortable over rough surfaces. Entry Air variants are seen as strong value under $50k with usable real-world range, but the flagship GT-Line drifts close to $70,000 on-road, where reviewers feel it should offer more standard safety kit such as a surround-view camera.
pros: Locally tuned ride soaks up broken Melbourne road surfaces while staying composed at highway speed
Roomy, well-packaged cabin and a genuinely usable 460L boot (1250L seats folded) for a compact SUV
Air Long Range offers a genuinely long 604km WLTP claim while still pricing under $55,000
Five-star ANCAP rating and Kia's 7-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty (7yr/150,000km battery)
cons: GT-Line pricing approaches $70,000 drive-away yet still lacks a surround-view camera
Noticeable road and wind noise intrude at highway speeds on all variants
Modest DC fast-charging speeds mean longer top-up stops on road trips than key rivals
Entry Air Standard Range is rated to tow just 500kg braked, well below the 1000kg of Long Range variants

summary: Kia's first electric sedan takes the EV3's E-GMP hardware and wraps it in a low, long four-door body, arriving at $49,990 before on-roads to sit just under the cheapest Tesla Model 3. Australian reviewers are near-unanimous on the ride and steering — several rate the chassis above cars costing far more — and on the frugality, with independent testing returning under 14kWh/100km. Where they part company is value: the Air is criticised as sparsely equipped and plasticky for the money, and the 612km battery cannot be had below $59,190 because there is no Air Long Range.
pros: Air Standard Range lists at $49,990 before on-road costs, $4910 under the cheapest Tesla Model 3 and level with a BYD Seal
Long Range grades claim 612km WLTP from 81.4kWh, and testers recorded 13.7-13.9kWh/100km in the real world — better than the 14.9 claim
Ride and steering are the review consensus high point; CarExpert rated the passive damping better resolved than many luxury cars
Kia's 7-year/unlimited-km warranty is unconditional (no dealer-servicing strings), and 7 years of capped-price servicing totals $1929
490L boot opening out to 1435L with the rear seats folded, and 1000kg braked towing on both Long Range grades
cons: 400V architecture peaks near 128kW, so a 10-80% DC stop takes about 31 minutes — well behind the 800V Ioniq 6 and EV6
Headroom is tight in both rows: a 185cm-plus reviewer sat close to the roof front and rear, a consequence of the low sedan roofline
No Air Long Range on the Australian price list, so the 612km battery costs a $9200 jump to the $59,190 Earth
Blind Spot View Monitor and the surround-view camera are GT-Line only, and the Air also goes without powered front seats or wireless phone charging
Reviewers flag hard plastics and a 150kW front-drive powertrain (7.4-7.8sec to 100km/h) that runs out of puff on uphill highway overtakes

summary: Kia's China-built mid-size electric SUV has become one of Australia's best-selling EVs on the strength of space and familiarity: a 513L boot plus a 67L frunk, a conventional dashboard with real climate buttons, and ride comfort Australian reviewers rate highly over broken suburban roads. The trade-off critics keep returning to is charging and range, because the 400V architecture caps DC fast-charging at 140kW and long-term testers get about 424km from the 470km-claimed GT-Line. Reviewers broadly agree the Air grades are the value pick, and split on whether the $71,770 GT-Line's hard-plastic cabin justifies the money against a Tesla Model Y Long Range.
pros: 513L boot (1714L seats folded) plus a 67L frunk, one of the largest load bays among mid-size EVs and roomier than a Tesla Model Y
Air Long Range claims 555km WLTP for $61,170 before on-roads, undercutting the Model Y Long Range AWD while adding standard equipment
Keeps a separate physical climate-control panel and a conventional dash layout instead of burying HVAC in the touchscreen
Five-star ANCAP rating plus Kia's 7-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty and 7-year/150,000km battery warranty
CarExpert recorded about 17.0kWh/100km in the Air Standard Range and 18-20kWh/100km in the Earth AWD, better than the WLTP claims
cons: 400V architecture caps DC charging at 140kW, and only about 102kW on the Air Standard Range, so 10-80% takes roughly 38 minutes against about half that in a Kia EV6
CarsGuide's GT-Line long-termer averaged 19.8kWh/100km over 932km for a real 424km against the 470km WLTP claim, and carsales saw 23-25kWh/100km in the Earth AWD
Cabin uses a lot of hard plastic that reviewers call low-rent at $70,000, and the climate display is partly obscured by the steering wheel rim
Lane-keep assist over-reacts on country bends and the speed-limit chime fires constantly, both needing to be switched off at every start-up
Surround-view camera and wireless phone charging are reserved for higher grades rather than standard across the range

summary: The facelifted 2026 Kia EV6 remains one of the most engaging mid-size electric SUVs to drive, with Australian reviewers rating its handling and steering among the best of any EV regardless of price, backed by rapid 800V DC charging and a now-uniform 84kWh battery that lifts range across every grade. It reads more as an electric grand tourer than a family hauler, though: reviewers consistently flag a smaller-than-expected boot, tight rear headroom and a busy low-speed ride, and note the range is priced at a premium against newer rivals, with the flagship GT landing well clear of the top FBT exemption threshold.
pros: Genuinely excellent handling and steering feel, rated by multiple reviewers among the best-driving EVs at any price
800V architecture enables very fast DC charging, around 10-80% in 18 minutes
Larger 84kWh battery lifts WLTP range across the range, up to 582km on the entry Air RWD
Strong 7-year/unlimited-km vehicle warranty with 7-year/150,000km high-voltage battery cover
cons: 480L boot trails key rivals such as the Ford Mustang Mach-E despite premium pricing
Tight rear headroom and harder rear-seat plastics let down an otherwise upmarket cabin
Speed-limit and driver-attention warnings are persistent and reset every drive
Priced above many rivals, with GT-Line and GT grades pushing well past the $75,000 FBT threshold and the GT AWD clearing $91,661 outright

summary: Kia's flagship seven-seat electric SUV is consistently praised by Australian reviewers as one of the most family-practical EVs on sale, with a genuinely usable third row, fast 800V DC charging, and a plush, tech-laden cabin. It comes at a real cost though, with even the entry Air RWD pricing above the luxury-EV threshold and the range topping out with the performance-focused GT, which reviewers see more as a halo model than a value pick.
pros: Spacious, genuinely adult-friendly third row that few seven-seat EV rivals match
Fast 800V architecture supports rapid DC charging, useful for family road trips
High-quality, feature-rich interior with strong safety tech across the range
Strong 7-year/unlimited-km warranty backing the whole lineup
cons: Every variant is priced above the FBT exemption threshold, eroding novated lease appeal
Big and heavy, so real-world efficiency and around-town manoeuvrability suffer versus smaller EVs
Boot space behind the third row is tight when all seven seats are needed
GT flagship commands a large premium mainly for extra performance few buyers will use

summary: The Sorento plug-in hybrid is a genuinely large seven-seater with about 58km of WLTP electric range, and for 2026 Kia finally broadened it from a single GT-Line grade to a four-grade walk opening at $70,880. Australian reviewers consistently like the way it drives and rate the charge-sustaining economy — roughly 6.4-6.5L/100km once the battery is flat, which is real hybrid territory — but they are close to unanimous that the value case is thin, with the GT-Line asking around $17,500 more than the equivalent diesel and $12,500 more than the equivalent hybrid. The recurring complaints are structural rather than cosmetic: 3.3kW AC-only charging with no DC option, a 175-litre boot with the third row up, and a braked tow rating cut to 1010kg.
pros: One of only two seven-seat plug-in hybrids on sale in Australia under $90,000 — the Mitsubishi Outlander Aspire is the other, while the BYD Sealion 6, Mazda CX-60 PHEV and Ford Ranger PHEV are all five-seat — and unlike the Outlander's children-only third row this is a full-size large SUV body

Charge-sustaining economy is genuinely good for a 2.1-tonne seven-seater: CarExpert measured 6.5L/100km and Carscoops 6.4L/100km over a week without plugging in, so the car still behaves like a proper hybrid when the battery is empty rather than reverting to petrol-SUV consumption

Kia's seven-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional — it is not tied to servicing inside the Kia dealer network, unlike the conditional 10-year offers from Mitsubishi and MG — and the high-voltage battery carries its own separate seven-year/150,000km cover

For 2026 the PHEV is no longer GT-Line-only: S, Sport, Sport+ and GT-Line are all offered in AWD, each priced exactly $11,500 above the equivalent all-wheel-drive hybrid grade, so a buyer can get the plug-in drivetrain from $70,880 instead of being forced into the $86,790 flagship

Real-world electric range holds up against the claim — CarExpert saw 55km and Carscoops comfortably over 50km against the 58km WLTP figure — which covers a typical Melbourne school run and commute without starting the engine
cons: Charging is AC-only and capped at 3.3kW through a Type 2 port, with no DC fast-charging at all; Kia quotes 3 hours 26 minutes for 15-95 per cent, so a driver who cannot charge overnight at home has no practical way to keep the battery full

The 1.6L/100km label figure is meaningless in normal use: Carscoops recorded 6.4L/100km without charging against 6.0L/100km for the Sorento diesel, meaning an unplugged PHEV is slightly worse on fuel than the diesel it costs about $17,500 more than

Boot space with all three rows up drops to 175 litres because the battery sits under the second-row seat, down from 187 litres in the petrol and diesel Sorento, and the curtain airbags still do not extend to the third row

Braked towing was cut to 1010kg for the facelifted PHEV (down from 1350kg previously, and against 2000kg for the Sorento diesel), which rules out most camper trailers and is the single spec reviewers flag as a deal-breaker for towing families

Running costs are higher than the badge suggests: it requires 95 RON premium unleaded, and servicing falls due every 12 months or 10,000km at roughly $705-$765 a visit, short intervals for a family SUV

summary: The only plug-in Defender is the 110 P300e, a 221kW 2.0-litre petrol hybrid sold in two trims and no other body length. Reviewers agree it keeps everything that makes a Defender a Defender — the twin-speed transfer case, the air suspension, the 3000kg tow rating — and adds around 48km of quiet electric running that suits a Melbourne commute. Where they split is whether that is worth the money: the battery costs boot space, a third-row seat and roughly $13,000-$16,600 over the equivalent D350 diesel, and the fuel saving only materialises if the car is plugged in nightly.
pros: The only Defender you can plug in: about 48km of WLTP electric range covers a typical Melbourne commute, and it is one of the few PHEVs at any price with DC fast charging (40kW, 0-80 per cent in roughly 30 minutes) rather than AC only.

Keeps the Defender's touring hardware intact — 3000kg braked towing, a 90-litre tank, twin-speed transfer case and up to 900mm wading on air suspension — so the battery is added capability rather than a substitution.

Clears both Australian tax tests: 78g/km CO2 on the Australian label is well inside Victoria's 120g/km green-car duty threshold, and the 3.4L/100km combined figure sneaks under the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficient LCT limit that lifts the threshold from $80,809 to $91,661.

Five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty with five years of roadside assistance and six-year anti-corrosion cover, level with Volvo and BMW rather than the shorter terms Land Rover Australia used to offer.
cons: CarExpert measured 9.7L/100km on the same drivetrain once the battery was flat and never recharged — about 63 per cent above the 3.4L/100km label — so a buyer without home charging is running a 2.6-tonne car on a small four-cylinder engine and paying for it in fuel.
The pack eats the boot: Land Rover quotes up to 116 litres less loadspace than a non-hybrid 110 and a loadspace floor raised 36mm, leaving 853 litres behind the second row.
No third row. Land Rover does not offer the seven-seat Family Pack on the P300e, so a family that needs six or seven seats has to take a D350 110 or step up to a 130.
Braked towing falls to 3000kg against 3500kg for the D350 and P425, and the PHEV carries roughly 100kg more kerb weight, so it is the worst Defender in the range for a heavy trailer.

At $131,100 and $143,200 before on-road costs it asks $13,000-$16,600 more than the D350 X-Dynamic SE and HSE, and it is well past the $75,000 cap in the 2027 FBT phase-down as well as both LCT thresholds.

summary: The B10 is Leapmotor's small electric SUV, sold in Australia from $37,888 list in two pure-battery grades that undercut the BYD Atto 3, Geely EX5 and Kia EV3. Australian reviewers are unusually united on the chassis — carsales scored it 81/100 and CarsGuide 7.4/10, both crediting the rear-drive layout and Maserati-influenced suspension tune with more composure than anything else at the price, and CarPlay and Android Auto fix the omission that dogged the related C10. Where they part company is how much the rough edges cost it: the standard Linglong tyres, the intrusive lane-keep system and the touchscreen-only controls drew criticism from every outlet, and the B10 is also sold here as a range-extender under the same two badges, so a buyer has to check which powertrain a quote refers to.
pros: Cheapest way into a new electric SUV in Australia at $37,888 list, several thousand under a BYD Atto 3 Essential and a Geely EX5 Complete, with a 14.6-inch screen, panoramic roof, wireless charging and 360-degree cameras standard on the base Style

Rear-wheel drive with Maserati-influenced suspension tuning — carsales rated it 'one of the best value and most engaging small electric SUVs' at 81/100 and CarsGuide gave 7.4/10, both singling out ride and handling as ahead of the class
Apple CarPlay and Android Auto are fitted, unlike the Leapmotor C10, which still has neither on any grade
The $40,888 Design LR steps up to a 67.1kWh pack, 434km WLTP and 168kW DC charging (30-80% in about 18 minutes) against the Style's 56.2kWh and 140kW, for $3,000
Eight years of capped-price servicing at roughly $370 per visit on 12-month/20,000km intervals, plus eight years of roadside assistance and a five-star ANCAP rating
cons: Not rated to tow at all — braked capacity is 0kg on both electric grades, where the B10 range-extender is rated to 750kg and the larger Leapmotor C10 manages 1,500kg

Standard Linglong eco tyres were criticised by RACQ, carsales and CarsGuide alike for squealing and losing grip early under brakes, which reviewers say squanders the chassis the car is otherwise praised for
Lane-keep assist is intrusive enough that multiple Australian reviewers disable it every drive, and there are no physical controls — mirrors, vents and most functions live in the touchscreen
Six-year/150,000km warranty is unconditional but trails the seven years offered by Kia, MG, Geely and Chery in the same price bracket, after Leapmotor cut the term from seven years for MY25
Resale is the open risk: Leapmotor has around 20 Australian dealers, almost no local resale history, and launched the B10 on a $38,990 national drive-away offer that sat below the true on-road cost

summary: The C10 is Stellantis-distributed Leapmotor's mid-size electric SUV, sold in Australia as a deliberate value play against the Tesla Model Y and Kia EV5 with list prices from the mid-$40,000s. Australian reviewers broadly agree on the package — RACV, CarExpert and CarsGuide all praise its limousine-like rear legroom, Maserati-tuned ride comfort and equipment level, and CarsGuide's 2026 BEV Design review scored it 7.5/10 after an over-the-air update tamed the intrusive driver-assist alerts. Where they diverge is how much the usability faults matter: the missing Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, everything-in-the-touchscreen layout and fiddly key card drew consistent criticism, and Chasing Cars marked the related C10 down to 5.5/10 for grabby brakes and numb steering, while RACV explicitly warned buyers about brand risk given Leapmotor's tiny local volume.
pros: Roughly $10,000 under a Tesla Model Y and several thousand under a Kia EV5 Air, with a panoramic roof, 14.6-inch screen and 17 driver-assist systems standard even on the $45,888 Style
Class-leading rear legroom on a flat floor — reviewers consistently rate the second row as the C10's standout, ahead of the Model Y and EV5 — plus a 581L boot expanding to 1410L
Ride comfort was tuned with Maserati chassis input and RACV found it smothers poor surfaces rather than fidgeting like most cheap EVs on 20-inch wheels
The $49,888 Design LR gets an 81.9kWh battery, 800V architecture and 180kW DC charging (30-80% in about 22 minutes) for the same price the smaller-battery Design used to cost
Cheap to keep: five services capped at $2000 total ($400 each, 12 months/20,000km) and a five-star ANCAP rating from 2024 testing
cons: No Apple CarPlay or Android Auto on any grade, with mirrors, vents and most functions buried in the touchscreen and no physical console buttons
The entry Style is stuck on the old 69.9kWh pack and 84kW DC charging — roughly half the Design LR's peak rate — so the $4000 step up buys a materially different car, not just trim
Leapmotor cut the C10's warranty from seven years/160,000km to six years/150,000km for MY25, so it now trails the seven years offered by Kia, MG, Deepal and Geely

Weak resale outlook: Leapmotor delivered only 579 C10s in Australia in 2025 and 39 in the first two months of 2026, and dealers are already listing stock in the high-$30,000s against a $45,888 list price
Numb steering, grabby friction brakes that are hard to modulate in traffic, no frunk, and a key-card entry system reviewers called convoluted enough that Leapmotor has admitted a rethink

summary: The NX 450h+ is the only plug-in hybrid in the Lexus NX range — the far more common NX 350h is a conventional hybrid with no plug — and it pairs an 18.1kWh battery with a 2.5-litre petrol four for 227kW and all-wheel drive. Its distinguishing trait is that it stays frugal once the battery is flat: Australian testers record about 5.4-6.0L/100km in charge-sustaining running, where most European PHEVs of this size drink 8L/100km or more. Reviewers rate the refinement, build and the newly added $84,500 Luxury grade, but are consistently critical of the $96,000 F Sport's value against cheaper plug-in rivals, the 6.6kW AC-only charging with no DC option, and an official 87km range claim that is NEDC-derived and about 15 per cent above the European WLTP figure.
pros: Charge-sustaining economy is genuinely low for a 2.05-tonne premium SUV: Chasing Cars measured about 6.0L/100km running on petrol alone with the battery depleted over a ~1000km long-term test, and CarExpert saw 5.7L/100km across a mostly-highway week — so an owner who cannot plug in still gets Toyota hybrid consumption rather than the 8-9L/100km typical of European PHEVs

Adding the NX450h+ Luxury AWD at $84,500 in late 2025 cut $11,500 off the price of entry to the plug-in drivetrain, which previously required the $96,000 F Sport, and it keeps the same 18.1kWh battery, 227kW output and e-Four all-wheel drive as the flagship

Lexus Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, and the hybrid battery carries separate 10-year unlimited-kilometre cover that can be extended a further 10 years through annual health checks at a Lexus dealer

Boot space is not sacrificed to the plug-in hardware — the battery sits under the cabin floor, so the 450h+ keeps the same 520-litre boot as the NX 350h hybrid, unlike the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-60 PHEV which both lose volume to their packs

Real-world electric range is usable rather than token: Australian testers report 53-70km on a full charge, enough for a typical Melbourne commute, and the car will hold EV mode to 135km/h rather than firing the engine at highway speeds
cons: Charging is AC-only at a maximum 6.6kW with no DC fast-charge capability at all, and the supplied cable is a 10A domestic lead that CarsGuide timed at roughly six hours for 35-100 per cent — a buyer without a home wallbox has no practical way to keep the battery full, at which point the car is simply an expensive NX 350h

The advertised 87km electric range is an NEDC figure mandated by ADR 81/02 for the Australian energy label; the equivalent European WLTP figure is 70-74km, so the headline number overstates the range by roughly 15 per cent before real-world driving is considered

The 1.3L/100km label consumption is meaningless in normal use — EV Central measured 5.4L/100km and CarExpert 5.7L/100km — and the car requires 95 RON premium unleaded, so the fuel bill is roughly four times what the sticker implies

At $96,000 before on-roads the F Sport sits above the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold and draws direct comparison with the Audi Q5 and BMW X3; EV Central scored it 3/5 on the basis that it is 'just not that rare or special any more' against Chinese plug-in hybrids costing $40,000-$60,000 less

Braked towing is capped at 1000kg, well under the 2000kg-plus of comparably sized diesel and petrol SUVs, and the NX still carries its 2022 ANCAP rating without the centre front airbag newer rivals fit

summary: The RX 450h+ is the only plug-in grade in the Lexus RX range — the RX350h and the flagship RX500h are conventional hybrids with no plug at all — and it pairs an 18.1kWh battery with a 2.5-litre petrol four for 227kW and all-wheel drive. Australian reviewers rate it highly for refinement, the 612-litre boot and a charge-sustaining thirst of roughly 6.5-7.0L/100km once the battery is flat, which is well under what similarly sized European plug-ins drink. The recurring criticisms are the modest 67km WLTP electric range against a BMW X5 xDrive50e's 101km, AC-only 7kW charging with no DC capability, a 1500kg tow rating, and the fact that the $123,650 Sports Luxury asks flagship money for a car whose $105,350 Luxury twin shares the whole drivetrain.
pros: The $105,350 RX450h+ Luxury added in November 2025 undercuts the Sports Luxury by $18,300 while keeping the identical 18.1kWh battery, 227kW output and e-Four all-wheel drive — it drops 21-inch wheels, adaptive suspension, adaptive headlights, the hands-free tailgate and the premium audio, but nothing that affects range or running cost

Charge-sustaining consumption is genuinely low for a 2.1-tonne large SUV: EV Central measured roughly 6.5-7.0L/100km with the battery depleted and the US EPA rates it at 35mpg (6.7L/100km) in hybrid mode, so an owner who cannot plug in still gets Toyota hybrid economy rather than the 9L/100km-plus typical of a large European PHEV

The 612-litre boot (1678 litres seats-down) is unchanged from the petrol and hybrid RX because the battery sits under the cabin floor — the Kia Sorento PHEV and Mazda CX-60 PHEV both surrender load space to their packs
Lexus Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the hybrid battery is covered separately for 10 years, and servicing is capped at $695 per visit for five years or 75,000km

Unlike PHEVs that simply revert to the petrol engine when the battery empties, the RX drops into full Toyota-style hybrid operation and recharges the pack on the move, and it will hold EV mode to 135km/h rather than firing the engine at highway speed
cons: The 85km electric range Lexus Australia advertises is an NEDC figure carried by the ADR 81/02 energy label; the European WLTP figure for the same car is 67-69km, so the headline overstates the range by around 25 per cent before real-world driving is considered, and Australian testers recorded 55-60km

Charging is AC-only at 7kW with no DC fast-charge option, so a full recharge takes just under three hours on a wallbox and most of a working day on a household socket — a buyer without home charging is paying a large premium over an RX350h for a battery they cannot keep full

The 1.3L/100km label consumption is meaningless in use: it assumes every trip starts fully charged, where real Australian tests land at 4.8-5.1L/100km with regular plugging in and 6.5-7.0L/100km without, roughly five times the sticker

Braked towing is capped at 1500kg, below the 2000kg the same car is rated for in Europe and well under the 2400-2500kg of the Volvo XC90 T8 and Mercedes GLC/GLE plug-ins, and there is no spare wheel — only a repair kit

At $123,650 the Sports Luxury sits $32,000 above the fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold of $91,661 and buys a five-seat SUV with less electric range than a BMW X5 xDrive50e; CarsGuide called the EV-only range 'relatively short' for the money and the Luxury grade is the value pick by a wide margin

summary: The RZ is Lexus Australia's only battery-electric model, a five-seat mid-size SUV on the Toyota e-TNGA platform it shares with the bZ4X, and the 2026 update cut list prices by $36,559 to $42,059 a grade while adding power, a bigger battery and 22kW AC charging. Reviewers agree the repositioning transformed the car's value case — CarExpert calls the cuts the difference between an also-ran and a genuine contender, EV Central scored it 4/5 — and praise the ride, steering and cabin quality. The persistent criticism is range: 437-460km WLTP is short for the money when the BMW iX3, Volvo EX60 and Mercedes-Benz GLC EV are arriving with 700-800km claims, and road roar and thin front cabin storage draw complaints too.
pros: The 2026 update is a permanent RRP reduction, not a run-out campaign: the entry RZ500e Luxury fell from $121,059 to $84,500 and the Sports Luxury from $133,059 to $91,000, which puts both under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and so inside the FBT exemption for a novated lease — the outgoing car sat well above it

AC charging doubled to 22kW, so an owner with three-phase power refills the pack in about three and a half hours rather than seven; DC peak is 150kW for a 10-80 per cent stop of roughly 30 minutes, and the pack now has its own water-cooling circuit

Lexus Australia's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the drive battery is covered separately for eight years/160,000km, and capped-price servicing is $395 per visit at 12-month/15,000km intervals — Toyota's longer seven-year driveline term applies only if every service is completed on schedule within the dealer network
Rated to tow 1500kg braked, double the 750kg of the Toyota bZ4X 2WD and more than most mid-size electric SUVs at the price, and the 522-litre boot expands to 1451 litres with the rear seats down

The RZ550e F Sport is the first car sold new in Australia with a steering yoke and steer-by-wire; lock-to-lock is about 400 degrees total, which CarExpert found genuinely easier for parking and manoeuvring once recalibrated
cons: Range is the range's defining weakness: 460km WLTP for the RZ500e and 437km for the RZ550e F Sport, where the incoming BMW iX3 and Volvo EX60 claim around 800km and the Mercedes-Benz GLC EV 713km — CarsGuide and CarExpert both list sub-500km range as their headline dislike

The RZ550e F Sport at $105,000 sits above the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold, so it attracts luxury car tax and is not eligible for the FBT exemption on a novated lease, while the $91,000 Sports Luxury clears the threshold by just $661 — the yoke costs a buyer the tax break, not just the money

The predecessor's list price was cut by up to $42,059 in a single model-year change after what Lexus itself attributed to very low sales, which is a severe signal for residual values on both the outgoing car and the new one
There is no glovebox — EV Central notes it has been replaced by a passenger-side knee warmer — front cabin storage is limited, and there is no spare wheel of any kind, only a repair kit

The F Sport's Interactive Manual Drive simulates eight gears with synthesised engine noise that CarExpert called 'more grating than engaging' and switched off, and CarsGuide described as 'cringe-worthy'; road roar over coarse-chip surfaces is a consistent complaint across Australian reviews

summary: Lotus's first SUV is a 2.5-tonne, 450kW-to-675kW electric hyper-SUV that Australian reviewers rate genuinely well — CarExpert called it "really, ridiculously good" and praised air suspension that stays composed on coarse country roads — but CarsGuide scored it only 7.2 out of 10 and flagged limited cabin practicality and a driving character that no longer resembles a Lotus. A MY25 factory price cut of $49,010 to $35,010 a variant transformed the value case, dropping the entry car from $239,000 to $189,990, and it is that repricing rather than the engineering that reviewers now credit for making it competitive. The unresolved risk is ownership rather than the car: Lotus sold 12 Eletres in Australia in 2024, nine in 2025 and three to date in 2026, through a five-showroom network, so parts, resale and service depth are all unproven.
pros: Cut by $49,010 in MY25 — the entry Eletre fell from $239,000 to $189,990 before on-roads, undercutting a BMW iX M60 and Lamborghini Urus while offering 450kW and 4.5sec to 100km/h
800V architecture takes 350kW DC for a 10-80 per cent charge in about 20 minutes, well ahead of the 400V Audi SQ8 e-tron and Mercedes-AMG EQE SUV it is cross-shopped against
688-litre boot expanding to 1,532 litres and a 2,250kg braked tow rating, which is more than the BMW iX or Polestar 3 will pull
CarExpert rates the Unreal Engine 5 infotainment as "one of the best infotainment experiences available", ahead of Tesla's, backed by a 23-speaker 2,160W KEF system on the S
Two-year/30,000km service intervals with only cabin filter and brake fluid as mandatory replacements, so scheduled maintenance is unusually light for the price bracket
cons: CarExpert recorded 340km from a full charge in hard driving against a 490km WLTP claim on the R, so the 600km and 535km figures on these grades will not survive highway use
Lotus has no capped-price servicing in Australia and distributes through only five Simply Sports Cars showrooms, so warranty and repair access is thin outside the capitals
Resale is the weakest part of the case: 24 Eletres were sold new in Australia across 2024 and 2025 combined, and the MY25 price cut wiped up to $49,010 off MY24 cars overnight
Standard brakes are judged inadequate for the performance — CarExpert recommends the $32,199 carbon-ceramic upgrade, and options escalate a car that already carries heavy unrecoverable Luxury Car Tax
The flagship Eletre R at $279,990 sits above this calculator's modelling ceiling, and neither S nor base qualifies for the FBT exemption, so novated leasing offers no relief on any grade

summary: The Emeya is Lotus's electric four-door hyper-GT, and Australian reviewers agree it is a genuinely resolved luxury EV — CarExpert praises air suspension that "breathes nicely with the road" rather than feeling floaty, and CarsGuide rates the chassis agile enough to hold its own against a Porsche Taycan while offering far more rear legroom. Where they part company is on whether it is still a Lotus: at 2480-2575kg CarsGuide argues it "abandons Lotus' lightweight principles" and that the heaviness dulls its edge. The bigger buyer risk is commercial rather than dynamic — Australia bought 5 in 2024, 3 in 2025 and none year-to-date in 2026, making it the slowest-selling car you can actually walk in and order.
pros: Wheelbase is roughly 200mm longer than a Porsche Taycan's, so rear legroom is genuinely adult-sized where the Taycan and Audi e-tron GT are cramped
800V architecture charges at up to 350kW for a 10-80 per cent top-up in about 14 minutes, comfortably quicker than a Taycan on the same charger
Liftback tailgate gives 509 litres behind the rear seats and 1388 litres folded, plus a 34-litre frunk — far more usable than the sedan-booted e-tron GT
Unconditional five-year/150,000km vehicle warranty with eight years/200,000km on the battery, no dealer-servicing strings attached
Entry 600 grade is certified at 580km combined WLTP from a 98.9kWh usable pack, ahead of the 506km BMW i5 M60 at a similar price
cons: Australian volume is effectively nil — 5 sales in 2024, 3 in 2025 and zero year-to-date in 2026 — so there is almost no used-buyer base and resale risk is severe
Only five Lotus retailers nationally (Brisbane, Sydney, Melbourne, Adelaide, Perth), meaning no franchised service or warranty support outside a capital city

Documented heavy discounting: Carscoops reported in May 2026 that UK dealers were taking roughly 36 per cent off a $189K-equivalent Emeya, and the Australian entry price has already been cut from $189,990 to $177,990
Kerb weight of 2480-2575kg is close to a large SUV, and CarsGuide judges that the mass blunts the agility the badge implies
Lotus Australia publishes no prices on its website or configurator, so the grade walk above the entry 600 cannot be compared without visiting a retailer

summary: The Grecale Folgore is Maserati's first electric SUV and the fourth grade in an Australian Grecale range that is otherwise petrol and mild-hybrid, at $207,500 before on-road costs against $119,900 for the entry GT. Reviewers agree on the cabin and the pace — 410kW/820Nm and 4.1 seconds make it comfortably quicker than an entry Porsche Macan Electric — but split hard on whether the engineering justifies the money, with CarExpert calling it "oddly compromised" for its stiff ride, torque steer and 400V charging in a class that has moved to 800V. The bigger caution for an Australian buyer is commercial rather than dynamic: Maserati delivered just 101 cars nationally in the first half of 2026, and the car sold here is the pre-facelift version, with the longer-range MY26 update not due until early 2027.
pros: 410kW/820Nm and 0-100km/h in 4.1 seconds — CarExpert notes it has more power and torque than the entry Macan 4 Electric and is a full 1.5 seconds quicker to 100km/h
501km WLTP from a 96kWh usable pack, which is more certified range than a Genesis GV70 Electrified (462km) or a Polestar 3 Performance (593km is the exception, not the rule at this power level)
22kW AC onboard charging is double the 11kW almost every rival fits, so a three-phase home or destination charger refills it roughly twice as fast overnight
Rated to tow 1800kg braked, where most performance EV SUVs at this price are rated well under that or not at all
Maserati includes a home wallbox with the car, and the Econyl regenerated-nylon interior and 12.3-inch infotainment come standard rather than as option boxes
cons: 400V architecture caps DC charging at 150kW and takes 29 minutes for 20-80 per cent, where the 800V Porsche Macan Electric, Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6 do 10-80 per cent in 22 minutes or less
CarExpert's Australian review records a "stiff and brittle" ride and torque steer on uneven surfaces, concluding the car feels "oddly compromised" next to the Porsche Macan Electric
Three-year warranty is the unconditional term — half of Kia's and BYD's, and two years short of the five that BMW, Mercedes-Benz and Genesis give as standard at this price
Maserati sold 101 vehicles in Australia across the whole range in the first half of 2026, down 33.1 per cent, so the dealer and service network is tiny and resale support is thin

Australia gets the pre-facelift car: the MY26 update that lifts range to 580km and adds an AWD-disconnect and battery preconditioning is not expected here until early 2027, dating the car a buyer signs for now

summary: Mazda's return to the mid-size car segment is a China-built electric liftback that Australian reviewers rate as quiet, well-finished and unusually polished for the money, with a $49,990 entry price that undercuts every Tesla Model 3 and the BYD Seal. The 77kWh usable LFP pack's 560km WLTP range and 195kW peak DC charging are competitive, but local testers consistently criticise the Europe-tuned suspension as too soft, the steering as too light off-centre, and the near-total reliance on a 14.6-inch touchscreen as a step backwards from Mazda's usual ergonomics. Both grades sit far below the $75,000 FBT exemption threshold, so the only real decision is interior trim.
pros: GT's $49,990 list price undercuts the cheapest Tesla Model 3 RWD by $4,910 and the entry BYD Seal by $3,000, while claiming 560km of WLTP range
195kW peak DC charging takes the LFP pack from 10-80 percent in around 24 minutes, well ahead of the 80kWh NMC version sold in continental Europe
High-voltage battery is covered for eight years or 160,000km, on top of the unconditional five-year, unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty
Rear-wheel drive with near-even 47/53 weight distribution, and Chasing Cars recorded 459km of real-world range over hilly terrain against the 560km claim
Rated to tow 1,500kg braked, where most electric sedans in this price band are limited to 1,000kg or are not rated to tow at all
cons: 337-litre boot to the parcel shelf is small for a mid-size liftback, against 682 litres in a Tesla Model 3
Almost everything except the windows, hazard lights and gear selector runs through the 14.6-inch touchscreen, including the wipers; reviewers report 30-45 minutes just to learn the menus
Australian reviewers rate the Europe-tuned damping too soft and the steering too light around straight ahead, and the mirror and indicator stalks are still laid out for left-hand drive
Brand-new nameplate with no Australian resale history, and Mazda's only previous EV here, the MX-30, sold in tiny numbers and depreciated heavily

summary: Mazda's P50e plug-in hybrid pairs a 2.5-litre turbo petrol engine with a 17.8kWh battery for a claimed 76km of EV-only range and brisk 5.8-second 0-100km/h performance, wrapped in Mazda's most upmarket cabin. Reviewers rate the interior materials and safety kit highly and note the boot doesn't shrink for the battery pack, but they consistently flag drivetrain roughness — jerky low-speed transmission behaviour, occasional 'tug-of-war' shunt between engine and motor, and creaks reviewers say feel unresolved for the price. With the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids gone since April 2025, reviewers are also blunt that the economics only work for buyers who charge at home every night; leave it unplugged and fuel use climbs sharply.
pros: 76km claimed WLTP electric range (55-60km real-world per CarExpert) covers most Australian commutes on electricity alone, backed by a 241kW/500Nm combined output good for 5.8-5.9 second 0-100km/h
477L boot with seats up and 1726L seats-down is identical to the petrol and diesel CX-60 — unlike many PHEV rivals, the battery pack doesn't cost you cargo space
2500kg braked towing capacity matches the petrol/diesel CX-60 and beats most mid-size PHEV SUV rivals, plus a 1500W vehicle-to-load outlet in the boot
5-star ANCAP (2022, tested to Euro NCAP protocols) across the range, and the high-voltage battery carries an 8-year warranty on top of the 5-year vehicle term
Combined-cycle 49g/km CO2 and 2.1L/100km comfortably qualify every grade for Victoria's green passenger-car duty rate and the higher fuel-efficient LCT threshold
cons: Reviewers describe unresolved drivetrain manners: 'bunny hops' at low speed, a 'tug-o-war' sensation between engine and electric motor, and creaks CarExpert called 'not confidence inspiring' for a flagship-priced Mazda

Once the battery is depleted it's a ~2.2-tonne turbo-petrol AWD SUV — CarsGuide's real-world test (two charging stops over 600km) implies combustion-only running closer to 8-9L/100km versus the 2.1L/100km label, and reviewers note fuel use 'climbs a lot' if you can't charge at home

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease case that drives this site now hinges entirely on the fuel-efficient LCT and green duty concessions, not a tax-free benefit — several reviewers flag this as undermining the CX-60 PHEV's original value pitch
Azami Sp and Azami Takumi list at $83,990 and CarsGuide/CarExpert both flag CX-60 servicing costs as 'on the higher side' versus mainstream SUV rivals
200kg heavier than the equivalent G40e petrol CX-60 according to Mazda's own guide, which reviewers link to the firmer, occasionally unsettled ride reported even in Touring-spec cars

summary: The CX-80 P50e is the stretched three-row version of the CX-60 plug-in hybrid, using the same 2.5-litre petrol four, 17.8kWh battery and 241kW/500Nm combined output in a body long enough for seven seats. Reviewers rate it the best-riding and quickest CX-80 and praise the cabin quality and genuinely usable third row, but they are consistent that the electric range is modest for the money, the boot behind row three is small, and that a July 2026 price cut of $7,650-$8,119 reset the whole range downward. Opinion splits on ride: Chasing Cars calls the PHEV the best of the CX-80 line-up while other testers still find the secondary ride firm and the steering heavy around town.
pros: Now $68,100-$85,300 list after Mazda cut CX-80 PHEV prices by $7,650-$8,119 on 23 July 2026, putting the P50e just $5,000 above the equivalent G40e petrol or D50e diesel six

Every grade posts 2.7L/100km and 64g/km on the combined cycle, so all four clear both the 3.5L/100km fuel-efficient LCT test and Victoria's 120g/km green-duty ceiling — the $85,300 Azami SP pays no LCT as a result
The battery sits under the floor, so the 258L/566L/1971L boot figures are the same as the petrol and diesel CX-80 — no cargo penalty for the plug, and braked towing stays at 2500kg
241kW/500Nm makes it the quickest CX-80; Chasing Cars rates the PHEV's primary ride the best in the range, and 5-star ANCAP (2024, 92% adult occupant) covers all powertrains
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the high-voltage battery is covered for eight years, and capped-price servicing runs about $620-$700 a year over seven years
cons: 65km ADR (61km WLTP EAER) electric range is short for a $68k-plus PHEV — The Beep expects 55-60km in the real world and says nightly charging is 'essentially mandatory' to justify the $5,000 premium over the diesel

With the battery flat it is a 2237kg seven-seater on a 2.5-litre atmo four: Driving Enthusiast measured 7.0L/100km and Chasing Cars 'mid-to-high sixes', roughly two and a half times the 2.7L/100km label, so the case collapses for anyone without home charging
Only 258L behind the third row, well short of a Kia Sorento or Hyundai Santa Fe, and there is no spare wheel — just a repair kit
AC charging only at 7.2kW with no DC capability, so a depleted battery needs about 2.5 hours on a wallbox and cannot be topped up usefully on a road trip

PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and the GT at $75,100 sits $100 above the $75,000 cap that will matter for FBT purposes from 2027 — the Touring at $68,100 is the only grade with clear air beneath it

summary: The battery-electric CLA is the first car on Mercedes-Benz's MMA platform and the model that replaces the EQA and EQB as the brand's entry point into electric motoring here. Australian reviewers are near-unanimous that the efficiency and charging hardware are class-leading — an 800-volt system, 320kW DC peak and a 663km WLTP claim on the dual-motor grade — but equally consistent that the car is soft and remote to drive rather than sporting, and that the fastback roofline costs real rear-seat headroom. It reads as a car chosen for range, charging speed and a novated lease that stays inside the FBT exemption, not for driver engagement.
pros: The 350 4MATIC claims 663km WLTP, comfortably ahead of the BMW i4 eDrive35's 448km at similar money
800-volt architecture peaks at 320kW DC, enough to add roughly 300km in about ten minutes — nothing else near this price charges as fast
Both electric grades list below the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold (the 350 4MATIC by just $361), so a novated lease keeps the FBT exemption
CarExpert matched the 14.4kWh/100km consumption claim on test and rated the ride 'almost pillow-like' for refinement
A 101-litre front boot supplements the 405-litre rear boot, and both grades are rated to tow braked (1500kg and 1800kg)
cons: Rear headroom is tight for anyone over 1.8m and the high battery floor leaves thighs unsupported — the four-door-coupe roofline costs real space
CarExpert's verdict is that it is 'a bit ordinary to drive', with muted steering feel and early understeer even in the 260kW 350 4MATIC
The 800-volt-only design cannot use older 400V-limited DC chargers, including many Australian 50kW units, without the factory DC-DC converter
Mercedes EV resale in Australia has been weak: the EQA and EQB this car replaces both needed repeated local price cuts to sell
Almost every physical control has gone, with MB.OS moving climate and drive functions onto the touchscreens

summary: The EQA is Mercedes-Benz's entry-level electric SUV, essentially a battery-electric GLA with a front-mounted motor and the brand's usual small-SUV proportions. Australian reviewers consistently praise its refined, adaptive-damper ride and slick MBUX cabin, but mark it down for a WLTP range and boot space that trail cheaper, more spacious rivals now on sale locally. It reads as a car for buyers who want three-pointed-star badge appeal and a comfortable, quiet cabin rather than the last word in efficiency or outright value.
pros: Refined, well-damped ride quality even on larger wheels, reviewers say it feels bigger than its footprint
Smooth, linear power delivery from the single front motor makes it easy and relaxing to drive in town
Upscale MBUX cabin with twin 10.25-inch displays and quality materials typical of the brand
Now priced under the luxury car tax threshold across the range, helped by repeated local price cuts
cons: Reviewers note numerous rivals offer better range and/or value for similar or less money
Compromised rear legroom and a smaller-than-expected boot due to battery packaging
Divisive EQ-era styling elements, some reviewers say the design is starting to look dated
WLTP range and real-world efficiency trail newer competitors despite the premium price

summary: The EQB is a battery-electric version of Mercedes-Benz's boxy GLB small SUV, and its point of difference in Australia is a standard third row in a car under 4.7 metres long. Reviewers are consistent that it rides and insulates like a Mercedes and that the packaging is clever, but equally consistent that the third row is a 5+2 for children, that 100kW DC charging and roughly 350km of real-world range are behind the class in 2026, and that the money buys less car than the badge suggests. It is now a run-out model, with the GLB Electric replacing it locally in the final quarter of 2026.
pros: One of the very few seven-seat EVs on sale here under the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT cap, and the third row is standard on all three variants rather than the $2,900 option it once was
Rides pliantly and quietly even on the standard 20-inch wheels, with sound insulation Australian reviewers rate as a clear step above mainstream electric SUVs
Second row slides through 140mm of travel, so third-row legroom can be traded against boot space rather than being fixed
Compact 4,684mm length and 210mm ground clearance make it far easier to park and garage than a Kia EV9, which needs a $97,000 entry price for the same seat count
Advertised price includes a three-year service plan package and 12 months of Chargefox public charging, which offsets Mercedes-Benz's high standalone servicing costs
cons: Only 130 litres of boot space with all seven seats in use, which CarExpert put behind a Volkswagen Tiguan Allspace in every seating configuration
The third row is explicitly a 5+2: Mercedes-Benz specifies occupants under 1.65m tall, and headroom runs out for adults
DC charging peaks at just 100kW, around half what a Kia EV9 or Tesla Model Y will take, so long-trip stops are noticeably longer
CarExpert measured 19.1kWh/100km in mixed driving against the 536km WLTP claim, cutting realistic range to roughly 350km

Out of production since January 2026 and superseded locally by the GLB Electric in Q4 2026, which leaves resale exposed; at $90,000 the 250+ also has only $1,661 of headroom under the FBT-exemption cap, so one option pack can cost a novated-lease buyer the exemption

summary: The GLC 350e 4MATIC is Mercedes-Benz Australia's first non-AMG plug-in hybrid GLC, and its 25.28kWh usable battery is roughly a third larger than most rivals' — 107km of WLTP electric range is enough that many owners will use the petrol engine only on country trips. Australian reviewers are consistently positive about the calibration and the near-silent EV mode, and note that at $99,900 it undercuts both the GLC 300 petrol it outperforms and the BMW X3 30e. The recurring criticisms are the 2.3-tonne kerb weight, a boot that loses its underfloor storage and spare wheel to the battery, and a five-year service plan that Chasing Cars priced at $7350.
pros: 107km of WLTP electric range from a 25.28kWh usable battery is the longest of any plug-in hybrid SUV under $110,000 in Australia — roughly double the Lexus NX 450h+ (87km) and Volvo XC60 T8, and enough that a typical Melbourne commute never starts the engine

Charges properly for a PHEV: 11kW AC three-phase gets 0-100 per cent in about 2h45m, and it is one of very few plug-in hybrids on sale here with DC fast charging (up to 60kW, 10-80 per cent in about 29 minutes), so a driver without a home charger still has an option

At $99,900 before on-road costs it lists $5200 below the GLC 300 4MATIC petrol it comfortably out-accelerates — 230kW/550Nm combined, 0-100km/h in 6.7 seconds — which is unusual for a plug-in hybrid, and it is 10kW/100Nm up on the $104,800 BMW X3 30e
Braked towing is rated at 2400kg, well ahead of the Kia Sorento PHEV's 1010kg and the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV's 1600kg, so the battery has not cost it usefulness as a tow car
Mercedes-Benz Australia's five-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional and is not tied to servicing inside the dealer network
cons: The 1.2L/100km combined label is meaningless once the battery is flat: Australian testers recorded 7.3L/100km (Chasing Cars), 7.8L/100km (NRMA, CarsGuide) and 8.8L/100km (CarExpert) in charge-sustaining mode on 95 RON premium, so a buyer who cannot charge at home is running a 2.3-tonne petrol SUV and the whole case for the car collapses

The battery sits over the rear axle and takes the boot from the GLC 300's 620 litres to 590, removes the underfloor storage entirely and replaces the spare wheel with a repair kit — the floor is no longer flat

Servicing is expensive even by German standards: Chasing Cars quotes $7350 for a five-year plan on 12-month/25,000km intervals, roughly ten times what a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV costs to service over the same period

It sits well above both Luxury Car Tax thresholds at $99,900 and above the $75,000 FBT cap, and since the FBT exemption for plug-in hybrids ended on 1 April 2025 there is no novated-lease advantage left to offset that

Kerb weight is about 2316kg — some 200kg more than the GLC 300 — and reviewers note the extra mass in direction changes and under brakes, though the air-free steel-spring suspension copes better than expected

summary: The MG4 is consistently rated by Australian reviewers as one of the best-value small EVs on sale, combining sharp pricing with genuinely engaging rear-wheel-drive handling that punches above its budget-hatch positioning. The 2026 update fixed earlier interior gripes (better seats, more responsive touchscreen) and added the entry-level Urban variant, which reviewers praise for segment-busting cabin space and a surprisingly mature ride for the money. Common criticisms are a fiddly climate interface, an overactive speed-limit warning chime, and a boot that's merely adequate rather than class-leading.
pros: Sharp pricing relative to range and equipment, undercutting most EV rivals
Engaging, well-sorted rear-wheel-drive handling and steering feel
Spacious, upmarket-feeling cabin for the price, especially in Urban trim
Strong standard safety suite (adaptive cruise, AEB, blind spot monitoring)
Quick DC charging (10-80% in around 25-30 minutes)
cons: Boot space is only middling for a hatch (350-382L)
Few physical controls; climate functions buried in the touchscreen
Overactive speed-limit and driver-attention warning chimes annoy some reviewers
XPower's real-world range drops noticeably under highway/AWD use

summary: The HS Super Hybrid is MG's plug-in version of its mid-size SUV, and its 120km WLTP electric range is the longest of any PHEV SUV under $55,000 in Australia — enough that most buyers with a driveway charger will rarely burn petrol. Reviewers agree the powertrain is the drawcard and that the car is comfortable and well equipped, but are consistently unimpressed by the chassis: 220kW through the front wheels overwhelms the standard tyres, and the steering is remote. The catch is charging, since the car takes AC only and cannot DC fast-charge at all, so the whole value case collapses for anyone who has to rely on public infrastructure.
pros: 120km of WLTP electric range from a 24.7kWh (23.2kWh usable) LFP pack beats the GWM Haval H6 PHEV's 106km, the BYD Sealion 6 Essential's 92km and the Jaecoo J7 SHS's 90km, and carsales and EV Central both verified 100km-plus of real-world EV running before the engine woke up.

MG advertises a 10-year/250,000km warranty, but that term is conditional on servicing exclusively within the MG dealer network; the unconditional cover a buyer gets regardless is seven years/unlimited kilometres, and the drive battery is covered on the same terms as the vehicle.
The 24.7kWh pack costs nothing in packaging: 507 litres seats-up and 1484 litres folded are identical to the petrol and Hybrid+ HS, where most PHEVs give up boot floor to the battery.

220kW/350Nm combined and a 6.8-second 0-100km/h make it the quickest thing in the price bracket, and carsales covered 809km on 49.95 litres plus one charge, supporting MG's 1000km-plus combined-range claim.
cons: There is no DC fast-charging capability at all — AC only, at up to 6.6kW — and carsales measured 16 hours 16 minutes for a full recharge on test, so this is a car that only makes financial sense if you can leave it plugged in at home overnight.

Once the battery is flat it is just a heavy petrol SUV: the NRMA recorded about 6.0L/100km over 230km of suburban running in hybrid mode and carsales saw 5.9L/100km on a long highway leg, against MG's 'under 5.0L/100km' claim and a 0.7L/100km combined label figure that is meaningless as a running cost.

Reviewers at carsales and the NRMA both single out traction: the standard tyres cannot put 220kW through the front axle in the wet, and the steering is described as disconnected — the Sealion 6 Premium AWD and Haval H6 PHEV AWD have driven axles at both ends for similar money.

Advertised pricing swings hard — MG cut $5,000 off the range for an EOFY campaign in June 2026, taking the Excite to $42,990 drive-away — which is good for a buyer timing a deal but poor for resale, and PHEVs lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025 so there is no novated-lease tax shelter to offset it.

summary: The IM5 is the sedan half of 'IM Presented by MG', a premium sub-brand sold through MG's own dealer network — a 4931mm five-seat liftback that undercuts the Tesla Model 3 and Polestar 2 on kilowatts, standard equipment and charging speed. Australian reviewers do not argue about the hardware: 800V charging up to 396kW on the Platinum and Performance, a 655km WLTP Platinum, rear-axle steering and a 3.2-second flagship are unusual at $60,990 to $77,990 drive-away, which is the only basis MG quotes for the IM range. They disagree sharply about whether it earns its premium billing, with Chasing Cars and carsales calling the cabin 'premium-lite' over cheap lower plastics and a knees-up rear seat while WhichCar and The Driven rate the chassis, refinement and self-parking as genuinely competitive; the reservation they share is real-world consumption near 20.6kWh/100km against an 18.9kWh/100km claim, and an unconditional warranty of only five years.
pros: Platinum and Performance run an 800V SiC architecture with a 396kW DC charging peak, giving a 30-80 per cent top-up in about 15 minutes against roughly 25 minutes for a Tesla Model 3 and 30-plus for a BYD Seal

Warranty runs to seven years/unlimited km provided every scheduled service is completed inside the IM/MG dealer network within 30 days and 2000km of the due interval — five years/unlimited km applies otherwise — plus an eight-year/160,000km high-voltage battery warranty and five-year cover on the air suspension and four-wheel steering

Performance's 572kW/802Nm dual-motor AWD hits 100km/h in 3.2 seconds for $77,990 drive-away — about $74,000 before on-road costs, undercutting the $80,900 Tesla Model 3 Performance by roughly $6,900 list-to-list while adding air suspension, four-wheel steering and a 20-speaker stereo as standard
Five-star ANCAP (2025) across the range with 89 per cent adult and 91 per cent child occupant protection, and 1500kg braked towing — 500kg more than a Tesla Model 3 and equal to a Polestar 2

Every grade gets the 26.3-inch display, panoramic roof, rear-axle steering with a 9.98m turning circle, heated front seats and 6.6kW vehicle-to-load, so the entry Premium at $60,990 drive-away is not stripped out to make the price
cons: The unconditional warranty is five years, not the seven MG's own badges carry — the seven-year term is forfeited the moment a service is done outside the dealer network or falls outside the 30-day/2000km window

Real-world consumption lands well above the claim: carsales measured 20.6kWh/100km against the Performance's 18.9kWh/100km WLTP figure, returning about 485km rather than 575km, and The Driven recorded 21.1kWh/100km on the highway

A high battery floor leaves rear passengers sitting knees-up with what Chasing Cars calls 'non-existent toe room', and the letterbox rear window makes over-the-shoulder vision poor in a car 4931mm long

Cabin quality is the consistent criticism — cheap lower-door and lower-console plastics, no glovebox at all, and a 10.5-inch central touchscreen mounted too low to use without looking away from the road

No Australian resale history exists for the IM sub-brand, and MG dealers were already advertising $3,000 cashback on the Platinum within twelve months of the July 2025 launch, so this dataset assumes depreciation steeper than the mainstream EV default

summary: The IM6 is the SUV half of the IM sub-brand that MG Australia sells through its own dealers as 'IM presented by MG' — a 4.9-metre, 2.3-tonne electric crossover whose specification-per-dollar Australian reviewers consistently call extraordinary, with 800V charging, air suspension and four-wheel steering at XPeng G6 and Zeekr 7X money. The consensus splits sharply on whether it drives like the money: CarExpert and the NRMA rate the cabin, comfort and equipment highly, while Chasing Cars scored the Performance 5.5/10 for a lumpy air-sprung ride, disconnected steering and intrusive driver aids. Reviewers converge again on ownership: real-world consumption of 22-27kWh/100km against WLTP claims, a five-year unconditional warranty well short of the MG-badged cars, and no Australian resale history yet.
pros: 800V architecture on Platinum and Performance takes up to 396kW DC for a claimed 30-80 per cent in 15.2 minutes — roughly triple the peak rate of a Tesla Model Y or XPeng G6; the 400V Premium is capped at 153kW and about 20 minutes
665L boot and 1640L folded on Premium and Platinum (646L/1621L on the Performance) plus a 32L frunk, comfortably ahead of the XPeng G6's 571L and the Zeekr 7X's 539L
The Performance's 572kW/802Nm dual-motor drivetrain claims 0-100km/h in 3.4 seconds at $77,990 drive-away, undercutting a Tesla Model Y Performance by roughly $17,000

Rear-axle steering with up to 12 degrees of angle gives a 10.18m turning circle, and Advanced Air Suspension with continuous damping is standard on the Performance and a $4,990 factory option on Premium and Platinum
Warranty extends to 7 years/unlimited km if every scheduled service is completed inside MG's dealer network, and the high-voltage battery is covered 8 years/160,000km however the car is serviced
cons: IM does not get MG's headline 10-year warranty: the unconditional term is 5 years/unlimited km (7 only with in-network servicing), behind the 7 years on MG's own cars, Kia and Chery, and the NRMA notes not every MG dealer is set up to service IM

Thirsty even on paper: the Performance's declared WLTP consumption is 23.4kWh/100km, against roughly 17.5kWh for a Zeekr 7X Performance and 14.5kWh for a Tesla Model Y Performance, and testers did worse again — CarExpert averaged 24.1kWh/100km and carsales 27kWh/100km, putting realistic touring range nearer 400km than the claimed 505km
Chasing Cars scored the Performance 5.5/10, describing the air-sprung ride as 'knobbly or lumpy' over ordinary urban surfaces and the steering as short on feedback despite the hardware
Rear vision is poor enough that CarExpert calls the mirror setup 'one of the worst', and the driver-assist warnings reset to on at every restart with no explanation of what triggered them

Ownership risk is unpriced: no spare tyre, servicing every 12 months/20,000km averaging $585.80 across the first five visits, and a brand with no Australian resale record that has already cut Platinum and Performance by $2,000-$3,000 each inside 12 months and is running $3,000 cashback on top
