summary: The MG S5 EV is the ZS EV's rear-drive replacement and is widely described by Australian reviewers as MG's most convincing model to date: a conventional, well-resolved small-to-mid electric SUV with a 453-litre boot, five-star ANCAP and pricing that sits under the Kia EV3. Reviewers agree the 62kWh car is the one to buy — the 49kWh Essence's 335km WLTP range draws consistent criticism as thin for the money — and the MY26 update added 25kW and 25km of range to the 62 at an unchanged $47,990. Opinion splits on the chassis: CarExpert and Chasing Cars rate the body control and steering response highly, while CarsGuide finds the steering too light and the styling derivative, and several testers note a ride that turns brittle over sharp-edged bumps.
pros: Up to 10 years/250,000km warranty (7 years/unlimited km if serviced outside the MG dealer network) — matching the 7-year cover from Kia, Chery and Geely and beating BYD's 6, with more on offer if you stay with MG servicing
MY26 Essence 62 gained 150kW/350Nm (up from 125kW/250Nm), cutting 0-100km/h from 8.6 to 7.0 seconds and lifting WLTP range 425 to 450km, at the same $47,990 list price
453L boot with underfloor storage, expanding to 1441L seats-down, plus a flat rear floor and genuine three-across rear seating — well ahead of the MG4 hatch's 350-382L and level with the Kia EV3
Five-star ANCAP (2025) with 90% adult occupant protection, and an MG Pilot Custom shortcut that lets you switch off individual driver-assist chimes without menu-diving
150kW DC charging gives a 30-80% top-up in about 19 minutes, and the LFP chemistry tolerates routine 100% charging
cons: Essence 49's 335km WLTP range is the range's weak point — CarExpert's verdict is that the '62 battery is far better than 49', and the $5000 step up buys 115km
The 10-year warranty is conditional on every scheduled service being done inside the MG dealer network; miss one and cover reverts to 7 years
Suspension can be harsh over sharp-edged urban bumps, and CarsGuide criticises steering that is 'too light and lacks communication'
No child presence detection, which cost it points in ANCAP's child occupant and safety assist categories (79% safety assist)

Weak Australian resale for the brand — used MG4s are retaining around 50% at three years against a ~60% EV market average, and MG's recurring drive-away and $1000-off campaigns keep resetting the market price

summary: MG's mid-size electric SUV undercuts the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7 by several thousand dollars while claiming more WLTP range than either, and reviewers broadly agree it is the value pick of the segment. The disagreement is over the ride: every Australian test criticises a firm, busy low-speed tune, but opinions split on whether it settles acceptably above 50km/h. The dual-motor version is the weaker buy, adding $7000 for pace few family buyers need and giving up 45km of range.
pros: 530km WLTP range from the rear-drive version beats the Tesla Model Y RWD and BYD Sealion 7 Premium on paper, and does it from a car priced thousands below both.

MG's unconditional cover is seven years/unlimited kilometres, and it extends to 10 years or 250,000km only if every scheduled service is done inside the MG dealer network — miss one and it reverts to seven.
Keeps physical climate and volume controls rather than burying them in the touchscreen, a point CarExpert, carsales and Chasing Cars each singled out.
581 litres of boot with the seats up (1690 folded) plus an 86-litre frunk on the RWD, with rear legroom reviewers rated as class-leading for six-footers.
Rated to tow 1500kg braked, where the smaller MG S5 EV manages only 750kg.
cons: 144kW peak DC charging and a 38-minute 10-80 per cent stop are slower than the Sealion 7 and Model Y, and it is the criticism every reviewer makes.
Low-speed ride is firm bordering on harsh over patchy surfaces; carsales also reported cabin rattles and resonances in a car with just 500km on it.
No over-the-air software updates, and the 12.9-inch touchscreen is laggy on start-up.
The driver-assist alerts, including a speed-sign warning that fires at 1km/h over, must be switched off again at every start.
The $56,990 drive-away AWD is poor value against the RWD — $7000 more for 45km less range — and battery cover is only seven years/160,000km, short of the segment norm.

summary: The Aceman is Mini's five-seat electric crossover, slotted between the Cooper hatch and the Countryman, and Australian reviewers broadly agree it delivers the brand's go-kart handling in a shape that finally has usable back seats — Chasing Cars scored the SE 8.0 and made it its 2025 Premium Small Car of the Year. The recurring objection is price against size: $60,990 before on-roads buys a 4.07-metre car when a larger Volvo EX30 opens at $49,990, and Mini deleted the cheaper Aceman E from the local range in 2025 after discounting it heavily, leaving the SE as the entry point. Opinion splits on the ride, which is firm on the standard 19-inch wheels, and on whether the JCW E's extra 30kW justifies $5,000 and a 51km range penalty.
pros: Sharply tuned front-drive chassis that reviewers rate as genuinely fun — Chasing Cars called the SE a 'tenacious corner carver' and scored it 8.0/10, well clear of a BYD Atto 2 or Zeekr X on driver appeal
Far more usable than the Mini Cooper Electric it shares a platform with: five seats and a 300-litre boot expanding to 1005 litres, against the Cooper's four seats and 210 litres
406km WLTP from the SE's 49.2kWh usable pack is competitive for a 4070mm car, and Chasing Cars still recorded 351km in real-world Australian testing
Both variants clear the $75,000 FBT exemption cap with room to spare — even the $65,990 JCW E has almost $9,000 of headroom, so a novated lease keeps the full exemption
High-voltage battery covered for 8 years/160,000km on top of the 5-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty
cons: Expensive for the metal: $60,990 for the SE against $49,990 for a longer-range Volvo EX30 and $46,080 for a Zeekr X, both roomier cars
95kW peak DC charging is modest — around 31 minutes for 10-80 per cent, where rivals at this money manage well over 150kW
Firm damping on the standard 19-inch wheels is the most consistent criticism in Australian reviews; CarExpert flagged ride quality at speed and Chasing Cars found it harsh in town
Rear-seat space and outward vision are compromised for a five-seater — CarsGuide notes tight rear legroom and a large B-pillar blind spot, and tyre noise is 'far from best in class'
Resale risk is real: Mini cut the entry Aceman E by $11,500 to $51,990 drive-away and then deleted it within months of launch, and Mini's total EV volume here is tiny at 159 Aceman sales in Q1 2026

summary: Mini's third-generation electric Cooper hatch is, by broad Australian reviewer consensus, the most entertaining EV in its price bracket — CarsGuide scored the driving experience a perfect 10 and Chasing Cars called it one of the most enjoyable electric cars on sale here — but the same reviewers keep landing on the same objection: it is a very small, very expensive car. Mini Australia deleted the cheaper Cooper E in 2025, so the range now opens at $58,990 before on-road costs for the 400km Cooper SE, roughly $20,000 above an equivalently sized MG 4. Opinion splits hardest on the ride: some testers treat the taut, fidgety damping as part of the go-kart appeal, others find it wearing on suburban roads, and the JCW E does without the adaptive dampers the petrol JCW gets.
pros: Genuinely engaging chassis — sharp steering and go-kart agility that no other electric hatch near the price matches, per CarsGuide (10/10 driving) and Chasing Cars
Quick for a small hatch: 160kW/330Nm and 0-100km/h in 6.7s in the Cooper SE, 190kW and 5.9s in the JCW E
The 9.4-inch circular OLED touchscreen is a real design statement rather than a generic tablet, and reviewers rate the interface fast and genuinely fun to use
Every variant sits well under the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so a novated-lease buyer keeps the exemption even on the top JCW E at $63,990
High-voltage battery covered for 8 years on top of the 5-year unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty
cons: 210-litre boot is among the smallest of any EV on sale in Australia — under half the 470 litres of a Skoda Elroq, and only 800 litres with the rear seats folded
Strictly a four-seater with token rear legroom; CarExpert's 185cm tester could not sit behind his own driving position, and CarsGuide called the rear backrests too upright for adults
Real-world consumption of 17-18kWh/100km against the 14.7kWh/100km claim drops usable range to roughly 300km from the 49.2kWh battery
Expensive for the metal: an MG 4 Essence 64 is $37,510 and a Tesla Model 3 RWD $54,900, both far more practical, and Mini offers only one interior trim on the SE
95kW peak DC charging is modest — 30 minutes for 10-80 per cent, where similarly priced rivals manage well over 100kW

summary: Mini's largest model is also its most practical EV, and Australian reviewers broadly treat it as a BMW iX1 in a more entertaining suit: near-identical hardware and a 230kW dual-motor drivetrain in SE All4 form, but sharper steering, less body roll and a list price $10,000-$15,000 below the BMW. The March 2026 technical update raised usable battery capacity to 65.2kWh and WLTP range to 501km for the front-drive E and 467km for the SE All4, which answers the biggest criticism levelled at the launch cars. Where reviewers still divide is the circular OLED interface and the roughly 130kW DC charging peak, both of which draw complaints at this price, and whether the SE All4's extra motor justifies stepping over the $75,000 FBT line.
pros: Same 66.5kWh/65.2kWh-usable pack and 230kW dual-motor drivetrain as the BMW iX1 xDrive30, for $10,000-$15,000 less on list price
March 2026 silicon-carbide inverter update lifted WLTP range from 462km to up to 501km (E) and 433km to up to 467km (SE All4) with no change to the pack's physical size
Rated to tow 1200kg braked as the SE All4 (750kg for the front-drive E), where the Mini Cooper Electric and many small electric SUVs are rated at zero
Six-year capped-price servicing quoted by CarExpert at $1,753 all up, cheap for a European-badged EV
Five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, with separate eight-year/100,000km high-voltage battery cover
cons: SE All4 Favoured ($76,990) and JCW Sport ($79,990) list above the $75,000 FBT exemption cap that the SE All4 Classic clears by only $1,010, so a novated lease can cost more for the higher trim than the price gap suggests
DC charging peaks at about 130kW and takes roughly 29-34 minutes for 10-80 per cent, slow against similarly priced rivals
CarExpert recorded 18.9kWh/100km on test in the SE All4, giving under 400km real-world, and the JCW Sport's 20-inch wheels push Mini's own WLTP figure to the worst end of its 15.7-17.4kWh/100km band
Apple CarPlay appears as a small pop-up box on the 9.4-inch circular OLED rather than filling it, and climate control is touch-only and fiddly on the move
460L boot is 45L smaller than the petrol Countryman's and front-cabin storage is poor, with an armrest that looks like it hides a bin but does not

summary: The March 2026 update gave Australia's longest-serving plug-in hybrid a 22.7kWh battery, 221kW and a locally developed suspension and steering tune, and reviewers agree the ride and steering are genuinely better than the pre-update car even if 20-inch wheels still let sharp bumps through. Where they split is value: the extra 86km of WLTP electric range and the unique seven-seat Aspire earn praise, but prices rose $1700-$3000 and the range now sits well above cheaper Chinese plug-in rivals that offer more EV range for less. The charging hardware is the consistent complaint, with a CHAdeMO DC port on a standard that is disappearing from Australian chargers and only 3.6kW AC charging.
pros: 86km of WLTP electric range from the new 22.7kWh pack, up from 20kWh and 84km NEDC on the pre-update car; CarsGuide saw about 80km in real-world urban running, enough to cover a typical Melbourne commute without starting the engine
The Aspire is the only seven-seat plug-in hybrid at this price - the BYD Sealion 6, Mazda CX-60 PHEV and Toyota RAV4 PHEV are all five-seat only
1600kg braked towing across the whole PHEV range, roughly double the BYD Sealion 6 Essential's 750kg and enough for a small camper or box trailer

Mitsubishi advertises a 10-year/200,000km warranty and 10 years of capped-price servicing (about $550 a year), but that term is conditional on every scheduled service being done inside the Mitsubishi dealer network; walk away from the dealer and the cover reverts to 5 years/100,000km. The drive battery is separately warranted for 8 years/160,000km

Springs, dampers and steering were re-tuned in South Australia for the 2026 update, and Australian reviewers report noticeably less float and better-weighted steering at speed than the car it replaces
cons: DC fast charging uses a CHAdeMO plug, a standard being decommissioned across Australian public charging networks, and AC charging is capped at 3.6kW so a full recharge takes about 6.5 hours on a home wallbox

The 1.2L/100km NEDC label figure only holds if you start every trip fully charged - Mitsubishi's own battery-depleted figure is 6.7L/100km, and CarsGuide measured around 10L/100km when the engine is actively charging the pack, so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging

The 2026 update added $1700-$3000 across the range, putting the ES at $58,990 and the Exceed Tourer at $74,490; reviewers call the flagship overpriced next to cheaper plug-in rivals with more electric range

The Aspire's third row leaves only 191 litres of boot behind it and is not covered by the curtain airbags, which extend to the first two rows only - it is a children-only occasional space, not a genuine seven-seater
The 2.4-litre engine is audibly coarse when it cuts in, described by reviewers as sounding like a vacuum cleaner from inside the cabin

summary: Nissan's only EV in Australia is a quiet, comfort-tuned mid-size SUV that finally went on sale here in September 2025, roughly six years after its global reveal, and Australian reviewers consistently rate it competent rather than class-leading. Its strongest cards are the 10-year/300,000km conditional warranty, better-than-claimed real-world efficiency and a 1500kg tow rating on the dual-motor Evolve; against that, 130kW DC charging and a fidgety ride over sharp bumps leave it behind newer rivals. Verdicts diverge on value: testers praise the drivetrain refinement and cabin isolation, but most call the list pricing optimistic next to a Tesla Model Y, BYD Sealion 7 or Kia EV5.
pros: 10-year/300,000km warranty if every service is done at a Nissan dealer, with $299 capped-price servicing; stay outside the dealer network and it reverts to 5 years/unlimited km, short of Kia's unconditional 7
Real-world efficiency beats the WLTP claim: Australian testers recorded mid-17kWh/100km around town and 557km from the 87kWh Advance+ against its 504km WLTP figure
Evolve e-4ORCE is rated to tow 1500kg braked — five times the Kia EV5 Air's 300kg — and does 0-100km/h in 5.6s from 290kW/600Nm
Unusually quiet cabin and comfort-biased seating, backed by a 5-star ANCAP rating and a nationwide Nissan dealer network rather than an online-only channel
cons: DC charging peaks at only 130kW, so 10-80% takes 35-40 minutes — roughly double an 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 or Kia EV6
Engage and Advance are stuck with 385km WLTP from the 63kWh pack; the 87kWh battery costs $63,840 in Advance+ form, an $8,000 step up from the base car
Suspension reacts abruptly to sharp bumps and the Evolve's 20-inch wheels make the ride busy on coarse Melbourne surfaces
No front boot on any variant, a high rear floor that leaves rear passengers knees-up with negligible toe room, and wired-only Android Auto
Resale risk is real: 127 deliveries in 2025 and ~104 in the first four months of 2026, with factory bonuses near $7,000 and $49,990-$53,990 driveaway offers appearing within a year of launch

summary: The Omoda 9 SHS is Chery's flagship in Australia and is sold here in a single $61,990 Virtue AWD grade, pairing a 1.5-litre turbo petrol with three electric motors for 395kW, a 4.9-second 0-100km/h claim and 145km of WLTP electric range from a 34.46kWh battery — roughly double the electric range of a BYD Sealion 6 or Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV for similar money. Australian reviewers are consistent that the powertrain, equipment list and cabin quality are the strongest part of the car and that the chassis is not: CarExpert, CarsGuide, Chasing Cars and carsales all criticise vague steering, loose body control and a busy, head-tossing ride, and none rates it as a genuine premium drive. It is a compelling equipment-and-range package with a hard ceiling on driving polish, and with no resale history in a brand that launched here in 2025.
pros: 145km of WLTP electric-only range from a 34.46kWh usable battery — around double a BYD Sealion 6 Premium AWD (81km) or a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV, and enough that most Melbourne buyers would rarely start the engine
395kW/650Nm from a 1.5-litre turbo petrol and three motors gives a claimed 4.9-second 0-100km/h, quicker than any PHEV SUV near the price and quicker than most $100k performance SUVs
70kW DC fast charging (30-80 per cent in about 25 minutes) plus 6.6kW AC — the Sealion 6 and Outlander PHEV have no DC capability at all, so an Omoda 9 can top up its electric range on a road trip

Eight-year/unlimited-kilometre vehicle warranty with a matching eight-year/unlimited-kilometre high-voltage battery warranty guaranteeing at least 70 per cent residual capacity, plus eight years of capped-price servicing ($3343 total) and roadside assistance

1500kg braked towing and a 660-litre boot (1783 litres folded) — the Jaecoo J7 SHS has no braked tow rating at all and only 340 litres, and the seven-seat Chery Tiggo 8 PHEV leaves just 117 litres behind its third row
cons: Omoda's own figure for a depleted battery is 7.0L/100km, not the 1.4L/100km combined label, and a 2000km European test returned 7.2L/100km — a 2.2-tonne AWD SUV on 95-octane premium, so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home

Ride and steering are the near-universal complaint: CarExpert calls it a 'bouncy, head-tossing ride', CarsGuide marks it down for 'vague steering' and 'lacking body control', and Chasing Cars describes the steering as 'numb and lifeless' — it does not drive like the premium car its price and equipment imply
Five seats only, where a Chery Tiggo 8 Super Hybrid at $42,990 and several rivals at this money seat seven, and the front seats lack height and tilt adjustment despite being power-operated

Omoda launched in Australia in 2025 with one model and a small dealer network, and the flagship is already being advertised with a $5000 factory bonus — resale is unproven and the transaction price keeps resetting, which is why a steeper-than-average depreciation curve is assumed here
Only one grade is offered, so there is no cheaper way into the nameplate: the choice is $61,990 or nothing, roughly $20,000 above the closely related Jaecoo J7 SHS Track

summary: The Polestar 2 is a premium electric fastback that Australian reviewers consistently praise as a genuine driver's car — crisp steering, tidy body control and, in the rear-drive Long Range Single Motor, a 659km WLTP range that beats most rivals in this price band. Where opinion splits is liveability: the ride is judged disciplined by some and outright punishing by others, and nearly everyone marks down the cramped rear seat, a legacy of the combustion-derived platform it shares with the Volvo XC40. It is now a late-life car facing a clean-sheet replacement, which means heavy factory discounting today and correspondingly weak resale tomorrow.
pros: 659km WLTP range from the Long Range Single Motor — more than a Tesla Model 3 Long Range RWD or a BMW i4 eDrive35, from the cheapest car in the range
Rated a driver's car by CarExpert and Chasing Cars alike: crisp, direct steering and excellent body control that the softer Model 3 does not match
MY26 update lifted DC fast charging to 205kW on the 82kWh pack and fitted a much quicker Qualcomm infotainment processor, fixing the range's most-criticised software lag
Rated braked towing of 1500kg, which most electric sedans in this price band do not offer at all
5-year unlimited-kilometre warranty and 5-star ANCAP, with well-tuned driver-assist calibration reviewers do not complain about
cons: Ride is firm to the point of being abrupt over sharp bumps — Chasing Cars called it 'considerably firmer than you expect' for a premium car, and this is the single most repeated criticism across Australian reviews
Cramped rear seat: a high floor from the battery, an unsupportive bench, small windows and a wasted transmission tunnel from the shared combustion platform — a couple's car more than a family one
407-litre boot trails the BYD Seal and Tesla Model 3, and the panoramic roof has no blind
Costly options creep: a heat pump requires the $1500 Climate pack and a power tailgate the $4700 Plus pack, so a well-equipped car lands well above the list price
Late-life model with a clean-sheet next generation confirmed within about 12 months, and discounts of up to $13,000 already on offer — resale should be expected to be soft

summary: The Polestar 3 is a large five-seat electric SUV that shares its SPA2 underpinnings with the Volvo EX90 but is tuned to feel considerably more athletic, and the March 2026 update moved it to an 800-volt architecture with much faster charging and, on two of three variants, a lower price. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the ride, body control and cabin quality, and rate the rear seat as one of the roomiest in the class. Disagreement centres on practicality and interaction: the boot is modest for the car's 4.9m footprint, there is no third-row option, and almost every secondary control has been pushed into the touchscreen.
pros: 800-volt architecture charges at up to 350kW (310kW on the Rear Motor), taking 10-80 per cent to 22 minutes — more than 25 per cent quicker than the 250kW car it replaced
The MY26 update made the previously $9,000 Plus Pack and the Pilot Pack standard on every variant while cutting the Rear Motor's price $1,720 to $116,700 and the Dual Motor's $1,600 to $131,100
Ride and body control rated 'exceptional' by carsales, and Chasing Cars found the rear-drive chassis genuinely lively despite a 2.3-tonne kerb weight
Palatial rear legroom plus a 25-speaker Bowers & Wilkins system that CarExpert called among the best it has experienced
5-year unlimited-kilometre warranty with long 24-month/30,000km service intervals, about $2,251 for six years of capped-price servicing
cons: 484 litres to the seat backs (including a 90-litre underfloor bin) is small for a 4.9m SUV, and unlike the Volvo EX90 it shares a platform with there is no six- or seven-seat option — five seats only
Steering column adjustment, mirrors and climate all live behind touchscreen menus, with no physical climate controls
The Rear Motor cannot be optioned with air suspension at any price, and Chasing Cars described its passive steel-sprung ride as 'knobbly' around town
AC charging is capped at 11kW, so a 0-100 per cent home charge takes about 10 hours where some rivals accept 22kW
Every variant is well above the $91,661 FBT-exempt luxury cap, so novated-lease buyers get none of the EV FBT exemption that a Kia EV5 or Tesla Model Y attracts

summary: The Polestar 4 is a coupe-styled mid-size electric SUV that Australian reviewers rate highly for its involving, well-composed driving manners, spacious and upmarket cabin, and genuinely competitive pricing against premium rivals like the Porsche Macan Electric. Its standout talking point is the deletion of a conventional rear window in favour of a camera-fed digital mirror, a decision reviewers describe as a workable, even class-leading, trade for headroom but not a universally comfortable one. Value is undercut by a lengthy, pricey options list and a control layout that pushes nearly everything through the touchscreen.
pros: Involving, well-controlled ride and handling that belies the car's size, with the Single Motor judged the best-balanced everyday pick
Spacious, near-limo-like rear seat and a large, usefully square 526-litre boot
Classy, well-finished interior with a crisp 15.4-inch Android Automotive infotainment system
Strong ownership package: 5-year/100,000km free servicing and 5-year unlimited-kilometre warranty
Undercuts key premium EV rivals such as the Porsche Macan Electric on price
cons: No rear window: the camera-fed digital mirror lacks the depth perception of a real mirror, and at least one reviewer reported a passenger became carsick watching the live feed

Near-total reliance on the touchscreen and touch-sensitive steering wheel controls for basic functions like mirrors, seat heating and cruise control fine-adjustment, which reviewers flagged as fiddly and distracting
Lengthy, expensive options list (Plus Pack, Pro Pack, Nappa leather) means the well-equipped price climbs well past the base figure
DC fast-charging speed is competent but trails class-leading rivals
Polestar's smaller Australian dealer and service footprint compared to established luxury brands

summary: The Megane E-Tech is Renault's compact electric hatch, sold in Australia in a single Techno EV60 grade with a 60kWh battery and 454km of WLTP range. Australian reviewers consistently rate it as one of the better-driving and more genuinely efficient EVs in its class -- a long-term test returned 14.4kWh/100km over 2359km -- and repeated price cuts have taken it from a $64,990 launch price to a permanent $54,990 before on-roads. Where opinion divides is on whether the sharp styling and hatch-like driving manners make up for a firm ride on its standard 20-inch wheels, a tight rear seat, and an ownership package (5 years/100,000km, 7.4kW AC charging) that trails most rivals.
pros: Genuinely efficient in the real world: CarsGuide's long-term test averaged 14.4kWh/100km over 2359km and 13.6kWh/100km in city running, beating the 15.6kWh/100km WLTP claim, so the modest 60kWh pack stretches further than the spec sheet suggests

Drives like a hatch rather than a heavy EV crossover -- 4200mm long, 1642kg, quick steering and 0-100km/h in about 7.0 seconds -- and Australian reviewers rate it at or ahead of the Cupra Born and MG 4 for handling

The list price has fallen $10,000 from the $64,990 launch figure to a permanent $54,990 before on-roads, and Renault has repeatedly run drive-away campaigns as low as $45,990-$49,990, so there is unusual room to negotiate

130kW DC charging delivers a 15-80% top-up in roughly 30 minutes, quicker than most 60kWh-class rivals, and it carries a five-star ANCAP rating (2022 Euro NCAP) with AEB, blind-spot monitoring and adaptive cruise standard
cons: Warranty is 5 years/100,000km, not the 5 years/unlimited km nearly every rival offers -- a 20,000km-a-year driver runs out of cover in year five, and Kia's EV3 and MG's 4 both come with seven years
Ride quality on the standard 20-inch wheels and 215/45 tyres is the car's most-criticised trait; reviewers describe bumps and thumps making their presence felt on pock-marked urban roads
AC charging is capped at 7.4kW single-phase, so a full home charge takes over nine hours and a three-phase wallbox buys nothing -- CarsGuide's long-tester called it "a real bummer"

Rear accommodation and the 440-litre boot are tight for family use: toe room is close to non-existent with the front seat low, the centre rear seat is narrow, the boot lip is high and there is no spare wheel

Australian cars go without the connected-services app and some equipment offered in Europe, only the one Techno EV60 grade is sold here, and the updated model (46km more range, higher DC charging power) is not due locally until the first half of 2027

summary: The Scenic E-Tech is Renault's mid-size electric SUV, built on the same CMF-EV platform as the Megane E-Tech and sold in Australia in three front-wheel-drive grades from $55,990 to $65,990 before on-road costs. Australian reviewers rate it near the top of its class for ride comfort, rear-seat space and cabin quality -- Chasing Cars scored the Esprit Alpine 8.0/10 and singled out its damping and adult-sized rear seat -- and the 87kWh grades' 625km WLTP claim is the longest in the segment under $70,000. The disagreement is over whether that is enough against cheaper Chinese rivals, given a 130-150kW charging peak that is only average, soft brake feel, and a five-year/100,000km warranty that is the shortest of any mainstream EV brand here.
pros: The 87kWh grades claim 625km WLTP, more than the Kia EV3 Earth (563km), Skoda Elroq 85 (529km) and Tesla Model Y Long Range AWD (600km), and Chasing Cars still saw 518km in real-world testing

Genuinely usable as a family car in a way most rivals in the price band are not: 545 litres of boot (1,670 with the 40/20/40 rear seats folded), a rear bench Chasing Cars rated a 'real highlight' for full-size adults, and a 1,100kg braked tow rating against the Megane E-Tech's 900kg

Ride and refinement are the standout: reviewers describe the damping as smooth and sophisticated over urban bumps, a clear step away from the Megane E-Tech's much-criticised firmness on its 20-inch wheels

Android Automotive with built-in Google Maps and Google Assistant, plus ADAS calibration that Australian reviewers say works quietly rather than beeping constantly -- a specific complaint they level at most Chinese rivals in this class

The $4,000 step from Techno EV60 to Techno Long Range EV87 buys 27kWh more usable battery, 195km more range and 35kW more power, which most reviewers call the pick of the range over the $65,990 Esprit Alpine
cons: Warranty is five years/100,000km per Renault Australia's own disclaimer, not the unlimited-kilometre cover Kia (seven years), Skoda (seven years) and Tesla offer -- a 20,000km-a-year driver is out of cover before year five ends

DC charging peaks at 130kW (EV60) and 150kW (EV87) on a 400-volt architecture, giving a 10-80% top-up of about 37 minutes -- slower than the 800-volt Kia EV3 and Hyundai Ioniq 5 despite the far bigger pack

Brake pedal feel is the most consistent criticism: CarExpert called the travel spongey and hard to modulate progressively, and reviewers also report noticeable road noise from the Michelin tyres and a low-resolution 360-degree camera

At $65,990 before on-roads the Esprit Alpine is knocking on Tesla Model Y money without ventilated seats or a sunroof, and it adds 20-inch wheels that firm up the ride the cheaper Techno grades get right

Renault is a small-volume brand here distributed by Ateco, service pricing was still unconfirmed at launch, and the sister Megane E-Tech has already been cut $10,000 from its launch price -- a resale risk this car inherits

summary: Skoda's compact electric SUV undercuts every other European EV on price in Australia and reviewers consistently rate its efficiency, DC charging speed and conventional, button-rich cabin as class-leading. The split verdict is on ride and range: Australian testers find the fixed-rate suspension too firm for patchy suburban tarmac, and the entry 60 Select's sub-400km WLTP claim asks buyers to pay $7,000 more for the 85 Select to get genuine touring range. Cheap prepaid servicing and a seven-year warranty offset an equipment list that still omits surround-view cameras, sat-nav and a connected app.
pros: 60 Select lists at $48,990 before on-roads, making it the cheapest European-built EV on sale in Australia and priced against Chinese rivals like the BYD Atto 3 and Geely EX5
Genuinely efficient: CarsGuide's long-term 60 Select averaged 15.9kWh/100km, exactly matching the WLTP claim, and CarExpert saw 12.8kWh/100km in the 85
Fast DC charging for the money - the 60 Select peaks at 165kW for 10-80 per cent in about 24 minutes, the 85 at 175kW in about 28 minutes
Prepaid servicing works out to roughly $195 a year over 10 years, with a 7-year/unlimited-km warranty
Rear-drive chassis, 9.3m turning circle and retained physical climate controls; 470L boot expanding to 1580L with Skoda's usual clever storage
cons: Suspension is tuned too firmly for Australian roads - reviewers report a busy, thumping ride over road joins, and no adaptive dampers are offered on Select grades
60 Select's 395km WLTP range is sub-400km; a real-world long-term test returned only 371km, so the 85 Select's 529km costs an extra $7,000
No ANCAP rating as at July 2026 - it relies on a 2025 five-star Euro NCAP result, which can be a blocker for fleet and novated-lease policies
Select grades go without surround-view camera, satellite navigation, vehicle-to-load and a spare tyre, and lack the connected app, remote climate and over-the-air updates rivals include
Lane-keeping assistance is over-sensitive and needs resetting each drive, a common complaint across Australian first drives

summary: The Enyaq is Skoda's mid-size electric SUV and the larger sibling to the Elroq, sold in Australia as a conventional SUV and a fastback Coupe across 60 Select, 85 Sportline and dual-motor RS grades. Australian reviewers rate it highly for packaging, real-world efficiency and a cabin that keeps physical controls, with scores clustered around 8.3/10, but they consistently criticise a firm ride and coarse-chip road noise unless the optional adaptive dampers are fitted. The critical buying decision is the price ladder: everything up to the Coupe 85 Sportline sits under the $75,000 FBT cap for novated leasing, while both RS grades sit just above it.
pros: 85 Sportline lists at $60,990 for 547km WLTP and 210kW, undercutting a Tesla Model Y Premium Long Range AWD ($68,900) and a Kia EV5 GT-Line AWD ($71,770) on range per dollar
Genuinely efficient in Australian conditions: CarsGuide averaged 16.6kWh/100km over 970km in the 85 Sportline and saw 13kWh/100km in city running, against a 15.9kWh/100km WLTP claim
585L boot expanding to 1710L in the SUV with Skoda's Simply Clever storage, plus rear-seat head and knee room reviewers single out as class-leading against the Kia EV5 and BYD Sealion 7
Long, cheap ownership terms: 7-year/unlimited-km warranty (8-year/160,000km battery) with 2-year/30,000km service intervals and a prepaid 8-year/120,000km pack for $1,650, about $206 a year
The RS adds 250kW/545Nm, 5.4s to 100km/h and a bigger 84kWh (79kWh usable) pack charging at up to 185kW DC, so 10-80 per cent takes about 26 minutes
cons: Both RS grades ($76,590 SUV, $77,590 Coupe) sit above the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so a novated lease loses the exemption that the $66,990 Coupe 85 Sportline still qualifies for

Ride is tuned too firmly without the cost-optional adaptive dampers - carsales calls it 'a little too tied down' on bumpy roads and CarsGuide reports intrusive road noise on coarse-chip surfaces with the 21-inch wheels
Only 1000kg braked towing on the 60 Select and 85 Sportline (1200kg on RS), well short of a Tesla Model Y's 1588kg or a Zeekr 7X's 2000kg
No spare tyre at any grade, only a repair kit, and the surround-view camera plus semi-autonomous park assist are options rather than standard on Sportline

Safety rating leans on a 2021 five-star Euro NCAP result for the pre-facelift car with no fresh ANCAP assessment, and the MY27 60 Select's switch to a smaller 61kWh LFP pack has no republished Australian WLTP range yet

summary: The Kodiaq Select Plug-in Hybrid is the only plug-in grade in Skoda Australia's large-SUV range, and its 19.7kWh usable battery and 110km WLTP electric range are the longest of any plug-in SUV under $70,000 here — enough that a Melbourne commuter with home charging would rarely wake the 1.5-litre engine. Reviewers are near-unanimous that the drivetrain is smooth and the cabin genuinely large, and equally unanimous on the catch: this is the one Kodiaq you cannot have with seven seats or all-wheel drive, because the battery sits where the third row goes. Where they split is value — CarExpert notes the $8,500 premium over the petrol Select 4x4 buys you fewer seats and less traction, while Chasing Cars still calls it easy to recommend against a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV or BYD Sealion 6.
pros: 110km of WLTP electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery is the longest in the mainstream plug-in SUV class — Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV claims 86km, BYD Sealion 6 81km and Mazda CX-60 PHEV 76km
50kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in 25 minutes) plus 11kW AC is unusual on a plug-in hybrid; neither the Outlander PHEV nor the Sealion 6 can take DC at all

Seven-year, unlimited-kilometre warranty applies with no strings — Skoda Australia made it standard across the range in September 2022 and it is not tied to buying a service pack or servicing inside the dealer network; the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km
745 litres behind the second row and 1,945 litres with it folded is more usable space than most five-seat rivals, and the second row slides and reclines
At $63,490 before on-roads it sits below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold, and at 42g/km CO2 it clears Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car test, so stamp duty is charged at the flat green rate
cons: Five seats only — the battery occupies the third-row well, so the one Kodiaq a large family would most want is the one that cannot carry seven; the petrol Select, Sportline and RS all seat seven and even the cheaper mild-hybrid offers a seven-seat option for $2,000

The 1.9L/100km label figure only survives if you plug in every night; Chasing Cars measured roughly 800km from the 45-litre tank with a brimmed battery on an interstate run, and UK owners report 32-40mpg (7-8.8L/100km) once the battery is flat, so the economics collapse for a buyer who cannot charge at home
Front-wheel drive only and 1,800kg braked towing, against 4x4 and 2,300kg on every petrol Kodiaq — CarExpert lists 'loses all-wheel drive' among its three headline dislikes
No spare wheel: the PHEV gets a tyre inflation kit where every other Kodiaq gets a space-saver, and it also loses the head-up display and the 289-litre third-row boot area

Plug-in hybrids lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, and Skoda Australia is already advertising the car at $59,990 drive-away against a $68,990 launch drive-away published in its own April 2026 spec sheet — roughly $9,000 off within months of launch, which is a real resale-value warning

summary: The smart #1 is a 4.27m electric crossover built on Geely's SEA platform and styled by Mercedes-Benz, sold in Australia by LSH Auto out of just three Mercedes-Benz showrooms in Sydney, Melbourne and Brisbane. Australian reviewers consistently rate the driving experience above its price -- a well-damped ride, quick 200kW rear-drive response and a rear seat that slides 15cm and genuinely fits adults -- and it now undercuts a Volvo EX30 on list price. Where opinion turns hostile is the software: nearly every function lives behind a 12.8-inch screen guarded by a fox avatar, and CarExpert singled out the speed-sign warnings and driver-monitoring camera as among the most intrusive it has tested.
pros: Undercuts its SEA-platform sibling the Volvo EX30 (from $49,990) while giving 200kW and 343Nm to the EX30 Plus's 200kW, and undercuts a BMW iX1 by roughly $29,000

150kW DC charging takes 10-80 per cent in under 30 minutes, and the Premium and BRABUS add 22kW three-phase AC -- a real advantage over the Pro+'s 7.4kW single-phase for anyone on a three-phase home supply
Rear bench slides 15cm and folds to 976 litres, so a 4.27m car carries adults in the back with legroom rivals like the Zeekr X cannot match
Rated to tow 1,600kg braked -- the same as an EX30 and unusual for a sub-$50,000 EV of this size
Five-star ANCAP rating, with a heat pump standard on Premium and BRABUS
cons: Climate, mirrors and most vehicle settings are buried in the 12.8-inch touchscreen behind an animated fox avatar; CarExpert found menu navigation deliberately obfuscated and could not reduce the adaptive cruise to plain cruise control

Driver-assist calibration draws repeated complaints: the speed-sign reader misread a 110km/h zone as 70km/h and chimed continuously, and the driver-monitoring camera flagged ordinary glances as distraction

Only three dealerships nationally (Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane) -- there is no smart service point in WA, SA, Tasmania, the ACT or the NT, which also narrows the resale market outside those three cities
Servicing is expensive for an EV: smart's own capped-price schedule runs $1,998 (Pro+) to $2,231 (BRABUS) over five years, with a $666-$701 single visit in years three and four

Residuals are an open question -- list prices were cut about $4,000-$5,000 within two years of the August 2024 launch, on top of near-continuous clearance campaigns, and the brand has no modern Australian resale history to price against

summary: The smart #3 is the coupe-roofed, 4.40m sister car to the smart #1, sharing that car's Geely SEA platform, 66kWh NMC pack and 200kW rear motor but stretching 130mm longer and sitting lower. Australian reviewers rate it as a quiet, well-damped semi-premium cruiser rather than the sports SUV the styling and the 3.7-second BRABUS suggest -- CarExpert's verdict is that it 'isn't a performance car' and 'is no corner carver', while praising the suspension and cabin isolation. The reservations are structural rather than dynamic: three showrooms nationally, a heavily discounted first two years on the market, and a 12.8-inch screen that swallows most vehicle functions.
pros: Costs $2,910 more than a smart #1 Pro+ for 15km more WLTP range (435km vs 420km), a 370-litre boot against the #1's 313 litres, and 130mm more length -- the practical pick of the two smart SUVs
Undercuts its SEA-platform cousin the Volvo EX30 while matching its 1,600kg braked towing rating, which is unusual for an electric SUV of this size
Premium and BRABUS add 22kW three-phase AC charging over the Pro+'s 7.4kW, cutting a 10-80 per cent AC top-up to under three hours; all three grades take 150kW DC for a sub-30-minute 10-80 per cent
Five-star ANCAP rating under the 2023 protocols (90 per cent adult, 85 per cent child occupant protection), applying to every #3 sold here since September 2024

The high-voltage battery carries a separate 8-year/150,000km warranty with a 70 per cent state-of-health guarantee, on top of the unconditional 5-year/150,000km vehicle cover -- but the battery cover requires servicing every 20,000km or 12 months at a smart-appointed dealer
cons: LSH Auto Australia runs just three showrooms -- Alexandria NSW, South Melbourne VIC and one in Brisbane -- so there is no smart sales or service point in WA, SA, Tasmania, the ACT or the NT, and clearance offers have been restricted to those three states

List prices were cut $5,000 across every grade within two years of the 2024 launch ($57,900/$61,900/$70,900 down to $52,900/$56,900/$65,900), on top of runout campaigns that put a Pro+ at $50,990 drive-away -- a saving CarExpert put at up to $11,500
Capped-price servicing runs four years/80,000km and totals $2,445 (Pro+) to $3,120 (BRABUS), which is expensive for an EV with 20,000km intervals
The coupe roofline costs rear headroom and rear visibility, and the boot is shallow with a high load lip; folding the 60/40 bench leaves a sloping floor rather than a flat one
Almost every vehicle function lives in the 12.8-inch touchscreen, and CarExpert found smart's claimed single-pedal e-Pedal mode 'fell just short' of actually stopping the car

summary: The facelifted 2026 Solterra addresses the original car's biggest weaknesses, gaining a larger 74.7kWh battery, more power (252kW combined) and up to 566km of WLTP range, backed by two rounds of price cuts in six months that make it far more competitive. Australian reviewers rate the driving experience highly - composed, quick and comfortable - and praise the upgraded, more premium-feeling cabin, though they still mark it down for tight practicality, some cabin ergonomic quirks and a ride that could use further tuning. Several reviewers suggest the entry AWD variant is the sweet spot of the range, rather than the higher-priced Touring.
pros: Major step up over the outgoing model: bigger battery, +92kW more power and notably longer range
Composed, quick and engaging to drive - CarsGuide rated the driving experience 9/10
Upgraded, more premium-feeling interior with a redesigned console and larger touchscreen
Two price cuts within six months have made it meaningfully more competitive against rivals like the Tesla Model Y and BYD Sealion 7
Standard AWD on both variants with a useful 1,500kg tow rating, unusual for a mid-size EV SUV at this price
cons: Practicality trails rivals - CarsGuide scored it just 5/10 on practicality, citing tight boot space and no passenger-side glovebox
Ride quality still needs further tuning - reviewers describe it as firm with more bounciness than ideal
Cabin ergonomic quirks, including an instrument display that can be partly obstructed and an intrusive driver-monitoring system
Repeated price cuts so soon after launch raise doubts about resale value and initial pricing
Touring grade seen as poor value next to the base AWD, which reviewers say is the better buy in the range

summary: The Trailseeker is a longer, boxier take on the Solterra that Subaru pitches as an electric Outback: 280kW, 4.5 seconds to 100km/h and 211mm of ground clearance, with a 609-litre boot and a 1,500kg braked tow rating. Australian reviewers rate the drivetrain and comfort highly - CarsGuide gave it 8.1/10 - but consistently mark it down for efficiency, noting it travels less far than the smaller Solterra on the same battery. Opinion splits on whether it earns its price: Chasing Cars argues Subaru stopped short of real off-road hardware and that a petrol Outback makes more sense for most buyers, while CarsGuide sees the $63,990 base AWD as the pick of the two grades.
pros: Subaru's fastest production car sold here - 280kW and 0-100km/h in 4.5 seconds, quicker than a Tesla Model Y Long Range
211mm ground clearance with dual-mode X-Mode, plus a 1,500kg braked tow rating that most mid-size EVs cannot match
609L boot (595L on the Touring) expanding to about 1,694L - larger than the Solterra's 410L and the bZ4X's 452L
Capped-price servicing at roughly $197 a visit over 5 years/75,000km, and 22kW three-phase AC charging on both grades
Subaru cut both grades by $4,000 on 14 May 2026, so the Touring lands at $69,990 and the whole range stays under the $75,000 FBT threshold
cons: Range is the weak point: 533km WLTP on the base AWD and only 488km on the Touring's 20-inch wheels, less than the smaller Solterra gets from the same pack (74.7kWh gross, 71kWh usable)
150kW peak DC charging is slow for the money - 10-80% takes about 30 minutes when rivals at this price do it in 20
No spare wheel on either grade, only a puncture repair kit, which undercuts the all-terrain positioning
A $4,000 price cut within a month of launch, on top of two Solterra cuts in six months, points to soft resale for Subaru's EVs
5-year/unlimited-km warranty trails Kia's 7 and BYD's 6, and there are no over-the-air updates or connected-car services

summary: Subaru's third and cheapest EV is the electric twin of the Toyota C-HR+ and lands in Australia as a single, fully-loaded dual-motor AWD grade at $59,990 before on-roads, with 252kW, a 74.7kWh gross (71kWh usable) battery and 522km of WLTP range. Australian coverage so far is launch pricing and specification analysis rather than road tests - no local drive review had been published at the time of writing - and the consensus argument is about value: it is quick, generously equipped and the only genuine all-wheel-drive small electric SUV near the price, but a Kia EV3 starts more than $12,000 below it. Overseas first drives praise the ride and body control while flagging the fastback roofline's cost to rear headroom and boot space.
pros: Only one grade and it is the loaded one: 20-inch alloys, 14-inch touchscreen, 10-speaker Harman Kardon audio, heated front and rear outboard seats, heated wheel, power tailgate, 360-degree camera and 1500W V2L are all standard
252kW dual-motor Symmetrical AWD for a 5.0-second 0-100km/h, with 211mm of ground clearance and dual-mode X-Mode - no front-drive-only rival at the price offers both
22kW three-phase AC charging (0-100% in about four hours) alongside 150kW DC, where most small electric SUVs cap AC at 7-11kW
Uses the same 74.7kWh gross battery pack and 252kW output as the larger Solterra AWD in a lighter, quicker body for $2,000 less list price
Five-star ANCAP rating published June 2026 (88% adult, 86% child occupant protection), carried across from Euro NCAP testing of the Toyota C-HR+ and bZ4X
cons: Subaru Australia's own specification sheet lists no braked or unbraked towing rating at all, where the Solterra and Trailseeker are both rated to 1,500kg

403 litres behind the rear seat and 1,089 litres folded is small for the money, and the fastback roofline costs rear headroom - the panoramic roof cuts the to-ceiling figure further, from 1,323 to 1,304 litres
$59,990 is top-of-segment for a small electric SUV: a Kia EV3 opens at $47,600, and Subaru's own recommended drive-away is about $65,400-$65,600 depending on postcode
Subaru cut Solterra prices twice and Trailseeker prices by $4,000 on the very day the Uncharted was priced, which is an uncomfortable precedent for early-buyer resale
16.0kWh/100km WLTP is only average efficiency for a compact SUV, and the 20-inch wheels are the sole fitment - there is no smaller-wheel, longer-range configuration as offered overseas

summary: Suzuki's first battery-electric car in Australia is a 4.28m small SUV built in India on a BYD-supplied LFP battery, sold in Victoria as the 49kWh front-drive Motion and the 61kWh dual-motor Ultra. Reviewers broadly agree it drives well and feels a class above its price inside, and broadly agree it is priced above what its 344-395km WLTP range and 70kW DC charging justify against BYD, MG and Kia rivals. Suzuki publishes drive-away pricing only and no list price, and the launch figures rose $2,000-$3,000 once the 100-car introductory allocation ended.
pros: Five years/unlimited kilometres of warranty with no servicing conditions attached — Suzuki Australia advertises no longer conditional term, unlike MG, Nissan or Hyundai, so the headline number is the number you actually get; the traction battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km.
The Ultra's ALLGRIP-e dual-motor all-wheel drive makes 135kW/307Nm and runs 0-100km/h in 7.4 seconds; the BYD Atto 2, MG S5 EV and Kia EV3 rivals it is cross-shopped against are front-drive only.

The rear bench slides and reclines, so boot space moves between 238 litres with maximum rear legroom and 306 litres with the bench forward, and 562 litres with the seats folded — you choose legroom or luggage per trip.

Capped-price servicing is covered by Suzuki's 5-year/100,000km Genuine Service Program at 12-month/20,000km intervals, and a Type 2 AC charging cable Suzuki values at over $1,000 is standard on both grades.
Suzuki has one of the larger established dealer and parts networks in regional Australia, which is a real difference from the newer Chinese brands the e Vitara is priced against.
cons: At $49,990 and $58,990 drive-away post-introductory, it is roughly $10,000 dearer than a BYD Atto 2 and above the MG S5 EV and Kia EV3 while offering less range than any of them — CarExpert and EV Central both make price the central criticism.
CarsGuide measured about 295km in the Ultra against its 395km WLTP claim, a shortfall near 100km, and recorded 17.9kWh/100km against the 16.5kWh/100km official figure.
DC charging peaks around 70kW for a 45-minute 10-80% stop on both battery sizes — slow for 2026 — and there is no vehicle-to-load outlet.
Four stars from ANCAP in 2026, with 77% adult occupant protection and no head-protecting centre airbag; most direct rivals hold five stars.

Victorian buyers get two grades only. The 61kWh front-drive Ultra — the longest-range e Vitara at 426km WLTP, at $54,990 drive-away — is sold solely by the separate Suzuki Queensland distributor covering Queensland and the Northern Rivers of NSW, and cannot be ordered here.

summary: Australian reviewers regard the updated Model 3 as the class benchmark among electric sedans, praising a noticeably quieter cabin and softer ride than earlier versions alongside brisk performance and strong efficiency. The Long Range RWD's 750km WLTP claim makes it the longest-range EV sold in the country, while the screen-only control layout continues to split opinion. The Performance variant's near-$81,000 list price also pushes it close to the FBT exemption threshold that keeps novated-lease buyers interested in the cheaper variants.
pros: Long Range RWD offers the longest WLTP range of any EV on sale in Australia at 750km
Access to Tesla's extensive Australian Supercharger network plus regular over-the-air software updates
Recent refresh brings a quieter cabin and noticeably improved ride comfort over the outgoing model
Strong outright performance, with the dual-motor Performance variant hitting 100km/h in around 3.1 seconds
cons: Touchscreen-only interface, including indicators and gear selection on some builds, remains a sticking point for reviewers
Comprehensive insurance premiums tend to sit at the higher end of the EV market due to repair and parts costs
Performance variant's list price sits close to the $75,000 FBT exemption threshold, eroding some of the novated-lease tax advantage

summary: The Model Y is Australia's highest-volume EV, and since the 2025 'Juniper' overhaul Australian reviewers broadly agree it fixed the old car's crashy ride without surrendering its efficiency or Supercharger advantage. The range now runs from the $58,900 Premium RWD to the $89,400 Performance, plus a $74,900 six-seat Model Y L that lands just $100 under the $75,000 mark a novated-lease buyer cares about. Where reviewers split is the cabin: some rate the 16-inch-screen minimalism as fast and uncluttered, others call the car soulless and will not forgive the absence of Apple CarPlay at any price.
pros: Range per dollar leads the segment: $68,900 buys 600km WLTP in the Premium Long Range AWD, and even the $58,900 Premium RWD claims 466km
The Juniper update's adaptive dampers and extra sound deadening are the specific thing CarExpert and Chasing Cars single out as fixing the pre-2025 car's harsh ride and road noise
Model Y L adds a genuinely adult-usable third row and 3.3kW vehicle-to-load for $74,900 — around $20,000 under a Kia EV9 and still inside the FBT-exempt window
Every variant is rated to tow 1,588kg braked, including the entry RWD, and all carry the 5-star 2025 ANCAP result
Tesla lifted its Australian warranty to 5 years/unlimited km for cars delivered from 1 January 2026 (previously 4 years/80,000km), with 5 years of roadside assistance
cons: No Apple CarPlay or Android Auto on any variant — the single most repeated criticism in Australian reviews and a deal-breaker for some buyers
Wipers, mirrors, glovebox and drive modes all live in the 16-inch touchscreen; the Juniper update brought the indicator stalk back but nothing else
The $89,400 Performance costs $20,500 more than the Long Range for 20km less WLTP range, and it is the only variant that pushes a lease past the $75,000 mark
Resale carries Tesla-specific risk: the entry car's list price fell roughly $16,000 across 2023-24, and Tesla now sells a guaranteed-future-value product locally to reassure buyers about it

summary: The updated bZ4X is a much stronger car than the one Toyota launched: a 74.7kWh battery lifts the front-drive model to 591km WLTP and Toyota cut $10,010 off its price, so at $55,990 before on-roads it now undercuts a Tesla Model Y RWD while claiming 125km more range. Australian reviewers agree it is efficient, quiet and far better value than before - scores land between 6.5 and 8 out of 10 - but they split on the chassis, with CarsGuide and carsales calling the ride comfortable and nicely balanced while CarExpert and Chasing Cars find it lumpy above 40km/h with numb steering. The recurring complaints are ergonomic rather than mechanical, and the entry 2WD on 18-inch wheels is the grade most reviewers single out as the pick of the range.
pros: At $55,990 before on-roads the 2WD undercuts a Tesla Model Y RWD ($58,900) and a Kia EV5 Air Standard Range ($56,770) while claiming 591km WLTP against their 466km and 400km
Genuinely efficient rather than just optimistic on paper: 138Wh/km WLTP, and Australian testers recorded 14.4-14.9kWh/100km in mixed driving, so 500km between charges is realistic
AC charging doubled to 22kW three-phase, filling the 74.7kWh pack in about 3h30m - unusually quick for AC and useful if you have three-phase at home
Battery cover extends to 10 years with on-time servicing and the electric motors are warranted for 7, beyond the 8-year/160,000km battery-only cover most rivals stop at
AWD and Touring are rated at 1,500kg braked towing, and the Touring adds a 603L boot and 211mm of running ground clearance without the usual EV load-lip
cons: Its mechanical twin undercuts it: the Subaru Solterra AWD lists at $61,990 against the bZ4X AWD's $67,990, and Subaru bundles five years of scheduled servicing where Toyota charges roughly $180-$190 per 12-month/15,000km visit - the Toyota's counterarguments are the cheaper FWD grade, the longer motor and battery warranty, and a dealer network roughly twice the size
452 litres seats-up is small for a mid-size SUV (a Kia EV5 has 513L, a Model Y 854L) and there is no frunk and no conventional glovebox, so cabin storage is genuinely short

The 7-inch instrument display sits far forward and is partly obscured by the steering wheel rim for taller drivers - flagged by CarExpert, carsales, Chasing Cars and CarsGuide alike, and not fixed by this update
DC fast charging is still capped at 150kW, with Toyota quoting 10-80% in about 45 minutes for the 2WD, so road-trip stops are longer than in an 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 or Kia EV6

Cuts of $10,010 (2WD) and $6,910 (AWD) inside a single model year gutted residuals on earlier bZ4X stock, and no Australian reviewer lists resale as a strength; there is also no spare wheel on any grade, only a repair kit

summary: Australia's first battery-electric HiLux went on sale in May 2026 as a dual-cab only, dual-motor 144kW/468Nm ute in SR and SR5 pick-up form, and reviewers agree it is a genuine HiLux everywhere except the numbers that matter to a tradie: 245km of WLTP range, 2000kg braked towing and a 715kg payload. Where they part company is who it is for — CarExpert, Chasing Cars and RACV all read it as a depot-charged fleet and mine-site tool rather than a diesel replacement, while EV Central and WhichCar give it more credit as a first step that finally brings five-star safety and Toyota's dealer network to the electric-ute segment. Toyota itself expects only 500 sales in 2026, and fewer than ten of the first 300 orders went to private buyers.
pros: The only electric ute in Australia with a five-star ANCAP rating (2025 datestamp), which included assessment of high-voltage battery integrity in the crash tests — the LDV eT60 and its ilk have nothing comparable.

Reviewers rate it the quietest and smoothest HiLux ever sold: the twin-motor drivetrain removes the 2.8-litre diesel's clatter entirely, and it holds full-time AWD capability that survived Toyota's own off-road demonstration loop.
Fleet-friendly charging for a ute — 10kW three-phase AC fills the pack in about 6.5 hours overnight at a depot, and 150kW DC does 10-80 per cent in roughly 30 minutes.

Both pick-up grades list below the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and the 715kg payload keeps it under the one-tonne limit, so it qualifies as a car for the electric-car FBT exemption on a novated lease.

Toyota's 5-year/unlimited-km warranty stretches to 7 years on the driveline and the traction battery cover to 10 years — but only if every scheduled service and the annual battery health check are completed by a Toyota dealer.
cons: 245km WLTP range, and Australian testers averaged 23-24.5kWh/100km for about 220km in practice; a Ranger PHEV or Shark 6 covers 800km-plus before it needs anything.
2000kg braked towing against 3500kg for the diesel HiLux, the Ford Ranger PHEV, the GWM Cannon Alpha PHEV and the Shark 6 Performance — a 1.5-tonne cut in the headline number ute buyers shop on.
715kg payload versus 985kg for the equivalent diesel SR5, so a loaded tray plus five occupants can put it over GVM on a vehicle that already weighs about 2.45 tonnes.
Roughly $17,000 dearer than the equivalent diesel HiLux, and it gives up the low-range transfer case and rear diff lock while sitting 6mm lower on ground clearance.
Servicing every 6 months or 10,000km at about $450 a visit, near $2200 across five years — unusually short intervals for an EV, and reviewers still criticise the unladen ride as rough.

summary: Toyota's first plug-in hybrid for Australia, launched on the country's best-selling SUV nameplate in late June 2026: a 22.7kWh pack, 113-121km of WLTP electric range and 50kW DC charging, in three grades from $58,840 to $66,340. Reviewers agree the powertrain sets the class benchmark for electric range and refinement and that the car is genuinely quick, but they are just as consistent that once the battery is flat it drinks about 6L/100km - no better than the cheaper conventional hybrid. The argument against it is price rather than execution: it undercuts nothing from BYD or Chery, and without home charging the plug-in premium is money wasted.
pros: 121km of WLTP electric range on the XSE 2WD and 113km on the AWD grades, against 84km for a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and 81km for a BYD Sealion 6 - enough to cover a week of average Melbourne commuting between plug-ins.

50kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in about 30 minutes) and 11kW three-phase AC are standard across the PHEV range, where most plug-in rivals in the class top out at 3.7kW or 6.6kW AC and cannot DC charge at all.
227kW combined in AWD form makes this the quickest RAV4 sold in Australia at around 5.7sec to 100km/h; the 2WD still musters 201kW.
The battery costs less boot than in most plug-in rivals - 655L VDA versus 705L for the non-plug-in RAV4, a 50L penalty rather than the 80-100L several competitors give up.

Five years/unlimited km warranty with no servicing strings attached (driveline cover extends to seven years if you service in the Toyota network), and capped-price servicing at about $325 per visit for the first five services.
cons: Once the battery is depleted it is simply a heavy hybrid: RACV measured 6.0L/100km in HEV mode on an undemanding rural route, no better than the cheaper non-plug-in RAV4, and Toyota specifies 95 RON premium.

Toyota's 0.7L/100km ADR combined-cycle figure is a laboratory artefact that assumes you start every trip fully charged - CarsGuide calls it 'fanciful' - so the running-cost case collapses for anyone who cannot charge at home overnight.
Plug-in hybrids lost the FBT exemption on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease maths is far weaker than for a battery-electric rival at the same money, including Toyota's own bZ4X.

At $58,840-$66,340 the PHEV asks roughly $5,000 more than the equivalent hybrid RAV4 and thousands more again than a BYD Sealion 6 or Chery Tiggo 8 PHEV; multiple Australian reviews call the pricing uncompetitive against the Chinese plug-ins.

There is no driver-selectable mode that meaningfully recharges the drive battery on the move, the AWD PHEV carries about 285kg more than the hybrid, and the new-generation RAV4 has no ANCAP rating at launch.

summary: The ES90 is Volvo's first electric passenger car for Australia, a five-metre liftback that Australian reviewers agree is priced to embarrass the segment: it opens roughly $46,000 below a Mercedes-Benz EQE 300 and $67,000 below a BMW i5 while matching them on claimed range. Testers rate the cabin, refinement and driver-assistance calibration highly and the driving experience merely competent, with the steer-by-wire rack and the Ultra's 22-inch wheels drawing the most comment. What reviewers disagree on is whether anyone will buy it, because it is a big non-SUV in an SUV market, it carries no ANCAP rating yet, and its own EX90 sibling does nearly everything it does with a 655-litre boot.
pros: The Plus opens at $88,880 before on-road costs, which is $46,320 under a Mercedes-Benz EQE 300 ($135,200) and $67,020 under a BMW i5 eDrive40 ($155,900), and it lands under the $91,661 luxury-car tax and electric-car FBT exemption threshold that both German rivals clear by a wide margin

Volvo's first 800-volt car: 554km of range from an 88kWh usable pack, with a 10-80 per cent DC recharge quoted at 22 minutes on a 300kW charger and up to 300km of range added in 10 minutes, against roughly half an hour for the 400-volt BMW i5
Rated to tow 1,600kg braked, more than a BMW i5's 1,500kg and far more than the large electric sedans that carry no tow rating at all

The liftback tailgate is the practical argument for the shape: 424 litres expands to 1,427 litres with the second row folded, against 785 litres for a BMW i5's boot-lid sedan, plus a 27-litre front compartment for charge cables

CarsGuide scored the safety package 9/10 and called Volvo's driver-assistance integration industry best practice, noting the systems 'only work if you need them in an emergency' rather than beeping constantly - and MY2026 cars drop the roof-mounted lidar pod after Volvo split with the supplier, keeping five radars, seven cameras and 12 ultrasonic sensors
cons: No ANCAP or Euro NCAP rating at the research date, which is an awkward gap for a car sold on Volvo's safety reputation; the case for it rests on the related EX90's rating rather than a test of this body

The Ultra at $107,990 sits $16,329 over the $91,661 threshold, so it attracts luxury car tax and loses the electric-car FBT exemption the Plus keeps - and the $19,110 step buys 22-inch wheels, active air suspension, pixel LED headlights and a 25-speaker Bowers & Wilkins system, not a metre more range

Australia gets only the 245kW single-motor rear-drive car; the 500kW Twin Motor and the larger 106kWh battery sold in Europe are unconfirmed here, so there is no long-range or performance grade to step up to

Steer-by-wire needs acclimatising - CarsGuide found it 'literally feels like an old computer game steering wheel set-up, with very little resistance' during parking manoeuvres - and lane-keeping assist 'has a tendency to move in the lane slightly too much'

Volvo runs only about 28 dealer and service points nationally and had not published capped-price servicing for its EVs when the ES90 launched, so everything beyond electricity and tyres is an unquantified running cost

summary: The EX30 is Volvo's compact electric SUV, praised by Australian reviewers for punchy, agile handling, a well-damped ride and a distinctive, upmarket cabin featuring wool-blend seat trim. Sharp price cuts through 2026 have pushed the single-motor Plus below $50,000 before on-roads, making it one of the more attainable premium-badged EVs on the market, and it carries a five-star ANCAP safety rating. It is let down for family duty by a tight rear seat and modest boot, and reviewers are split on whether that's a fair trade-off for its style and driving manners.
pros: Agile, well-controlled handling and a comfortable ride, with brisk acceleration even in the base single-motor form
Distinctive Scandinavian interior design with higher-grade materials, including wool-blend seat trim, that feels a step above rivals
Aggressive 2026 price cuts (Plus from $49,990 before on-roads) bring a premium-badged EV within reach of mainstream buyers
Five-star ANCAP safety rating and strong standard safety tech
cons: Almost every function -- climate control, mirror adjustment, even the glovebox -- is buried in the portrait touchscreen with no driver instrument display; some reviewers call this the car's biggest flaw and report the screen lagging or crashing, while others say it becomes tolerable after a week of familiarity, so opinion is genuinely split rather than uniformly negative
Window switches are relocated to the centre console instead of the doors, one of several cost-saving control choices reviewers find awkward
Small rear seat and boot space limit its practicality as a family car
DC fast-charging speeds are competent rather than class-leading

summary: The EX40 is the renamed XC40 Recharge, a petrol-car-derived compact SUV that Australian reviewers consistently describe as sensible rather than exciting: comfortable, easy to live with and generously equipped, but behind purpose-built EVs on efficiency and packaging. April 2026 price cuts of $7,000 across the range dropped it to $69,990 and $74,990 before on-road costs, which reviewers treat as its strongest argument against a BMW iX1 or Mercedes-Benz EQA. Where opinion divides is whether an eight-year-old platform, a lapsed crash rating and the imminent EX60 make this a run-out bargain or a car worth waiting out.
pros: Both grades were cut by $7,000 in April 2026 to $69,990 and $74,990 before on-road costs, undercutting a BMW iX1 xDrive30 by roughly $8,000 and a Mercedes-Benz EQA 250+ by roughly $11,000 for comparable equipment

Volvo includes five years of complimentary scheduled servicing at 2-year/30,000km intervals plus five years roadside assistance, and covers the drive battery for 8 years/160,000km, so the only routine cost for the warranty period is tyres and electricity
Rated to tow 1,500kg braked as a Single Motor and 1,800kg as a Twin Motor, well clear of the 750-1,000kg typical of compact electric SUVs

There is only one equipment level and it is the top one: panoramic roof, 360-degree camera, Harman Kardon audio and Pilot Assist are standard, with paint, wheels and interior trim the only choices on the configurator

Volvo quotes a 28-minute 10-80 per cent DC recharge on a 200kW charger, and Australian testers recorded 17-18kWh/100km on the road after the 2024 motor and battery update cut the AWD car's consumption from nearly 24kWh/100km
cons: The five-star ANCAP rating it inherited from the petrol XC40 was datestamped 2018 and expired in December 2024, so the EX40 is now sold with no current crash rating -- an odd position for a car bought largely on Volvo's safety reputation

410 litres with the seats up trails a Kia EV6 (480L) and is barely half a Tesla Model Y (854L), and because the body was designed around a petrol drivetrain the front boot is only 31 litres and the load lip is high
The sole Ultra grade rides on 20-inch wheels; reviewers found the ride noticeably firmer than on the 19s the earlier single-motor cars wore, thudding over sharp bumps around town
Regeneration is a single on/off one-pedal switch with no selectable levels, where Hyundai and Kia rivals give you steering-wheel paddles

It is a run-out: the EX60 replacement is due in Australia in late 2026 or early 2027, EX40 sales fell about 40 per cent to 743 units in 2025, and two rounds of price cuts inside a year point to soft resale
