summary: The EX90 is Volvo's electric flagship and, alongside the six-seat Cadillac Vistiq, the only luxury-badged three-row battery SUV on sale in Australia. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the cabin, the quietness and the safety case -- ANCAP tested it in 2025 and it returned the highest adult occupant protection score of any vehicle rated that year -- while splitting over the ride, which is terse on the passive Plus and floaty-then-bouncy on the Ultra's air springs. The MY26 rebuild onto an 800-volt architecture with a 106kWh pack and 350kW DC charging fixed the launch car's biggest weakness, but at $124,990 and $134,990 before on-road costs the range clears the $91,661 FBT threshold by a wide margin and Volvo is about to reopen it $18,000 lower with a single-motor base grade.
pros: ANCAP rated the EX90 five stars on 2025 test protocols with 92 per cent adult occupant protection -- the highest score of any vehicle ANCAP rated in 2025 -- plus 94 per cent child occupant protection, 82 per cent vulnerable road user and 84 per cent safety assist

Ownership costs are close to nil beyond tyres and electricity for five years: a 5-year/unlimited-kilometre unconditional warranty, 8 years of drive-battery cover, 5 years roadside assistance, and scheduled servicing to 5 years/150,000km included in the purchase price at $0

The MY26 switch from 400 to 800 volts lifted DC fast-charging from 250kW to a 350kW peak, and Volvo Australia quotes 10-80 per cent in about 24 minutes -- a Cadillac Vistiq, its only luxury three-row electric rival here, peaks at 130kW

Rated to tow 2,200kg braked and genuinely seats seven adults on individual sliding second-row seats, in a segment where the Audi and BMW alternatives at this money are five-seaters and a Mercedes-Benz EQS SUV starts at $197,200 before on-road costs

Volvo quotes a 0.29 drag coefficient and Australian testers single out the cabin as one of the quietest they have measured, with CarExpert rating its Pilot Assist and lane-keeping calibration ahead of the Polestar and Zeekr cars that share the same Geely software stack
cons: Neither grade comes near the electric-car FBT exemption: the cheapest EX90 is $124,990 before on-road costs, roughly $33,000 above the $91,661 fuel-efficient luxury car tax threshold, and about $10,000 of that sticker is luxury car tax

Volvo replaces the entry Plus Twin Motor with a $106,990 Plus Single Motor in September/October 2026, an $18,000 cut to the range's opening price within months, on top of a MY26 change from 400V to 800V that leaves every launch car on the slower architecture -- both point to weak early resale
Australia gets the EX90 as a seven-seater only, with no six-seat captain's-chair layout of the kind offered on the Kia EV9 GT and Cadillac Vistiq, and only 324 litres behind the third row

Reviewers agree the primary ride never settles: CarExpert found the passively sprung Plus on 20-inch wheels 'a little busy and jittery' over pockmarked roads, and CarsGuide found the Ultra's twin-chamber air suspension 'bouncy over bigger bumps, especially over the rear axle'

At 2,764kg and a claimed 22.8kWh/100km it is thirstier than a Hyundai Ioniq 9 or Kia EV9 on the same duty cycle, and its 521km WLTP range is well short of the 570km the pre-update launch cars advertised

summary: The XC60 T8 is the plug-in half of Volvo's mid-size luxury SUV range, sold in Australia only in Plus and Ultra Dark trim alongside the non-plug-in B5 mild hybrids. Reviewers are consistent that it is the calmest and best-finished car in its class and that its 79km WLTP electric range is among the longest of the mainstream premium plug-ins, but they split on whether the money makes sense: at $92,990-$101,990 it is priced against a BMW X3 30e xDrive and a Mercedes-Benz GLC 350e while carrying an ageing cabin architecture and an expired ANCAP rating. The economics rest entirely on charging at home, because with the battery flat it drinks like the petrol SUV it becomes.
pros: 79km of WLTP electric range is well ahead of a Mazda CX-60 PHEV's 62km or a Kia Sorento PHEV's 58km, and Chasing Cars measured just over 70km in real driving — enough that a typical Melbourne commute never wakes the engine.
340kW/709Nm and 4.8sec to 100km/h make the T8 quicker than any petrol XC60 and quicker than the BMW X3 30e xDrive it is priced against.
Rated to tow 2250kg braked, which is 250kg more than a Mazda CX-60 PHEV and unusually strong for a plug-in hybrid.
Five-year unconditional unlimited-kilometre warranty, with the drive battery separately covered for 8 years/160,000km.
Reviewers repeatedly single out ride comfort and noise isolation as the car's real advantage over the German plug-ins rather than outright pace.
cons: The 1.6L/100km label figure only holds if you plug in every night; once the battery is depleted the T8 runs at roughly 8.4L/100km, so a buyer without home charging is paying luxury-PHEV money to run a 2.2-tonne petrol SUV.
AC charging only at 6.4kW and no DC fast-charging, so a full recharge is about three hours on a wallbox and around seven from a household socket — you cannot usefully top up on a road trip.
The battery pack costs 15 litres of boot (468L against the petrol XC60's 483L) and raises the centre tunnel enough that Chasing Cars called the middle rear seat close to unusable.

Both grades sit above the $91,661 fuel-efficient LCT threshold and far above the $75,000 FBT cap, and PHEVs lost the electric-car FBT exemption on 1 April 2025 — the novated-lease case that carried this car in 2024 no longer exists.
CarExpert notes the XC60's ANCAP rating expired in December 2023 and that the platform is showing its age against newer rivals on cabin tech.

summary: The T8 is the only plug-in XC90 — the B5 grades alongside it are 48-volt mild hybrids with no charge port — and it is currently the only seven-seat plug-in hybrid sold in Australia above $100,000, which is most of its case. Australian reviewers are close to unanimous on the driving: 340kW, air suspension as standard and a ride-handling balance carsales rated among the best it has sampled in an SUV. Where they diverge is on whether a decade-old platform justifies $130,990, and they agree the numbers are dated — about 69km of WLTP electric range when newer plug-ins clear 100km, AC-only charging, and 7.7L/100km once the battery is flat.
pros: The only seven-seat plug-in hybrid on sale in Australia above $100,000: the Audi Q7, BMW X5 xDrive50e and Mercedes-Benz GLE 450e are all five-seat in their PHEV form, and the cheaper seven-seat plug-ins (Kia Sorento PHEV, Mazda CX-80) sit a full class below on price and equipment

Braked towing is 2400kg, unusually high for a monocoque plug-in hybrid — the Kia Sorento PHEV manages 1010kg and the Mazda CX-80 PHEV 2500kg — so the battery does not cost you a caravan the way it does in most PHEV rivals

Height-adjustable four-mode air suspension is standard on both grades, and carsales rated the resulting ride-handling balance as one of the best it has experienced in an SUV, achieved on 22-inch wheels without any Australian-specific retune

Charge it and the petrol engine barely runs: CarsGuide recorded 3.4L/100km across a week of mixed driving with regular home charging, against 8.1L/100km for the mild-hybrid B5 XC90 that costs about $25,000 less

Volvo's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, the high-voltage battery carries a separate eight-year/160,000km cover, and capped-price servicing runs $2380 for three years or $3870 for five on 12-month/15,000km intervals
cons: Charging is AC-only through a 3.6kW onboard charger with no DC capability at all — roughly three hours on a two-phase 6.4kW wallbox, and overnight on a household socket — so a buyer without off-street parking cannot realistically keep the battery full and is left running a 2.4-tonne petrol SUV

Once the battery is depleted it drinks like what it is: carsales measured 7.7L/100km over a week-long loan, and Volvo's own European data quotes 7.2-8.0L/100km with the battery empty, against a 1.8L/100km label figure that assumes you start every trip charged

Electric range is the weak spot of the package — about 69km on WLTP, and both CarsGuide and carsales ran out of battery in the low 60s against the 77km NEDC figure Volvo Australia advertises — at a time when several cheaper plug-in hybrids claim more than 100km

The third row is genuinely awkward: there is no boot-side release, so raising the seats means climbing into the load bay or reaching through a rear door to work a heavy lever, and CarsGuide described the process as too much effort to want to repeat regularly
Boot space behind the raised third row is 262 litres, and there is no spare wheel of any kind — only a repair kit — because of the packaging demanded by the battery pack

summary: The ID.4 is Volkswagen's mid-size electric SUV and its first battery-electric car sold here in volume, offered in exactly two grades: the 210kW rear-drive Pro and the 250kW dual-motor GTX 4MOTION. Australian reviewers land around 7.8/10 and agree on the strengths - ride comfort, the massaging front seats and genuinely good highway efficiency - but split on whether the cabin plastics and the missing built-in navigation are forgivable at the price. Both grades list below the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, so the real decision is whether the GTX's extra 40kW, all-wheel drive and 1800kg tow rating justify $10,000 and 33km of WLTP range.
pros: The $59,990 Pro claims 544km WLTP from a 77kWh usable pack, roughly 80km more than the Tesla Model Y RWD it is priced against ($58,900), and 15km more than a Skoda Elroq 85 Select
Efficiency holds up in Australian testing: carsales averaged 16.6kWh/100km over more than 1000km against a 16.7kWh/100km WLTP claim, so the Pro's real highway range lands near 450-470km

Adaptive dampers with 15 settings, Matrix LED headlights, a panoramic glass roof and heated massaging ErgoActive front seats are standard on the base Pro - a Skoda Enyaq Sportline charges extra for the dampers
Both grades DC fast-charge at up to 175kW, adding about 178km in 10 minutes, and 24-month/30,000km service intervals keep six years of maintenance to $1,785 (about $298 a year)
The $69,990 GTX adds 250kW/679Nm and 4MOTION for 5.4s to 100km/h plus an 1800kg braked tow rating, well clear of a Tesla Model Y's 1588kg and a Skoda Enyaq RS's 1200kg
cons: No embedded satellite navigation and no wireless Apple CarPlay or Android Auto, and no spare tyre at any grade - only a repair kit

Volkswagen has repriced the Pro three times in about a year on drive-away campaigns ($59,990, then $63,990, then $64,990) while still clearing run-out MY25.0 stock at $59,990 drive-away, which weighs on resale

400V architecture caps DC charging at 175kW against the 800V Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6, and real-world consumption stretches a long way past the claim - 18.7kWh/100km on Chasing Cars' hilly launch route and about 20kWh/100km for CarsGuide
Wind and road noise dominate at motorway speeds - CarsGuide rates the Ioniq 5, EV6 and Model Y as more peaceful - and multiple reviewers call the steering devoid of feedback
The five-star ANCAP rating carries over from a 2021 Euro NCAP test of the pre-update car, and Australian media have flagged an extensively revised ID.4, so the current car is late in its cycle

summary: The ID.5 is the coupe-liftback body of Volkswagen's ID.4, sold in Australia in only two grades - the 210kW rear-drive Pro and the 250kW dual-motor GTX 4Motion - both on the same MEB platform and 82-84kWh battery. Australian reviewers rate the Pro highly for real-world efficiency and ride refinement, with several calling it one of the better-driving mid-size electric SUVs, but they are close to unanimous that the GTX's $10,000 premium buys less range than it costs and that the sloping roof and haptic controls cost the car genuine practicality. Both grades list under the $75,000 FBT exemption cap, though the GTX clears it by only $2,010 before dealer delivery or options.
pros: The Pro lists at $62,990 for 543km WLTP from a 77kWh usable pack, $3,000 more than the ID.4 Pro but $4,000 under a Skoda Enyaq Coupe 85 Sportline ($66,990) with almost identical range

Beats its own efficiency claim in Australian conditions: CarsGuide's long-term Pro averaged 15.8kWh/100km against a 16.3kWh/100km claim, and carsales recorded 16.1kWh/100km in the GTX against 16.9kWh/100km claimed

Tows well clear of its MEB siblings: 1,200kg braked on the Pro and 1,800kg on the dual-motor GTX 4Motion (rated at a 12 per cent gradient), against 1,000-1,200kg for a Skoda Enyaq and 1,000-1,200kg for an Audi Q4 e-tron
Cheap scheduled maintenance: 2-year/30,000km service intervals with a prepaid 10-year/150,000km plan at $2,890 - about $289 a year - alongside an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty
GTX adds 250kW dual-motor 4Motion, 5.4s to 100km/h and a rear-biased torque split sending up to 80 per cent to the back axle, and CarsGuide rated the chassis 'resolved, refined' at 7.5/10
cons: The $72,990 GTX gives up 21km of range to the $62,990 Pro (522km v 543km) for 0.9s of 0-100km/h; both CarExpert and CarsGuide judge it the worse buy of the two

The coupe roofline is a real practicality cost, not just a style choice - CarsGuide's long-termer found child-seat installation awkward and tall loads won't fit, and folded volume drops to 1,561L against the ID.4's 1,575L

Haptic and touch controls for climate and volume draw consistent criticism (CarsGuide: they 'sometimes work and sometimes don't'), and there is no frunk, no vehicle-to-load and no vehicle-to-grid at either grade
The GTX sits only $2,010 under the $75,000 FBT exemption cap on list price, so dealer delivery plus one option can push a novated lease past the threshold the Pro clears comfortably
Five-star ANCAP rating is carried over from 2021 Euro NCAP testing of the pre-facelift ID.4, with no fresh local assessment of the updated car

summary: The Tayron eHybrid is the long-wheelbase Tiguan's plug-in sibling, and in Australia it arrives as two front-wheel-drive grades sharing a 19.7kWh usable battery good for a claimed 113-116km of WLTP electric range — among the longest of any plug-in hybrid on sale here, and enough that most Melbourne commuters would run it as an EV during the week. Reviewers are consistent about the appeal: a 705-litre boot, DC fast charging and genuinely usable EV range at $62,390, which undercuts a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV Exceed. They are equally consistent about the catch — the battery sits where the third row would go, so unlike every petrol Tayron the eHybrid is a five-seater only, and CarExpert judged it less polished than the smaller Tiguan eHybrid it is based on.
pros: 113-116km of WLTP electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery is the longest in the mainstream plug-in SUV class — a Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV claims 86km and a Mazda CX-60 PHEV 76km — and CarExpert covered a 50km loop at an indicated 0.0L/100km on battery alone
705 litres of boot with the pack installed beats a Hyundai Santa Fe Hybrid's 628 litres, and 1,915 litres with the rear seats folded is genuinely van-like for the class
40kW DC fast charging (10-80 per cent in about 30 minutes) plus 11kW AC is rare on a plug-in hybrid — the Outlander PHEV has no 11kW AC and most rivals have no DC capability at all

Volkswagen Australia's five-year unlimited-kilometre warranty is unconditional, not tied to servicing inside the dealer network, and the high-voltage battery is separately covered for 8 years/160,000km

Both grades sit below the $80,809 ordinary LCT threshold and rate 38-40g/km CO2 on the combined cycle, well inside Victoria's 120g/km green passenger car test, so no luxury car tax applies and stamp duty is charged at the flat $8.40 per $200 green rate
cons: The battery occupies the third-row well, so neither eHybrid grade can be had with seven seats — every petrol Tayron from the $48,950 110TSI Life up can, which makes the plug-in the wrong car for the family the nameplate is otherwise aimed at

The 1.7-1.8L/100km label figure assumes you start every trip charged; once the battery is flat it is a 1.5-litre turbo hauling about 1,930kg, and UK testing puts it at roughly 40-45mpg (6.3-7.1L/100km), so the running-cost case collapses for a buyer without home charging
Front-wheel drive only — there is no 4MOTION eHybrid — and NRMA found the 1.5-litre engine feels underdone against the kerb weight once it is doing the work on its own
The 200TSI R-Line asks a $14,160 premium over the 150TSI Elegance for 50kW, a 200kg-higher tow rating and trim, and it crosses the $75,000 mark that the 2027 FBT cap is set at
The plug-in hybrid FBT exemption ended on 1 April 2025, so the novated-lease advantage that made earlier PHEVs compelling no longer applies to this car at all

summary: Volkswagen's first affordable plug-in hybrid for Australia takes the third-generation Tiguan and adds a 19.7kWh usable battery for a WLTP electric range of 113-117km, roughly double what the Outlander PHEV and Sealion 6 offer. Reviewers rate the drivetrain refinement, the 11kW AC and 40kW DC charging and the fact that most buyers will rarely wake the petrol engine, but are consistently critical of inconsistent brake and steering weighting and of a 490L boot that gives up 162L to the petrol Tiguan. Opinion splits on value: it undercuts European rivals but is roughly $20,000 more than a BYD Sealion 6 with similar equipment.
pros: 113-117km of WLTP electric range from a 19.7kWh usable battery is the longest in the mainstream mid-size PHEV class - about double the Mitsubishi Outlander PHEV and BYD Sealion 6
40kW DC fast charging (10-80% in about 26 minutes) is rare among PHEVs, which mostly offer AC only; 11kW AC fills the pack in roughly 2.5 hours
At 1.6-1.7L/100km and 37-38g/km CO2 combined it clears the LCT fuel-efficient test and Victoria's 120g/km green-car duty threshold comfortably
The high-voltage battery carries an 8-year/160,000km warranty on top of the vehicle's 5-year unlimited-kilometre cover, which is unconditional and not tied to servicing at a Volkswagen dealer
200TSI R-Line is rated to tow 2000kg braked (1800kg on the Elegance), better than most plug-in hybrids in the segment
cons: The battery costs 162L of boot: 490L versus 652L in the petrol Tiguan, and the fuel tank shrinks from 58L to 45L, so touring range depends on plugging in

Once the battery is flat it is a 1873-1883kg SUV on a 1.5-litre engine - reviewers report roughly 5L/100km on a gentle launch loop and about 7L/100km in mixed European testing, so a buyer without home charging is worse off than in a plain 150TSI
Front-wheel drive only - there is no 4MOTION eHybrid, unlike the 150TSI and 195TSI petrol grades which are all-wheel drive
Five seats only, with no seven-seat option and no spare wheel (tyre inflation kit only); buyers needing a third row are pushed to the Tayron eHybrid
The $74,550 200TSI R-Line commands a $9,960 premium over the Elegance for 50kW and little else, and sits about $20,000 above a comparably equipped BYD Sealion 6

summary: The XPeng G6 is a mid-size electric SUV coupe pitched squarely at the Tesla Model Y, with reviewers praising its upmarket cabin, strong tech package and genuinely quick charging on the refreshed 800V architecture. Testers rate the ride and refinement highly and note the flagship AWD Performance model undercuts a comparable Model Y on price while offering vastly stronger acceleration. The main knocks are steering that feels heavy and artificial, a chassis that doesn't quite match the Performance variant's straight-line pace, and quirks like the lack of a glovebox and a fiddly steering-column gear selector.
pros: Upmarket interior fit-out and strong tech/safety suite for the price
Fast 800V/451kW DC charging with a 10-80% top-up around 12 minutes
AWD Performance variant offers Tesla Model Y Performance-rivalling pace at a lower price
Spacious rear seating with good headroom for a coupe-SUV shape
cons: Steering feels heavy and artificial, chassis doesn't fully back up the Performance model's speed
No glovebox and limited cabin storage
Counterintuitive steering-column gear selector
Newer brand with a history of distributor changes in Australia, which may concern some buyers on parts/service continuity

summary: The Zeekr 7X is a mid-size electric SUV that Australian reviewers treat as the most complete Tesla Model Y alternative on price, with an 800V platform, a 615km WLTP Long Range grade and a cabin most testers rate above the Volkswagen ID.4 GTX and Kia EV5 GT-Line for the money. Reviewers agree on the packaging, charging speed and equipment, but split hard on which grade to buy: CarExpert and Chasing Cars both criticise the top grades' adaptive air suspension for bouncing at freeway speeds and prefer the steel-sprung Long Range RWD, while Chasing Cars still rated the Performance AWD 8/10. Recurring complaints are unreliable powered doors, almost everything buried in the 16-inch touchscreen, weak air-conditioning on hot days, no spare wheel, and the unknown resale of a brand that has only sold cars here since 2024.
pros: The $63,900 Long Range RWD is the range sweet spot: 95kWh usable for 615km WLTP, more range than a Tesla Model Y Long Range AWD ($68,900) or any Kia EV5 and for less money, with The Beep recording 500-550km at a sustained 110km/h

800V architecture with a 450kW DC peak on the RWD and Long Range and 22kW AC charging across the range - Chasing Cars timed the Performance AWD's 10-80 per cent DC charge at 16 minutes, and 22kW AC is double or triple the 7-11kW most rivals accept

Rated to tow 2000kg braked on every variant, against 1588kg for a Tesla Model Y, 1250kg for a Kia EV5 and 750kg for a BYD Sealion 7 Premium, with a 539L boot, 1978L seats folded and a 62L frunk on a 2900mm wheelbase

Ownership costs are unusually well defined for a new brand: five-year capped-price servicing totals $2,385 ($477 a year) on 12-month/20,000km intervals, with five years unlimited-km warranty, five years roadside assistance and an 8-year/160,000km battery warranty carrying a 70 per cent state-of-health guarantee

Equipment at the price includes a 36-inch head-up display, 16-inch touchscreen, 21-speaker audio, heated, ventilated and massaging front seats and tri-zone climate on the Long Range and above, and the 7X scored five stars under Euro NCAP with 91 per cent adult occupant protection
cons: The $75,900 Black Special Edition adds only cosmetics over the $72,900 Performance AWD - black wheels, black exterior trim and black Nappa leather, with no mechanical change - yet it is the one variant that sits above $75,000, so it loses the full novated-lease FBT exemption that applies to the rest of the range from 1 April 2027; a $3,000 styling pack that can cost several times that in lease terms

Adaptive air suspension on the Performance AWD and Black Special Edition is the biggest single criticism: CarExpert calls it flimsy at freeway speeds, bouncing dramatically over bumps as it auto-lowers, and explicitly recommends the steel-sprung Long Range RWD instead; Chasing Cars separately found front seats short on lateral support

Powered doors are called unreliable by both CarExpert and Chasing Cars - they misbehave on steep driveways and CarExpert raises a finger-pinch concern - and almost every function including climate control sits in the 16-inch touchscreen with very few physical controls

Chasing Cars measured the Performance AWD at 18.1kWh/100km on the highway and 19.7kWh/100km around town against a 17.5kWh/100km WLTP claim, so plan on roughly 480-520km rather than 543km, and both it and CarExpert flag weak, noisy air-conditioning in Australian summer heat plus no spare wheel, only a repair kit

Resale is unquantified: Zeekr has only sold cars in Australia since 2024, and the sibling Zeekr X was repriced down $5,000-$10,000 in a single model year, so there is no evidence 7X list pricing will hold despite the 2,200 sales achieved by March 2026

summary: The Zeekr X is a compact premium-badged electric SUV that Australian reviewers rate highly for cabin materials, standard equipment and outright pace, with the MY26 update adding 50kW per variant and repricing the range to flat drive-away figures of $48,900 (RWD) and $57,900 (Performance AWD). Opinion is genuinely split on the chassis: CarsGuide rates it one of the more engaging small SUVs to drive, while CarExpert and EV Central find the ride firm and the body underdamped over broken Victorian back roads. The consistent criticisms are a menu-heavy touchscreen, hyperactive driver-assistance chimes, a 405-415km WLTP range that trails cheaper rivals on real-world testing, and the ownership unknowns of a brand that only arrived in Australia in 2024.
pros: MY26 repricing to $48,900 drive-away for the RWD lands it under the Volvo EX30 and well under a BMW iX1 while adding 50kW (now 250kW) and cutting the 0-100km/h claim to 5.6 seconds

Cabin is the standout at the price: quilted leather, 13-speaker Yamaha audio and heated front and rear seats are standard, with massaging front seats and a temperature-controlled fridge on the AWD, and reviewers consistently rate the materials above mainstream rivals such as the Geely EX5 and BYD Atto 3
The RWD's 61kWh LFP pack accepts up to 230kW DC charging for a 10-80 per cent top-up in about 18 minutes, comfortably quicker than the Volvo EX30 or Kia EV3 at similar money, plus 11kW AC
365kW Performance AWD claims 0-100km/h in 3.7 seconds, quicker than anything else in the small electric SUV class
Five-star ANCAP rating, a 1600kg braked tow rating and a 404L boot that is 42L larger than the MY25 car
cons: 405-415km WLTP range is short for the money, and Australian testers recorded 16.5-20.7kWh/100km against the 15.5kWh/100km claim (carsales measured 20.7), so plan on roughly 300-350km between charges rather than 400

Driver-assistance calibration is the near-universal complaint across CarExpert, carsales and CarsGuide: overspeed warnings that repeatedly cut the audio, an attention monitor that chimes on ordinary head checks, and lane-centring that tugs at the wheel

Almost every function including drive modes, seat adjustment and climate is buried in a menu-heavy touchscreen, and reviewers report the reversing camera hijacking the display and wireless CarPlay microphone dropouts

Service and support proposition is thin for a five-year commitment: about 16 Zeekr retail and service sites nationally (three in Melbourne plus Geelong, nothing in Tasmania or the NT), MY26 servicing moved to 12-month/20,000km intervals at roughly $614 a visit and $3,072 over five years, and the standard warranty is five years unlimited km now that the seven-year pre-order offer closed on 31 May 2026, where a Volvo EX30 includes five years of free servicing

Resale is an unquantified risk on a brand first sold here in 2024, and Chasing Cars notes MY26 prices dropped $5,000-$10,000 in a single model year, which immediately devalues the outgoing cars and gives no reason to expect the MY26 pricing to hold
